Homage to the Holy Guru!
Now follows the Determination of the Manifestations from the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
In the first chapter, I shall explain the definition of Prakṛti according to the scriptures, the conceptualization of the forms of the deities, and the characteristics of the Nigamas and Āgamas.
I shall declare the names of the Tantras in the second chapter as well;
in the third, fourth, and fifth chapters, I shall speak of the origin of creation.
In the sixth [chapter], I shall describe creation and dissolution; in the seventh, the characteristics of the houses (bhāvas);
and in the eighth, I shall describe conduct, the characteristics of a maiden, and the ritual procedure.
In the ninth chapter (ullāsa), I shall explain the definitions of the states of being (bhāva) and so forth;
in the tenth, the meditation on the venerable Guru; and in the eleventh, his defining characteristics.
In the twelfth [chapter], I shall explain the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava; then, in the thirteenth, devotion;
and in the fourteenth chapter, the supreme characteristics of the bali offering.
In the fifteenth chapter, I shall explain the complete perfection of the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), the conduct of the Vaiṣṇavas, and likewise the conduct of the Śaivas.

In the sixteenth [chapter], there is the definition of the hero and the animal sacrifice, the fivefold reality (pañcatattvaka), the secondary substitute for that very reality, and the sectarian mark (tilaka).
In the seventeenth chapter, I shall describe the characteristics of the King of Yantras and the sequence of Śākta practice according to the divisions of Vāma and Dakṣiṇa.
In the eighteenth [chapter], the characteristics of the reviler and the beast are described, as well as the characteristics of the practitioners and the divine wheel (divyacakra). || 9 ||
I shall describe the sequence of the Vīracakra in the nineteenth chapter:
the location of the circle, the seat, and the entry into the center of the circle.
I shall describe the characteristics of the divine wheel (devacakra) within twenty [chapters],
as well as the classification of castes within the center of the wheel and the determination of the materials.
(kh) By the grace and favor of the Guru, I shall also speak of that in the twenty-first [chapter],
as well as the characteristics of the vessel and the support in the twenty-second *ullāsa*.
I shall describe the majesty of the primordial reality (ādya-tattva) in the twenty-third [chapter],
as well as the non-difference of substances and the purification of power in the twenty-fourth.
In the twenty-fifth chapter (ullāsa), there is the purification of the primordial reality (tattva),
as well as the meditation on Ānandabhairava and likewise on Ānandabhairavī.
In this twenty-sixth chapter, I shall briefly explain the purification of substances:
the characteristics and the purification of meat, fish, and ritual gestures (mudrā). || 15 ||
Having meditated upon the dust of the Guru’s feet, I shall speak concerning the twenty-seven [tattvas];
and I shall also speak the characteristics of Śakti in the twenty-eighth.
In the nineteenth chapter on the unfolding of consciousness (ikollāsa), I shall describe the purification of power (śakti-śodhana);
and in the thirtieth chapter, the ritual procedure for the drinking of consciousness (samvid-āpāna).
I shall describe, in thirty-one verses, the various types of characteristics pertaining to the Śrīcakra, the vessel, and the support.
The description of the practitioner's vessels consists of thirty-two;
the offering to Vaṭuka and the others is proclaimed to be thirty-three and so forth.
The ritual of placement (nyāsa), the rite of libation (tarpaṇa), and the thirty-four characteristics [of the vessel] have been explained;
now, in the thirty-fifth [chapter], I shall describe the prayer and the veneration of the vessel.
In the thirty-sixth great chapter, the rule concerning the characteristics of the worthy recipient;
in the thirty-seventh chapter, the characteristics of the meditation upon the venerable Guru.
In the twenty-eighth expansion of the directions, the measurement for the offering of honey is forty-nine; such is the procedure for the fifth [mandala].
In the forty-first [chapter], the *Ikkollāsa*, I shall describe the characteristics of play (*krīḍā*) and so forth; in the forty-second, the characteristics of the fifth bliss-petal (*ānandadala*).
Forty-two is the characteristic of the bliss of the practitioner;
and forty-three is the bliss of the nine vessels.
(g) In the forty-fourth chapter, the definition of the fifth [chapter] is given;
thus, the forty-fifth is the supreme Ānanda-stotra. 25.
I shall now describe the sequence of consecrations (abhiṣeka), numbering forty-six and forty-seven,
for the practitioner who follows the right-hand conduct (dakṣiṇācāra).
Forty-eight, thus is the specific left-hand practice (vāmācāra);
therein the measure of the flowers is fivefold and sevenfold.
In the forty-ninth chapter, I shall describe the ritual for the purification of flowers;
in the fiftieth chapter, I shall describe the characteristics of women of the Kula.
The characteristic of sexual union is in the fifty-first unfolding;
the knowledge of power that illumines is in the fifty-second unfolding of the letter *i*. (29)
In the fifty-third chapter, the characteristics of the Siddhānta conduct are described;
in the fifty-fourth chapter, the specific nature of Full Bliss is presented.
The characteristic of the bliss of fullness (pūrṇānanda) shines forth in the fifty-fifth [vibration];
the characteristic of the bliss of power (śaktyānanda) is in the fifty-sixth, the vibration of the primordial source (ikolāsa). || 31 ||
In the fifty-seventh chapter, the supreme majesty of Śakti is described;
in the fifty-eighth chapter, the characteristics of the Haṃsa-bīja are given.
O Unshaṣṭika, I shall describe the greatness of Dhyānatra;
in the sixth chapter (ullāsa), I shall explain with certainty the sequence of divine conduct.
The wise author has described the Kaulācāra in the sixty-first [chapter],
while whatever characteristics and essential nature belong to Prakṛti are found in the sixty-second.
In the sixty-third [chapter], the knowledge of Brahman is presented; thereafter, one is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
In the sixty-fourth, the completion of the work is reached, as described in the "Exaltation" (ullāsa) section.
Thus ends the *Ullāsanirṇaya*, from the *Sarvollāsatantra*,
composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
First Chapter. Homage to the venerable Guru. [Kh: Homage to the Supreme Deity.
Having prostrated before the eternal Prakṛti, whose nature is the very self of the universe;
I shall speak of the Great Ecstasy (Mahollāsa), which is the ecstasy of all and the supreme ecstasy. || 1 ||
The conduct of being has been extracted from the Nigamas, Āgamas, and Śāstras, as spoken by the venerable Sarvānandanātha at the lotus feet of the venerable Goddess. (2)
In the Gaṇeśatantra, the illustrious Śiva said:
"O Goddess, you are the supreme, eternal one, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) and having the three qualities as your essence.
I shall now describe some characteristics of Prakṛti in your stead."
O Maheśvarī, if there were an excess of even one among the qualities (guṇas), there would be modification;
however, when the three qualities are in equilibrium, they constitute Prakṛti in its subtle form.
Even that which is equal is eternal; that goddess who is uneven is the eternally accomplishing one.
For the sake of awakening to both the eternal and the non-eternal, they should be understood as mutually the cause of one another.
Some conceive of it as gross and eternal in form, while others conceive of it as subtle;
the entire world, whether eternal or non-eternal, is permeated by the nature of the Self.
And the Self, O Supreme Goddess, is eternal and exists in three forms;
it is proclaimed as the Supreme Self (Paramātman), the External Self (Bāhyātman), and the Individual Self (Jīvātman). (7)

The individual soul (jīvātman) is of the nature of a subtle body (liṅga-rūpī) and has the form of the flame of a pure lamp; it is a vast form of radiant meditation, more brilliant and possessing a subtle form.
O Maheśvarī, whatever has been spoken by me through reasoning is all gross;
O Śivā, there is no meditation at all for anyone without the meditation on light (tejodhyāna).
O Maheśvarī, just as milk is the cause of the curdled whey that has been held,
so too is Dhruva the cause of the light, both gross and subtle.
O Supreme One! Even the mind is a gross manifestation of fire described by the senses;
yet that which transcends the mind is subtle, singular, and stainless. (11)
Stainless, possessing all forms, and the cause of all knowledge, that Brahman shines like a witness; O Śivā, it is both the primordial nature and its transformation.
Now, the definition of *nigama* is given in the *Yāmala*:
"Because it has emerged from the mouth of Śaṅkarī and entered the face of Giriśā, and is considered [the teaching] of the venerable Vāsudeva, it is therefore called *nigama*. (13)
Now follows the explanation of the names of the Nigamas:
the Kalpasāra, the Kalpatattva, and thereafter the Kalpadruma;
previously, the Kalpalatā and the Kalpānanda were taught—thus they are fivefold.
Now, the definition of *āgama*:
It has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone to the face of the Daughter of the Mountain;
it is esteemed by the illustrious Vāsudeva; therefore, it is called *āgama*. (15)
(p. 3) Now follows the discourse revealing the Āgamas and Nigamas.
Having heard that, Vāsudeva also spoke to Gaṇeśa regarding those words of Nandīśvara, which are in accord with the Nigamas and Āgamas. (16)
It must be proclaimed by Gaṇeśa as revealed in the Yāmalas;
thus, the Āgamas and the Nigamas are mutually pervaded upon the earth. (17)
O Śivā, the Āgama is said to be fourfold, the Nigama fivefold;
the Yāmala is declared to be fourfold, and from that, the scripture was revealed. (18)
Now, concerning the origin of the *Yāmala*: O Śivā, that which is stainless even in the subtle is the *Yāmala* in the gross;
the gross form described in the *Yāmala* is the awakening of all scriptures. (19)
Now, the origin of the scriptures: Sixty-four Āgamas have been proclaimed, as well as five kinds of Nigamas; the Yāmalas are said to be fourfold, and from these the scripture has been revealed. (20)
From the Nigama, the Āgama was born; from the Āgama, the Yāmala came into being.
From the Yāmala, that which is called the Veda was produced; and from the Veda, the Purāṇa was born. || 21 ||
From the Purāṇas arises the Smṛti, and from the Smṛti arise those various scriptures; one should grasp them with effort, for they are supreme according to their sequential or reverse order.
Now, regarding the practice of the scriptures according to the divisions of the ages:
in the Satya Yuga, the rites prescribed by the Śrutis; in the Tretā, those approved by the Smṛtis; in the Dvāpara, the Purāṇas; and in the Kali, that which is approved by the Āgamas. (23)
In the Kali age, a wise person should worship the gods according to the injunctions declared in the scriptures;
for the gods do not become pleased by blind ritual practices in the Kali age.
Now, the definition of the form of the deity according to the scripture:
The Veda is declared to be the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the individual soul (jīva) is cited [as its source];
the Purāṇas and the auxiliary sciences (aṅga-śāstras) are the limbs (aṅga), and the Smṛti is the minor limb (pratyaṅgaka). (25)
All other scriptures are like the hairs of the body and so forth in sequence;
it is by means of this scripture that the specific form of the deity is known.
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
"O Maheśānī, the Nigama is the Self; the Paramātma-āgama is certainly the [Supreme] Self;
the Jīvātma is declared to be the Yāmala; and the Bāhyātma is of the nature of the Veda. (27)
The Purāṇas are the limbs, O beloved, and the Smṛti is a limb of a limb; whatever other scriptures there are, O Pārvatī, they are the hairs on his body.
The form of the deity arises according to the scripture and the distinction of the ages.
Now, the account of the origin of the Vedas:
O Śivā, the Sāmaveda-mata originated from the Brahmayāmala,
while the supreme Ṛgveda originated from the Rudrayāmala.
Great. || 29 ||
O Kuleśvarī, the Yajurveda is born from the Viṣṇuyāmala,
and the supreme, great Atharvaveda is born from the Śaktiyāmala.
The doctrine of the Sāmaveda prevails in the Kṛta age, that of the Ṛgveda in the Tretā, O Śivā;
the Yajurveda in the Dvāpara, and the doctrine of the Atharvaveda in the Kali age.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter: Now, the Explanation of What is Called Tantra.
In the Toḍala [Tantra], the Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the masters of life, O bestower of liberation upon the worlds! Now I desire to hear the proclamation of the names of the Tantras.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, O beloved; I am your servant. Bound by your affection, I shall relate the narrative known as the Tantra.
O illustrious lady, this Tantra—which is dearer to me than life itself and bestows liberation upon the worlds—must not be spoken to a man who performs evil deeds or is an atheist. (3)
O Pārvatī, even at the end of the cosmic egg, I am not able to describe Ananta, the God of gods, nor indeed the infinite Tantra itself.
By your command, O Great Goddess, for the sake of protecting the worlds,
sixty-four tantras have been spoken by me alone, O lovely one: the Kālītantra, the Muṇḍamālā, the Tārā, and the Nirvāṇa, and so forth.
The Śivasāra and Vīratantra [deal with] the worship of the Liṅga and the worship of the creeper (liṅgārcana and latārcana).
O Maheśvarī, [there are] the Toḍala, the Nīlatantra, the Rādhātantra, the Viśvasāra,
that which is called Bhairava, and also the Bhairavītantra.
O Śivā, [I have taught] the Siddheśvara, the Mātṛbheda, the Samayātantraka,
the Guptasādhanatantra, and also the Mātṛkātantra.
The Māyātantra, the Mahāmāyā, the Akṣayātantraka in Śivā, the great tantra called Kumārī, and after that the Kulārṇava. (9)
O Śivā, [I have taught] the *Kālikākulasarvasva*, the *Kālikākalpatantra*,
the *Vārāhīyoginītantra*, and the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
The Sanatkumāra-tantra, the Tripurāsāra-tantra, the Yoginīvijaya, and the Mālinī-tantra, O auspicious one. (11)
The great tantra called Kukkuṭa, the tantra known as Śrīgaṇeśa, the Bhūta-tantra, likewise the Uḍḍīśa, and the excellent Kāmadhenu; || 12 ||
The great Vīrabhadra-tantra, the Vāmakeśvara, the Kulacūḍāmaṇi-tantra, and the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, O Dear One. (13)
O Maheśvarī, [I have studied] the Jñānārṇava, the Varadātātantra-cintāmaṇi, the Kālīvilāsaka-tantra, and the Haṃsa-tantra. 14.
Beyond this is the Cidāmbarataṭa Tantra, the Vijñāpana, the Phetkāriṇī, the Tantra known as Nityā, and that designated as Uttara. (15)
The Nārāyaṇīyamahattantra, the Ūrddhvāmnāyaka-tantra,
the Jñānadvīpa, and the Gautamīya-tantra are unsurpassed, O Śivā.
The Gāndharva, the Kuñjikātantra, and then the Tantramuktāvalī; the Vṛhat Śrīkramatantra, the Svatantra, and the Tantraka, O Śivā. (17)
The *Yonitantra* and the *Kāmākhyātantra* have been proclaimed, O fair-faced one;
sixty-four tantras have just now been spoken by me alone. (18)
O Pārvatī, there are sixty-four chapters in the *pratitantra*,
as well as innumerable tantras and various types of ritual procedures (*bhāva*).
The entire Yāmalasaṃgīta consists of sixty-four types;
this should be known as the primary [work], established according to the doctrine of the four ages. || 20 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Sarvollāsa*, composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter:
Now, the Exposition of the Origin of Creation.
At the Island of Knowledge (Jñānadvīpa), the venerable Pārvatī said:
O Lord of gods, O Lord of the masters of life, O bestower of liberation upon the worlds,
reveal the majesty of creation and dissolution in my abode.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśānī, without creation, what dissolution could there be?
And O Goddess, without dissolution, how could creation arise? (2)
Without a seed there would be no tree, and without a tree there would be no seed;
likewise, O Goddess, the conception of creation and dissolution is indeed eternal and non-eternal.
In conceptualization there is creation; in conceptualization there is dissolution.
The majesty of creation and dissolution cannot indeed be fully described. (4)
Only a small portion should be spoken, like the reflection of a form in water;
bound by my affection for you, I have revealed but a little. (5)
Formless and most formidable,
that Brahman consists of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa; even at the time of creation, it assumes the forms of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
O Śivā, this [universe] has the form of the momentary and consists of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa;
some say it is Prakṛti, while others say it is Puruṣa, O Śivā.
Some lords of yogis say that Brahman consists of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa; it is to be known as ineffable, beyond speech, and perfectly pure.
O Maheśvarī, that which transcends the mind, transcends action, and transcends speech—I shall explain it as the state of oneness relied upon for the sake of the practitioner’s knowledge. (9)
Everything arises from primordial nature (prakṛti) through the longing of the person (puruṣa);
everything also arises from the person through the longing of primordial nature. || 10 ||
Intoxicated by the madness of passion arising from desire, and resting in perfect bliss, she became the opposite even of Puruṣa; she became the creator. (11)
Mahākālī is thus proclaimed, and Mahākāla is Sadāśiva;
because he is dissolved here within Mahākālī, he is celebrated as Mahākāla. || 12 ||
Mahākālī is proclaimed here as she who is dissolved within Mahākāla;
the Great Goddess is one in both knowledge and ignorance, transcending all existence.
Having relied upon the state of power (śakti-bhāva), the manner of emanation has been described;
emanation is the form of power alone, the mere state that awakens [consciousness]. || 14 ||
O Dear One, the knowledge of Śakti is pure existence, while the Puruṣa is non-existence;
the state of being one in both is the essence of Prakṛti and Puruṣa. || 15 ||
The second became Tāriṇī, who, afflicted by desire, grants protection;
she yearned with a state of longing, "O Mother of the World, grant me a husband. (16)
Having heard this, Mahādeva gave forth a person from his own body;
having obtained him, that Great Vidyā resorted to him in a reversed manner.
The third is the Ṣoḍaśī, who has become sixteen years of age;
she is the Vidyā of the Queen of Queens, worshipped by all the gods. || 18 ||
With eyes filled with wine and ever imbued with the state of passion, grant me a husband united with the bliss that is the cause of Mahākālī. (19)
Having heard this, the imperishable Mahādeva Dakṣiṇāmūrti, taking recourse to his right side, remains stationed there forever. || 20 ||
Whatever consists of the nature of the five elements, according to the distinction between left and right:
on the left, the Ṣoḍaśī (the Sixteenfold Power) is to be known, and on the right, the imperishable Puruṣa. || 21 ||

O Maheśvarī, Brahman, which consists of both the eternal and the non-eternal, is the illuminator whose form is creation, for the sake of the welfare of the practitioner and for the sake of its own bliss.
The Great Vidyā Tripurā and the others are established in eight parts:
Bhuvaneśī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and Maheśvarī. (23)
O Śivā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā—
Sadāśiva is always conjoined with these eight powers as his eightfold aspect.
The eightfold division is thus encompassed in the sequence beginning from the south;
this, O beloved, has been told to you as the manner of the origin of creation, the mere knowledge of which is indeed the cause of liberation while living. (25)
In her various momentary forms, she is Tāriṇī, the bestower of protection;
her eyes are rolling with wine, and she is ever longed for by Madana.
Mahādeva, the bliss of desire, is established in Akṣobhya;
having attained her womb, he is always possessed of the creation of erotic passion (or joy).
Mahākālī has transcended all states of being and is united with the state of Tāriṇī;
Tripurā is the form of emanation, and O Śivā, she is one in three ways and threefold in each.
Kālikā is the form of the seed-syllable, and Tāriṇī is the form of the dark blue.
O beloved, Sundarī is the form of creation, and this entire world is the form of creation.
In the Rādhātantra, the account of the origin of creation:
In the Greatly Terrible (Mahāghora) [state] of perfect bliss, Prakṛti envelops the Person (Puruṣa). She, whose form is the shape of a moment, rests upon that which transcends all states of being.
"O Goddess, the self, the senses, and pleasure have as their sole authority the Self alone," said the Supreme Power: "O Beloved, manifest the erotic sentiment for me. (21)
Having heard this, Mahādeva said to Prakṛti:
"O Goddess, though I am drawn by him, O dear one, manifest the erotic sentiment for my sake. (32)
By the word of her and his, they did not contradict one another;
at that very moment, that Great Power became Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Goddess.
Having seen the male form of Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā became the Supreme Lord;
she should be known as the male aspect of Rādhā, while [Kṛṣṇa] assumes the form of Śakti from the aspect of Kṛṣṇa.
In the aspect of Kṛṣṇa, she is in the form of a woman; this is to be known as the form of creation, the certain doctrine of the Vaiṣṇava school. || 34 ||
Now, in the Tripurāsāra-tantra, follows the account of the origin of creation:
Mahākālī, of terrible form and devoid of bodily marks,
and Mahākāla, who was likewise without a sixth [limb], resorted to the state of desire to create.
They are based on the state of childhood; [kh: they are based on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) arising from that state]. || 35 ||
O Goddess, [I have taught] the great hymn of Mahākālī, along with its mantra, its yantra, the ritual procedures, the offering of oblations, and the preliminary course of practice (puraścaraṇa).
Now follows the *Śyāmāstotra* composed by Mahākāla:

O Mother, Consort of the Destroyer of Tripura, those who recite three times this seed-syllable of yours— which consists of the letter *ka*, devoid of the middle and final vowels, joined with the moon and the left eye— [attain success].

For those who have attained all perfections, words— both prose and verse— issue forth spontaneously from the cavity of their mouths, as beautiful as a rain-cloud charged with darkness. (37) Thus it is stated in these twenty-two verses beginning with this one.
Having heard this, Mahākālī became the Sovereign of Tripura;
she possessed supreme and wondrous beauty, was three-peaked, and endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). || 38 ||
Even upon seeing the form of Sundarī, Sadāśiva became beautiful;
he should perform various hymns of praise, enveloped in great devotion.

Now, the Sundarī-stotra: Salutations again and again to Tripurā, whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), who is threefold, who possesses the three points (bindus), who conceives of herself as the triad, who wears three ornaments, and who has three forms. || 40 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Tripurā composed by Mahākāla, as declared in these six verses.
Having heard the hymn, the Great Goddess spoke with full bliss;
that Great Vidyā, increasing her own splendor, acted according to her will. (41)
Mahādeva is the heroic state, the imperishable southern form;
when he is approached by Dakṣa, then that supreme one becomes Dakṣiṇā.
Having reached her womb, she withdraws the entire universe;
O Dear One, Mahākālī’s dissolution occurs within the center of Mahākālī’s womb.
The womb-place (yonisthāna) should indeed be known as Mahātripurasundarī;
its three lines should be known as Tripurā, whose nature is the triple city (tripura).
Tripurā, the goddess of Tripura, is accompanied by the enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
The void (śūnya), the moon (candra), and the phoneme (vārṇa) are conceived as Tripura. 45.
She who is the Great Goddess consisting of speech and whose nature is the form of desire,
eternally abiding as pure power, is the great digit known as Trikuṭā.
When Sundara pervades Sundarī and Sundarī [pervades] Sundara, then she is the Tāriṇī Vidyā, the supreme mistress of the most terrible. 47.
With eyes rolling from wine, afflicted by passion, and bestowing desire, she is that second Great Vidyā, the beloved in her state of fullness. (48)
"O Mother of the World, grant me a husband endowed with the fifth bliss.
Having heard this, Mahādeva, becoming agitated, would abandon her. (49)
Then Mahādeva, whose single self assumes two forms, pervades them both mutually as a single body and a dual body; and Tāriṇī likewise becomes his dual-natured self.

At that moment, Mahādeva, who possesses a dual nature, becomes the single-natured Tāriṇī; O Supreme Lord, one should then perform the hymn of praise to the Great Goddess Tāriṇī, which bestows protection through the division of the one essence. (51)
Now, the hymn to Tārā:
Tāriṇī shall be the giver of protection, whose very self is protection, who speaks of protection;
she is endowed with protection, she has enjoyed protection, and she is the ancient one who has enjoyed protection. (52) And so forth.
Having heard the hymn of praise, the supreme Great Goddess Tārā appeared, most formidable, four-armed, blue-colored, three-eyed, and carrying a corpse. (53)
Having seen this form of Tāriṇī, Kālikā—terrible and right-handed—appeared with four arms, black in complexion, three-eyed, and mounted upon a corpse. (54)
Having seen this rosary of fifty letters, the garland of severed heads, and the string of beads, one perceives the Vidyā of Kālikā, which is the Śrīvidyā whose essence is Tripurā. (55)
Four-armed, red in color, and three-eyed, she is adorned with five skulls;
devoid of beginning, end, and middle, she is eternal and worshipped by all. (56)
Mahākālī is of the nature of truth; worship performed in the Truth Age (Kṛtayuga) yields great fruit. Sundarī is of the form of the three [mantras]; she bestows the fruits in the Tretā Age.
In the Dvāpara age, Tāriṇī is to be worshipped as "Dvāparā," and Tāriṇī as well;
in the Kali age, the three deities are to be worshipped as Kālī, and Tripurā is the supreme among the three deities.
Kālī joined with Sundarī, and Kālikā joined with Sundarī;
when both are united, she is Tārā, who is the essence of both.
Indeed, for the sake of the practitioner's accomplishment, this single Vidyā is divided merely by name into three: Tamas, Sattva, and likewise Rajas. (60)
She is the triple deity and triple-souled, the dual deity and dual-natured; she is the single deity and single-souled, Kālītārā, the beautiful one.
(13) Everything exists as threefold in nature, yet it is the stainless radiance of the radiant one.
When one knows that which is the single self in its threefold state, then liberation and dissolution are certain. 62.
Even one whose nature is action, by meditating on that which is distinct from the self, shall attain residence in the same world (sālokya);
and through intense energy, O Maheśvarī, one may attain similarity of form (sārūpya) or even union (sāyojya).
Having meditated upon the stainless radiance— or rather, the state— of union, which is like a pearl,
one should thus meditate upon the fourfold [state], which is certain according to the doctrine of the four ages.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Fourth Chapter:
Now, an account of the origin of creation by another method.
In the *Jñānārṇava*, the venerable Pārvatī said:
O beloved of the Earth! when the moon and the sun [are no longer needed], and when there is no water such as the Gaṅgā, nor sacred fords, nor the distinctions of castes such as the Brāhmaṇas; || 1 ||
The Paśvācāra, the Śaiva, the Vīra, the Divya, as well as the Siddhānta and the Kaula—if these states of being do not exist [within it], then [it is not so]. (2)
By what means and where does origination occur, and by what means and in what place does dissolution take place?
O Lord of the Mistress of Life, tell me this, so that my doubt may perish. (3)
Śrī Śaṅkara said: O Supreme Goddess, the anus, the genitals, the hands, the feet, speech, renunciation, erotic passion, attraction, movement, praise, and contempt—[these are the ten]. 4.
Hearing, seeing, smelling, touching, and the perception of taste—these are declared to be the ten sense organs, O beloved; the mind is the eleventh.
This body is to be known as that which awakens one to bondage and liberation;
wherever the mind is firmly established, there the dissolution of the senses is certain.
Just as a shadow resting upon trees and such things is reflected in water and the like, when the water has vanished, that shadow dissolves back into the trees and such things once more. (7)
Likewise, when the activity of the senses ceases, they dissolve again into the mind;
within the mind, everything arises as an object endowed with the senses.
Furthermore, O beloved, when that state devoid of the senses dissolves into that [reality],
conduct arises from the movement of the senses.
(15) Conduct is to be known as action; yet what can truly arise from mere action?
The entire world is nothing but action, and the world is the seed of that [action] as well. (10)
Śrī Śaṅkarī said:
Caste is rooted in conduct; conduct is rooted in the scriptures;
the scripture is rooted in the word of the God; and the God is rooted in the practitioner. (11)
The practitioner has action as his root, and action itself is rooted in the fruit;
O God, the fruit is rooted in happiness, and happiness is rooted in bliss.
Bliss has knowledge as its root, and knowledge has the object of knowledge as its root;
the object of knowledge has reality as its root, for reality alone has Brahman as its root. || 13 ||
The knowledge of Brahman has oneness as its sole root, for oneness is indeed the root of all; O Supreme Lord, oneness is certainly transcendent of all states of being. (14)
How can everything, being merely an entity, be manifest from that which has transcended existence?
For where there is a seed, there arises a sprout, and from that, a tree in full bloom. (15)
Without the sprout, the seed did not exist; without desire, the lover did not exist.
O Lord, without the union of these two, nothing whatsoever is born. (16)
O Lord, when the one alone exists, the second and so forth do not arise;
and O Lord, when the second and so forth exist, oneness never arises. || 17 ||
O Mahādeva, it is the number itself that is intended to be expressed by the numbered;
O Mahādeva, it is the numbered object that is intended to be expressed by the number. (18)
Reveal to me its beginning and its end, and by what means and in what manner;
who am I and who are you, O Mahādeva? Tell me how and why this is so. (19)
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Indeed, existence (bhāva) would be of the nature of creation, while non-existence (abhāva) is devoid of creation;
yet that which is completely free from both existence and non-existence is both non-existence and indeed existence itself.
Existence that transcends existence, and existence that is supreme and transcends existence, just as the reflection and the act of seeing appear within the surfaces of mirrors. (21)
p. 16) Likewise, all [qualities] such as duality and so forth are observed in individual entities:
duality is conjoined with unity, and unity is conjoined with duality. (22)
And without number, it is simply impossible to cognize that which is numerable;
O Śivā, how can oneness arise without the state of duality? (23)
Without the state of oneness, how could the state of duality be manifested? Without one another, it is simply impossible to utter a sentence. (24)

Just as a substance is permeated by qualities and a quality is likewise permeated by a substance, so too there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from one another; it is not merely cognition alone anywhere. (25)
Without a producer there is no produced, and without a produced there is no producer;
without a fruit there would be no action, and without an action there would be no fruit. (26)
Likewise, O Great Goddess, both knowledge and the object of knowledge are mutually dependent; knowledge possesses existence, while the object of knowledge is devoid of existence. (27)
For one for whom knowledge and the object of knowledge are one, liberation is unimpeded.
That which is expressed as having two states is of a single nature; that which has two states is of a single nature. (28)
Indeed, you alone, distinct from the self, are the Self who embodies all forms;
without me, who am knowledge, you can never arise as knowledge anywhere.
Without you, knowledge does not arise anywhere; without me, knowledge is not produced. || 29 ||
Just as space, taking all forms, is present within all substances, so too am I and you, taking all forms, present within all substances. (30)

"You are said to be fragmentary knowledge (khaṇḍa-jñāna), whereas I am certainly complete knowledge (pūrṇa-jñāna). Just as this [fragmentary knowledge] exists, by that [complete knowledge] the world is pervaded, even when devoid of a fragmented self. (31)
Just as there is no division in space, even though it is characterized by a jar, so too am I and you are characterized by the body; for the body is certainly composed of that [Self]. 32.
Just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within the jar dissolves into the [great] space,
so too when the body is destroyed, "I" and "you" dissolve into the Supreme Self.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. 4.
The Fifth Chapter (Pañcamollāsa).
Alternatively, the description of creation according to another method,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
In the world of truth (satyaloka), she is formless, consisting of the nature of great light;
yet, for those whose self is veiled by illusion (māyā), she appears in the form of momentary manifestations.

Devoid of hands, feet, and the like, she has the form of the moon, sun, and fire; having cast off the bark-garment of *māyā*, she is divided into two, being composed of the world. (Note: The reading from the *Nirvāṇatantra* cited in the *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* is "having cast off the bark-garment of *māyā*, she is divided into two.")
When she has become intent upon that. || 2 ||
The conceptualization of creation arises through the division of Śiva and Śakti;
first, O Pārvatī, a son is born who is indeed named Brahmā.
Śrī Kālikā said:
"Listen, O son, O great hero [variant: O great wise one], perform the marriage with diligence.
Having heard this, O beloved, Brahmā then spoke respectfully.
"Without you there is no mother; grant me the power of beauty.
Hearing that, the Mother of the Worlds gave Mohinī from her own body.
She is that Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Sāvitrī, the supreme power;
having attained union with her, perform the expansion of the Vedas.
"May you become the effortless creator upon the circle of the earth;
in the second [birth], you are born."
His son was Viṣṇu, whose disposition was characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva).
The illustrious Kālikā said:
"Listen, O son, great hero; perform the marriage with diligence.
Viṣṇu said:
By the mere sight of you, a man becomes free from desire. || 8 ||
"O Mother, how shall I act? O Śivā, grant me delusion!
Having emerged from her body, Kālikā drew forth that power and gave it to him.
Relying upon that Vaiṣṇavī Mahāvidyā, the Śrīvidyā, the Supreme Goddess,
the Great Viṣṇu protects the entire universe.
In the third [birth], a son is born who is a great yogi, Sadāśiva;
seeing him, Mahākālī then becomes filled with joy. (11)
"Listen, my son, great yogi; take my words to heart.
Who else but you is a man, and who else but me is a woman?
Therefore, O Śiva, grant me the supreme bliss of marriage. (12)
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Mother, what you have said—that there is no enchantress (Mohinī) apart from you—is true; O Mother of the World, likewise there is no man apart from me."
"And while this body remains, I shall not perform the marriage;
O Mother, if you have compassion, take on another body. (14)
At that moment, Mahākālī gave Bhuvanasundarī;
as Kālī was the primordial being, so too was Bhuvanasundarī.
Relying upon that, the great yogin withdraws the entire universe;
Śakti exists through an eightfold division, and each part likewise becomes eightfold. (Gh:
The divisions of Śambhu are eightfold, and Śakti likewise becomes eightfold.)
This is the reading from the Mudritanirvāṇa Tantra: "Through the division of powers, [the state] of Śambhu becomes eightfold. (16)
O Supreme Goddess, by this [means] the great Vidyās beginning with Kālikā [are attained].
Thus, O Beloved, I have told you the description of the creation according to its origin;
it should be concealed with effort, just as the arising of the Vidyā [is hidden].
O beloved, O beloved! || 17 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
The Sixth Chapter: Now begins the Section on Dissolution (Laya). In the Island of Knowledge (Jñānadvīpa), the Śrī Devī said:
O Lord, in what form did the dissolution occur, and finally, where did the creation take place?
O Lord of my life, tell me this in my presence if you have grace toward me. (1)
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess, just as water is indistinguishable from water, milk from milk, and ghee from ghee,
so too should the non-difference between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) be understood.
Just as milk has a single color, so too is the Supreme Lord one;
yet, just as a cow may possess various forms, so too is dissolution manifold in nature.
The individual soul (jīvātman) consists of the five elements, and the external self (bāhyātman) is joined with those;
the external self is of gross form, while the individual soul is of subtle nature.
Upon the destruction of both the gross and the subtle, that alone remains as the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 4 ||
Just as there is the space within a jar, so too is there the embodied soul within bodies;
just as there is sound within a machine, so too is there the mere word "I" within the body. (Or, according to the *gh* and *ṅ* recensions: so too is there the word "embodied soul" within bodies.)
When that has perished— even as these [perish]— in Śiva, who is like the hearing of space or the form of a crow,
there is indeed only the manifestation of division, which, though dissolving, is non-differentiating.
(6) The Holy Goddess said:

For what purpose is that which is described as having the form of a moment, characterized by duality in some [texts]? What is the nature of the commencement of creation, and what is the nature of that which effects destruction? (7)
In the Mahānirvāṇatantra, the illustrious Śiva said:
"Mahākālī is the Supreme Self, whose form is the appearance of a moment;
she [resides] within that [Self], which has its nature veiled by Māyā, through a state of equanimity. (8)
He alone is the Great Rudra, the Self; he indeed is the Great Viṣṇu;
he alone is the Great Brahmā, the Self—the distinction being merely one of names.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the three names of a single form;
for one whose mind perceives them as diverse entities, liberation does not exist.
O fair-eyed one, hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs are born there;
therein Brahmā, therein Viṣṇu, and therein Rudra are established.
Some say he is Brahmā; some proclaim him to be Viṣṇu;
others say he is Rudra—that one God who is stainless.
The Lord, joined with the primordial power, has the form of a wheel;
endowed with a mass of bliss, the Master assumes the form of Prakṛti.
O Dear One, he is the manifest abode of the Guṇa-less and the abode of Mahākālī.
Right there, it exists eternally in the form of a chickpea.
Her form is supreme and eternal, higher than the highest supreme bliss;
O Goddess, Kālikā stands on the right, bestowing eternal joy.
The primordial power, Mahāmāyā, who brings about the manifestation of the gods, is born upon the earth and dissolves back into the earth like a tree. (16)
Just as a bubble born from water dissolves back into the water, and just as lightning produced in a cloud dissolves back into the cloud; || 17 ||
p. 22) Likewise, the gods beginning with Brahmā are born from Kālikā;
likewise, at the time of dissolution, they are dissolved back into her. || 18 ||
O Goddess, without the knowledge of Śakti, liberation is rendered a mere mockery;
by one portion He becomes Brahmā, and by one portion Janārdana. (19)
O fair-eyed one, Śambhu exists as one part of Kālikā;
the other part is Mahākālī, who is like the ocean to rivers and the like. (20)
Just as water in a cow’s footprint is to [the waters] of the gods beginning with Brahmā, so too,
O Śivā, what could a cow’s footprint know of the water of the ocean?
Therefore, Brahmā does not know her; what indeed does Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara know?
For when the gods and others are protected by Kālī, the creator of the universe. || 22 ||
Then, at the time of dissolution, he is dissolved back into her;
therefore, Kālī is the bestower of liberation and the giver of bliss to the Puruṣa. (23)
The mind-made light appears in the form of momentary aspects;
just as the sun illumines the world, so too is the object of knowledge momentary. (24)
The single Śakti, having become twofold, spoke as a Puruṣa in the middle; again, at the time of dissolution, she became one twofold, concealed by the Puruṣa. 25.
The person (puruṣa) is twofold, based on the two states of permanence and impermanence;
yet, when permanence and impermanence are of one essence, that is the single form of Brahman.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Seventh Ullāsa. Now, the praise of *bhāva*: In the *Nigamakalpananda*, the venerable Śiva said:
O Supreme Goddess, having gathered together the conventions of conduct as well as the conventions of inner being, which have been indicated, please speak out of compassion.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Indeed, in all Tantras and Vidyās, there is the very convention of *bhāva*;
nevertheless, in the Śakti Tantras, there is a special [method] which is the means for accomplishing everything."
The means of accomplishment is indeed mere intention; through intention one becomes possessed of what is to be accomplished.
Without conduct, intention never arises at all. (3)
Śrī Śiva said:
From what does existence arise, and into what is existence dissolved?
Is the possessor of existence the enjoyer of the fruit, or by what means does one become possessed of right conduct?
The Goddess said:
Since *bhāva* is a mental state (*mānasa-dharma*), how can it belong to sound?
Something of its nature must be explained, at least by way of showing a general direction.
O Lord, O Mahādeva, just as the sweetness of sugarcane or molasses is perceived by the tongue,
so too is the true nature [of reality] contemplated by the mind.
An entity arises in the mind; it dissolves in the mind.
An entity that abides in the mind dissolves again into the mind. (7)
Just as trees, creepers, and so forth undergo creation, maintenance, and dissolution upon the earth, so too, O Great Lord, all existence resides only within the mind; of this there is no doubt. (8)
Just as a reflection born from water dissolves back into the waters, O beloved,
so too does a mental state arise in the mind and dissolve back into the mind.
An entity would be characterized by action, like a bracelet or other ornaments made of gold. (9)
Praise of the state described in the scriptures—
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the Goddess said:
"O Lord of gods, O Master of the life-force, O bestower of existence upon the worlds!"
In what form does even a person in the world become a partaker of the fruit? || 10 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
O lady of excellent hips, without *bhāva* (inner feeling), sound is never manifested;
*bhāva* has sound as its root, for *bhāva* is indeed the root of everything.

O Śivā, even a man who is ignorant of the internal state (bhāva) and who, upon hearing the chest [of the mantra], performs a slight action, becomes like a woman wearing male attire, with his limbs trembling. 12.
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform ritual action after having understood the internal state (bhāva).
O Great Goddess, if one were to become a partaker of the fruit without the internal state, [it would be in vain].
Does a beloved woman increase the joy of her husband when he is a eunuch? || 13 ||
Existence is rooted in action, and action is likewise rooted in existence;
O Supreme Goddess, one who is endowed with existence and empowered by action is the partaker of the fruit.

The Śrī Devī said: O Lord, you are dearer to me than my own life-breath and are free from praise or blame. It is said that action is rooted in intention; how can there be action without intention? (15)
Śrī Śiva said:
Action is rooted in disposition, and action itself is rooted in disposition;
they cannot exist without one another, just as knowledge and the object of knowledge cannot, O beloved. (16)

(25) O Great Goddess, neither through extensive recitation nor through fire-offerings, nor through the detailed practice of bodily mortifications and the like, will there be success; even ritual action does not yield fruit. 17.

What is the use of hundreds of thousands of heroic rites (vīrasādhana), what use are the various types of magnetizing rituals (ākarṣaṇa), what use is the worship of sacred seats (pīṭha), and what use is the feeding of virgins and so forth? || 18 ||
What is the use of bestowing love upon one's own wife, or likewise upon others;
what is the use of self-control over the senses, or of performing the duties of family tradition?
If there were purity of intention, one would not be intent merely upon the fruits [of action].
Through devotion one attains liberation; through devotion, the family prospers.
Through devotion there shall be an increase in lineage; through devotion, the family is purified.

What is the use of elaborate ritual deposits (nyāsa), what is the use of extensive purifications of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and likewise what is the use of worship, if the state of being [the divine] does not arise? 21.
By whomsoever this Vidyā is worshipped, by none is it not fully worshipped;
yet, O Goddess of Gods, due to the absence of fruit, the state of both existence and non-existence arises.
The yogi who has entered into the savor of meditative cultivation becomes a great poet;
even one who is dull-witted attains purity by being intent upon the savor of cultivation. (23)
O Goddess of gods, one certainly obtains the pure and the impure through one's state of being (bhāva);
likewise, one also obtains bondage, liberation, and even the state beyond both through one's state of being.
O Supreme Goddess, one certainly attains everything—be it an animal, a hero, a divine being, or a kaula—through one's state of being, as well as both sin and merit. (25)
O Maheśvarī, through one's own state of being, one indeed attains honor and dishonor, happiness and suffering,
as well as the individual self and the supreme self. (26)
Whether it be joy or the absence of joy, drink or the absence of drink, eating or fasting—one certainly attains these through one's state of being. (27)
O Supreme Goddess, one attains these—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—through one's state of being; and through that very state of being, one perishes.
By means of one's inner disposition, one attains these—the subtle, the gross, Śiva, Śakti, the object of worship, the act of worship, and the worshipper; yet in that same disposition, one perishes.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"The entire universe is merely *bhāva* (being/mental state), which brings about its creation, maintenance, and end.
Among these, reveal that most excellent *bhāva* within my own abode. (30)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Maheśvarī, existence-in-itself is indeed fourfold, and conduct-in-itself is likewise fourfold; light-in-itself is threefold, consisting of both existence and conduct.
Now, the characteristic of the fourfold states:
the inferior ones bring about bodies; the middling ones bring about the individual soul (jīva);
the superior ones bring about liberation; and those beyond the states are the highest of all. || 32 ||

The lowest are those whose conduct follows their own family traditions; the middling are those whose conduct follows the revealed scriptures (śruti); the superior are those whose conduct grants liberation; and those even higher than them follow their own will.
Worship with images is inferior; recitation, hymns, and the like are mediocre; worship of one's own self—and that is mental worship—is superior; and "I am He" is the highest of all worships.
Here, the inferior see the external form, while the mediocre see the supreme time.
Those who are supreme perceive liberation, while those who are most supreme do not perceive it.
The base are afraid of action; the mediocre are afraid of devotion;
the excellent are afraid of liberation; but for those who are most excellent, there is no fear.
Human birth is to be known as the lowest; births among gods and others are middling;
the man of knowledge is said to have the highest birth; there is no birth higher than that. (37)
The lowest is reckoned as having many births, the middling has birth after birth, and the highest has but a single birth; there is no such thing as a "highest-of-the-high" beyond that.
The artificial machine is the lowest; the machine of flowers and so forth is middling; the yoni-machine is the best, and it is the most excellent among all machines. (39)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Eighth Chapter (Ullāsa). Now, the definition of the conduct (*ācāra*) regarding the three types of states (*bhāva*).
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*, the venerable Śiva said:
But existence, O Goddess, is threefold, according to the sequence of the Divine, the Heroic, and the Fettered;
the threefold conduct, O Goddess, has been illustrated by me in due order. || 1 ||
O Dear One, there is only one great reality that assumes manifoldness;
through the distinctions of states such as the supreme (para) and so forth, the differentiation of reality is also threefold.
This single reality is the Supreme Brahman, the destroyer of all obstacles.
In the *Kumārītantra*, the Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, benefactor of the worlds!
O Lord, reveal to me how the state of oneness [is attained] in my own abode."
Śrī Śiva said:
From two years of age up until eight years,
a girl is renowned there as a *kumārī*, bestowing the fruits of *yantras* and *tantras*.
Up until the sixteenth year of her life, she is called a young woman (*yuvatī*);
therein, that state which is luminosity is considered the supreme state (*bhāva*).
O Maheśvarī, a woman over ten years of age is known as a *yuvatī* up to sixteen years; worship offered to her yields great fruit. (6)
In the sixteenth year, the digit is full; in the sixteenth year, the digit is established.
At the end of that sixteenth year, O Śivā, the digit is the digit to be accomplished (sādhyakalā).
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Compassionate One, you who are dearer to me than my own life!
O Supreme Lord, reveal to me what this *kalā* is in my own abode. (8)
The illustrious Śiva said:
The place of the womb (yonisthāna) should be known as the *kalā* when it is joined with the wind of desire (*kāmavāyu*). If it is devoid of the wind of desire, there is no fitness for worship.

O Goddess, one should worship the maiden with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth, both in the state of the *vibhava* and the *paśu*; one should worship her with the sentiment of desire (*kāma-bhāva*).
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Ninth Chapter (Ullāsa). In that interval, the venerable Goddess said:
[The five verses beginning with "O Lord of Gods" and ending with "arising from this" are found in manuscript *gha*.]
It is not in the book; however, this reading is seen there: In the *Nārāyaṇītantra*, the venerable Śiva said:
"The threefold conduct and the threefold disposition are the cause of the Kaula practice."
The Paśvācāra, the Vīra, and the Divya are undoubtedly Kaula;
O Maheśānī, even the Siddhānta is based upon the Kaula state. || 1 ||
The Goddess said: O Supreme Lord, tell me how there are six types— namely Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Divya, Siddhānta, and Kaula.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O beloved, the conduct of the bound soul (paśvācāra) is to be known as threefold; the conduct of the hero (vīrācāra) is threefold;
and the divine (divya) and kaula [conducts] are fourfold each, pertaining to both the Śakti and the Puruṣa."
The Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, the Divya, the Paśu endowed with the Kaula state,
the Dakṣiṇa, the Vāma, the Siddhānta, and indeed the Śākta joined with the Kaula;
O Lord of the Mistress of Life, Beloved of Pārvatī’s life!
Tell me, what is the sixfold conduct, the four states of being, and the Kaula knowledge? || 1 ||

Śrī Śiva said: O Śivā, the conduct of the bound soul (paśvācāra) is to be known as threefold, the conduct of the hero (vīrācāra) is threefold, and that of the manly one (pauruṣa)— meaning the practitioner whose deity is the Supreme Person— is likewise so.
For the Śākta practitioner—that is, for one who practices the deity Śakti—from that which is endowed with the fourfold state. || 2 ||
(30) The Kaulas who possess the state of the bound (paśubhāva) are the Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and [others];
the Kaulas who possess the state of the hero (vīrabhāva) are the Siddhāntas of the Left and Right.
And the bound one, O Goddess, is of two kinds: that which possesses its own nature (sabhāva) and that which is devoid of nature (vibhāvaka).
And the hero, O Goddess, is of two kinds: the excitant (vibhāva) and the natural (sabhāvaka). || 4 ||
Thus, there are four kinds of states, and the fifth is the divine state;
all of them depend upon the Kaula path, just as rivers and other streams depend upon the ocean.
O Supreme Goddess, the Kaula indeed consists of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa;
it transcends duality, transcends action, is absolute, and is devoid of mental states.
For in the Kaula systems, even mere ritual action leads to the state of liberation regarding the Kaula goal.
Now, the cause of the Kaula-knowledge:
in the Jñānadīpa—“The Vedas are superior to all; among the Vedas, the Vaiṣṇava is supreme.”
The Śaiva is superior to the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śākta is superior to the Śaiva.
And the Śākta, O Goddess, is of two kinds through the division of Vāma and Dakṣiṇa;
the Vāma is superior to the Dakṣiṇa, and the Siddhānta is superior to the Vāma.

The Kaula is superior to all established doctrines (siddhānta), for there is nothing higher than the Kaula. The practice of the Kaula is the seed of all; the universe consists of the practice of the Kaula.
The practice of the Kaula is mere being, yet the Kaula is indeed devoid of being.
By these practices, the one qualified for yoga is described as follows:
like an ant, a small creature, a large creature, a frog, an animal, a monkey, a bird, and a wakeful man.
And through the power of right conduct, the Vedic scriptures and other authorities will come into being, and the qualification for yoga will be gradually established.
Thus says Nāgabhaṭṭa. Now, regarding the practice of the Paśus:
in the *Samayācāra-tantra*, the illustrious Śiva said:
One should worship the God according to the Vedic injunctions, preceded by the mental resolve for one's desires.
That which is indeed the Vedic practice is itself the practice of the bound soul (paśu).
O Goddess, there is no eating of fish, nor should one even mentally recall women.
One should have no greed for another's property, nor should one even mentally long for its enjoyment. || 11 ||
On the banks of a river, in a forest, on a mountain, or in a divine abode;
at the foot of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, or in a beautiful and holy field. || 12 ||
The deity should be meditated upon with a pure disposition and well-composed mind;
one should not look upon a Śūdra and should abandon crookedness far away. (13)
One should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day and perform the recitation (japa) at the three junctions;
however, one must never touch the yantra or the rosary at night.

One should not engage in talk concerning the deeds of heroes, nor should one revile the Guru. Reviling is to be understood as conceptualizing [the Guru] as another Guru. Just as the conceptualization of the Self is the cause for the knowledge of reality regarding the individual soul (jīva), so too is the Guru. || 15 ||
In the Guru-tantra, it is said that reviling the guru is a fault:
"Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one guru to another. (16)
O Dear One, the Guru is of two kinds according to the distinction between initiation (dīkṣā) and instruction (śikṣā).
One who is still possessed of the state of a bound soul (paśu) should not act as a Guru of instruction.
A woman joined with the state of a bound soul (paśu) does not conceive of her husband as a husband; likewise, O Goddess, a bound soul does not conceive of the Guru as the Guru’s consort. 18.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Tenth Chapter:
The Characteristics of the Guru in the Gurus’ Tradition. The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the Master of Life, I bow at your lotus feet;
tell me, by what means shall the world, filled with various modes of conduct, be transformed?
O Lord of Gods, in what form does the conduct of the bound soul (paśvācāra) arise?
Tell me that: how do the Vīra, Divya, Kaula, and Siddhānta [traditions] come to be? || 2 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said: O Supreme Goddess, when the Guru conducts himself with joy according to the prescribed conduct,
the practitioner of mantra will likewise be endowed with that conduct in age after age.
In the *Niruttara*:
"One who has received the mantra from a guru who is a bound soul (paśu) is undoubtedly still a bound soul;
one who has received the mantra from the mouth of a hero (vīra) is undoubtedly a hero. (4)
The Siddhānta is obtained through mantras; this is the Siddhānta, of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, apart from the conduct of the bound soul (paśvācāra), the five principles (pañcatattva) are auspicious when joined [with it].
One should recognize that he who reviles the five principles (pañcatattva) follows the conduct of a bound soul (paśu);
therefore, with every effort, one should not perform initiation for such a bound soul.
O Goddess, without the five principles (pañcatattva), the mantra of power (śaktimantra) becomes useless;
for this very reason, one who possesses the disposition of a hero (vīrabhāvī) should not perform initiation for a bound soul (paśu).
If a Śākta is the teacher of Paśus, or if a Paśu is the teacher of Vīras,
it is like a young wife for an old man, or an infant husband for an old woman. (8)
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*:
"There is no form even for this [consciousness], nor is it the manifestation of a real entity; for form and the real entity always exist as its own nature."
Just as water, O Śaṅkara, appears in various colors through the quality of its substances, and is indeed heavy according to its characteristics.
Now, the praise of the Śākta Guru:
"O Hara, having received the mantra from a Kaulika and performing the rite of recitation, if liberation does not arise, then my word is in vain. (10)
One devoted to the Kula-dharma should not perform the initiation of a paśu (bound soul).
Merely by the sight of a paśu, the ritual efficacy of the Kaulikas is destroyed.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the initiation of a paśu. || 11 ||
In the Bhairavatantra:

"O Supreme Goddess, a practitioner endowed with the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) should avoid initiating those bound souls (paśu) who possess both natural dispositions (sabhāva) and artificial dispositions (vibhāva). (12)
The Hero undergoes initiation even for the manifestation and dissolution of all natures;
having taken refuge in the Kulanātha, he should perform the initiation once again.
When initiated into a mantra in its true nature (sabhāva), it is terrifying with disease, grief, and fear;
when initiated into a mantra in its manifested nature (vibhāva), it consists of fear alone. || 14 ||
A Brahmin who delights in the conduct of his lineage and knows the true meaning of the scriptures of his family—
by hearing from his mouth, the mantra becomes the bestower of all accomplishments.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a guru of noble lineage.
Now he states the characteristics of the Guru:
"O Śivā, the Guru is threefold in Śiva—as gross, as radiant, and likewise as subtle;
O beloved, he who contemplates the Guru as one in these three ways, beyond all mental constructs. (16)
Sometimes that Guru, who is to be meditated upon through mantra, resides in the thousand-petaled lotus;
sometimes in the heart-lotus, and sometimes within the range of one's vision. (17)
Subtle meditation is in the thousand-petalled lotus, the fiery meditation is in the heart, O Dear One;
gross meditation is in the external region—such is the threefold fruit born of meditation.
Now, the subtle meditation on the venerable Guru.
In the *Gurugītā*:
[He is] the bliss of Brahman, the bestower of supreme happiness, the absolute embodiment of knowledge.
It transcends all dualities, is like the sky, and is the objective indicated by such statements as "That thou art. || 19 ||
I bow to that true Guru, who is one, eternal, stainless, and immovable; who is forever the witness, beyond all states of being, and devoid of the three qualities. 20.
I bow to the Guru, who is Brahman—eternal, pure, free from appearance, changeless, untainted, eternally awakened, and the bliss of consciousness. 21.
Now, the meditation on the splendor of the venerable Guru:
[He is] seated upon the pericarp in the lotus of the heart,
his divine form established upon a lion-throne.
One should meditate upon the Guru, adorned with the crescent moon, who is pure consciousness and bliss, and the bestower of desired boons. || 22 ||
Clad in white garments and anointed with white unguents, his divine form is adorned with strings of pearls;
he rests upon the seat of his left lap the divine Śakti, possesses a gentle smile, and is a treasury of perfect compassion. (23)

I perpetually bow to the venerable Guru— the Lord of Yogis, worthy of praise, the physician for the disease of worldly existence— who is blissful, the source of bliss, serene, whose nature is knowledge, and who is endowed with innate awakening. (24)
Now, the gross meditation upon the venerable Guru:

O Supreme Goddess, by whose command the gross energy and the subtle principles [are manifested], that Guru who is established in meditation through this threefold meditation is the one of gross form. (25)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Sarvāllāsa*, composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. The eleventh chapter begins.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, by your grace, the threefold meditation has indeed been heard.
Now, O beloved, I wish to hear the characteristics of the true Guru."
Now, the characteristics of the True Guru.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Great Goddess, the meditation on the Guru, who is the abode of the three, is likewise threefold.
O Supreme Goddess, [it is] in the thousand-petaled lotus of the heart, and also externally.
The word *sat* is applied to both gross and subtle light;
and without the word *sat*, O auspicious lady, the word *guru* is never used anywhere. (3)
O Supreme Goddess, the true Guru is captivating in his pure attire;
he is complete with all auspicious marks and adorned with every beautiful limb. || 4 ||
He knows the true meaning of all scriptures, is proficient in all treatises,
causes delusion in the world, and reveals the nature of the deities.
O Dear One, the true Guru is said to be endowed with such characteristics as these.
And the Guru, O Supreme Goddess, is the sole and supreme enlightener;
he is like a golden earring that possesses the word "sat" (real/excellent), which is both excellent and most excellent.
O Goddess, in the unsurpassed [tradition], existence is threefold according to the sequence of the divine, the hero, and the bound soul; likewise,
the gurus are said to be of three kinds, as are the deities of the mantra.
O Goddess, many gurus are remembered who are devoted to the Kula scriptures;
however, a guru who truly knows the established principles of the Kula-tattva is indeed rare.
In the *Vāmakeśvara*:
"O lady of excellent hips, there are indeed infinite gurus endowed with the threefold conduct; one obtains such a teacher through good fortune, provided they are possessed of true devotion. (36.9)
O Supreme Goddess, if by good fortune one obtains a true Guru, then one should perform the Kula initiation; one should not do so merely by seeing or hearing [of it]. 10.
In the Kulārṇava:
"The hosts of Yoginīs, becoming enraged, destroy the lineage of one who performs the Kula practice merely after seeing it written in a book. (11)

Having recognized the Guru, one who is endowed with devotion and conducts himself according to the accepted discipline shall attain the perfection of his own desired vidyā, just as the body serves the embodied soul.
Having seen such conduct, one who is not filled with devotion should not follow a Guru nor the Kula path.
His conduct would be in vain; there is neither salutation nor the sprinkling of water for him. || 13 ||
O Maheśānī, if one becomes a partaker of the fruit without a guru, then a woman will become pregnant with a son even without a husband. 14.
Therefore, one should appoint a teacher according to the prescribed method of their true nature;
by hearing [the teachings] from his mouth, a person becomes a partaker of the fruit in the performance of the rite. || 15 ||
A man devoted to the Kaula conduct, according to the method taught by his guru, worships the supreme Goddess and attains the highest goal. (16)
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"Indeed, a single Guru endowed with thirteen qualities is difficult to find;
among them, O Goddess, a Guru possessed of even one quality is rare. (17)
The Guru, endowed with the thirteen qualities, is Sadāśiva himself;
by the mere sight of him one is liberated from sin, and even one's ritual action becomes fruitful.
The Śrī Devī said:
O Kuleśa, O Lord of the Life-force, please tell me the thirteenth characteristic in its proper place, if you have grace toward me. (19)
Śrī Śiva said:
One who is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, wearing pure attire, of pure conduct, well-established, clean, capable, and highly intelligent; (20)
One who belongs to a stage of life (āśramin), is steadfast in meditation, is proficient in the mantras and tantras,
and is capable of both restraint and grace— such a person is recognized as a guru.
Now, regarding the peaceful one (śānta):
he who is content with whatever comes his way and is highly skilled in ritual action—he is indeed the peaceful one, ever joyful in mind and devoted to the Divine at all times. (22)
Now, regarding the self-controlled:
he imparts the words of knowledge with joy, whether [the disciple] has offered food or not;
endowed with compassion and free from attachment—this is the characteristic of a self-controlled guru. (23)
Now, O Īśvarī, one who is of noble lineage (*kulīna*) is a teacher who follows the family tradition, possesses family knowledge, imparts the reality of the family (*kula-tattva*),
and is engaged in the ritual practices within the family abode.

Now, regarding the disciplined one (vinīta): O Goddess of gods, by means of compassionate speech, he repeatedly utters words of wisdom; the disciplined one, who generates devotion in those who are not yet devoted, possesses the characteristics of a guru. || 25 ||
(p. 38) Now, regarding the pure attire: O Goddess, the Guru who is devoted to the conduct of whichever deity he wears the ornaments of should himself possess that same pure attire. (26)
Now, regarding pure conduct: If one follows the conduct of whichever deity [he worships], being entirely free from praise and blame, he himself is a teacher of pure conduct. (27)
Now, regarding Supratiṣṭha:
O Goddess, when served with pure devotion and pure knowledge,
the Guru Supratiṣṭha is the perpetual protector of bliss.
The bestower of all bliss. || 28 ||

Now, O Goddess, a teacher who is pure and skillful— one who is endowed with proper conduct despite being previously lacking in it, who has no attachment to sacred bathing places, who is pure and skillful, and who is adept in all undertakings— is [fit]. (29)
Then, O Supreme Goddess, the highly intelligent individual soul merges into the Supreme Self; O Goddess, that highly intelligent Guru—[realizing] "I am He"—his [dualistic] knowledge perishes. (30)
Now, regarding the householder (āśramī):

O Īśvarī, the householder guru is one who, having taken refuge in the bliss found within that [world] consisting of all desired forms—the relationship with wife, children, and so forth—is established therein. (31)
Now, regarding the one established in meditation:
if one should worship the Self by relying upon the threefold meditation, O Supreme Goddess, that teacher shall certainly be one established in meditation. (32)
(39) Now, O Supreme Goddess, he who is proficient in mantra and tantra, who protects the mind and destroys mental doubt— he is a guru proficient in mantra and tantra. (33)
Now, regarding the capacity for restraint and grace:
"One who can bestow bondage upon the liberated and grant liberation to the bound—one capable of both restraint and grace is recognized as a Guru. (34)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twelfth Chapter: Now, the Vaiṣṇava conduct.
"Abandoning all duties, devotion to the Beloved arises."
That indeed is the Vaiṣṇava conduct, free from desire and mental constructs. || 1 ||
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"A Vaiṣṇava should worship the Supreme Lord with a state of mind [characteristic of] a *paśu* (bound soul).
O lady of excellent hips, in the *Śakti-tantra*, the state of a *paśu* is terrifying. (2)
If one worships the God while in the state of a beast, even if endowed with devotion toward Śiva,
or if one should worship the Goddess [in that state], his exertion is in vain.
O Maheśānī, in the state of Paśu, the mantra has the nature of phonemes;
even in the state of Vīra, that same mantra bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
If a practitioner of mantra, relying on the state of a bound soul (paśu), should worship Kālī,
he goes to the Raurava hell until the dissolution of all created beings.
Now follows the prohibition regarding the worship of animal sacrifices with power (śakti).
In the Kulārṇava:
"Having eaten meat, having drunk liquor, and having approached a woman in her menses..."
One should worship the goddess Kālikā; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
One should not worship the Goddess while fasting; one should worship the Goddess after having eaten.
By worshipping while fasting, one is born as a worm in excrement.
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should not perform the worship of Śakti;
O Great Goddess, when performing the worship of another deity, one should worship with this intention.

(41) O Supreme Goddess, one should avoid treating devotion to worship as one thing and the act of propitiation as another; one must avoid censuring noble women or heroes, seizing the property of others, showing anger toward women, and striking them. 9.
In Picchilā—
having received the command of the Guru, a man with a purified inner self,
while praising his own chosen deity, should not worship another deity. (10)
O Supreme Goddess, one should avoid wandering to sacred fords, worshipping deities, performing libations, and so forth; one should not contemplate anyone other than the Guru.
Now follows the meditative absorption (samādhi) of a Vaiṣṇava:
having known another form as being one's own chosen form, one should perform the ritual action;
for just as a reflection appears in mirrors, so too does the form of another deity.
O Goddess, there is no god on the surface of the earth except for the one God, just as there is no sun in this world except for the one Sun. || 13 ||
O beloved, just as the sun appears many when reflected in water contained in many vessels,
so too is the Lord seen in many forms within those possessing manifold states of being.
Regarding the truth of the Nigama:
"O Great Goddess, the nature of Dharma is the ancient seed of all worlds; having abandoned Dharma, what has he resorted to as his support? (15)
The Śrī Devī said:
Having abandoned all dharmas and taking refuge in the single dharma, one should contemplate the Self of Dharma, the Self of the Deity, and one's own Self. (16)
One's own chosen Vidyā is the embodiment of Dharma, eternal, and self-illuminating; just as the nursing of a child at the breast increases both its physical body and its spiritual nature. || 17 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter:
Now, on the subject of devotion to the chosen deity (iṣṭabhakti),
the venerable Śiva spoke in the Nigamatattva:
O Goddess, you are supreme, perfect, and the bestower of the fruits of all prosperity;
whatever desire or devotion there may be, please reveal it to me in this place.
The Goddess said:
The Lord resides within the mouth of the Guru, and He alone is the form of the desired deity; even ritual action (kriyā) occurs through His word—such is the conception of devotion.
Whatever action there is, that too is devotion; and whatever is devotion, that too is action.
One's own chosen Vidyā is the very form of devotion; without devotion, it is not attained. (3)
Without devotion, that knowledge is not attained; therefore, devotion is proclaimed [as the means].
That devotion, O Lord, is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
O Maheśvara, devotion is threefold: sattvic devotion is the highest, rājasic devotion is middling, and tāmasī devotion is the lowest. (5)
Mental devotion is characterized by *sattva*, external devotion by *rajas*,
and hypocritical devotion by *tamas*; I shall now describe their distinctions.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*, the Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of gods, O Sovereign of the life-force, O benefactor of the worlds!
Please describe the characteristics of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) according to the distinctions of their inner disposition (*bhāva*)."
The venerable Śiva said:
O Dear One, practitioners are declared to be of three kinds—the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa*—O Maheśānī; I shall describe their characteristics to you. (8)
Now, the characteristics of the sāttvika practitioner:
One who is pure within and pure without, always devoted to the Lord,
and endowed with compassion for all living beings, O Goddess, is sāttvika.
O Great Goddess, he is of the nature of sattva and is always devoted to the deity. || 9 ||
Now, the characteristics of the rājasika practitioner:
One who worships oneself as the deity with faith through very fine garments and other offerings,
and who is always satisfied by passion, is proclaimed to be rājasika.
O Great Goddess, he is of the nature of rajas, consisting of passion and desiring passion. || 10 ||
Now, the characteristics of the *tāmasa* practitioner:
one who is full of anger, talkative, hostile toward others, and deceitful—who worships the God without faith—is proclaimed as *tāmasa*. (11)

Having fashioned a deity from a poor material, one may sacrifice with either faith or lack of faith; yet such a person, being devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in the performance of the rite, possesses the characteristics of the tamasic type.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the venerable Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, in what form does the practitioner become a partaker of liberation?
Tell me, O Lord of the Life-force, if you have grace toward me. (13)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Devotion may indeed have worship as its root, yet without worship one does not possess devotion.
That worship is declared to be threefold: superior, middling, and inferior. (14)
O Śivā, there are three kinds of *sāttvika* worship, three kinds of *rājasa* worship, and three kinds of *tāmasa* worship; I shall now describe their distinctions. (15)
Now, the characteristics of the threefold *sāttvika* worship:
"I alone am the Supreme Goddess; this entire world is within me"—this is to be known as *sāttvika* worship, hidden amidst all forms of worship. (16)

O Beloved of Prāṇa, that worship which one performs in the heart by means of the mind, visualizing the form of the deity as it truly is, should be known as the Sāttvika worship; it is the middling [type]. [Thus it is said.]
One should worship the Goddess with mental offerings and with services performed with faith;
that worship is to be known as *sāttvika*, while the inferior one, O Beloved of my life, is [the external]. (18)

Now, the characteristics of the threefold rājasa worship: One should worship the Goddess with faith and ritual offerings as if she were oneself; worship free from desire and mental constructs is the highest rājasa. (19)
One should worship the Goddess with ritual services solely for the sake of pleasing Her;
O Beloved of the Vital Breath, that is the Rājasa form of worship for the Goddess, which is considered middling.
One should worship Śivā with faith, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others;
however, worship performed while joined with desire and worldly resolve is of the nature of passion (rājasa) and inferior.

Now, the characteristics of the threefold *tāmasī* worship: One who, for the sake of hypocrisy, worships Śivā—whether for oneself or for another—being endowed with faith yet possessed of desire, that worship is the highest *tāmasī*. (22)
O Beloved of Prāṇa, that worship of Śivā performed with a ritual resolve for worldly gain or for the sake of hypocrisy is to be known as tāmasī; it is considered mediocre. (23)
O beloved of my life, if one worships Śivā with faith for the sake of harming others for one's own gain, that worship is to be known as *tāmasī* and is the lowest. (24)
And that worship which is devoid of faith does not yield fruit;
devotion has worship as its root, for worship indeed has devotion as its root.
Without one another they would not exist, just as knowledge and the object of knowledge do not exist apart from each other, O beloved. (25)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Fourteenth Chapter: Now, the Offering of the Sacrificial Feast (Balidāna).
In the Jñānārṇava, the Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of knowledge upon the worlds,
explain the characteristics of the offering of oblations (balidāna) according to the distinctions of inner disposition.
Śrī Śiva said: O Goddess, Kali is of three kinds: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
O Goddess, without the offering of a *bali*, there is no fitness for worship.
O Great Goddess, the offering of a sacrificial oblation (bali) according to the prescribed rite is the essence of worship;
for if one possesses knowledge, the offering of the bali becomes the very core of the ritual.
