Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should offer the bali-oblation with great effort;
what on this earth cannot be accomplished by offering the bali according to the prescribed rite? || 4 ||
Now follows the *sāttvika* offering.
The *sāttvika* offering is declared to be devoid of meat, blood, and the like;
for by what action could one cause harm to a body that is composed of Brahman? (5)
Indeed, the existent reality is merely creation, manifested as mere being;
within that existence, Śiva is the initiator of creation, the offering of the sacrifice, and the dissolution.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the offering of a *bali* with pure goodness (*sattva*)—an offering of *bali* devoid of flesh, blood, and the like—yields auspicious fruit. (7)
In the Kali age, the human horse-sacrifice, liquor, and injury to living beings must be avoided by the twice-born who are wise;
for what was not virtuous in the Satya age was not auspicious in the Tretā or the Dvāpara either.
(47) Since no one possessing knowledge would perform the human horse-sacrifice in the Kali age,
[one should instead perform] a buffalo as a substitute for the human, and a goat as a substitute for the buffalo.
O Śivā, for a goat there is the preparation of a sheep; for a sheep, a bird;
for a bird, a fish; and for a fish, merely an insect.
O auspicious lady, in the Kali age, one may abandon the secondary ritual options in the absence of the required materials.
Even by giving a buffalo in this secret rite, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
The practitioner of mantra becomes a sharer in the fruits [of his merit] if he offers the oblation according to the prescribed rule.
O Goddess, without the offering of an oblation, all violence is condemned everywhere.
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "One should never cut this [linga] without following the prescribed rule;
yet, even by killing a twice-born man, a cow, or one's mother according to the rite, one is not tainted by sins. (13)
Nevertheless, O Supreme Goddess, the man of knowledge is not at all a hunter;
yet sacrifice is to be understood as twofold—listen to me regarding the distinction between these two. (14)
The *bali* offering is the first; the gift of living beings (*prāṇidāna*) is the second.

When the *nivṛtti* [path] has ceased, there should be the *pravṛtti* [path], O Beloved, involving an animal for the *bali*. Any worship that is devoid of the *bali* is not a worship that yields fruit.
Now follows the rājasika bali:
The rājasika bali is described as being well-adorned and full of passion;
it is provided with meat, blood, and the like, and is especially black in color. (16)
Having thus offered a complete sacrificial offering (bali) that is black in color, free from missing or extra limbs, and healthy, the practitioner obtains the full fruit.
By offering a child as a sacrifice, Caṇḍikā kills one's son;
by an old man, she kills an elder; likewise, by a thin man, a kinsman; by one with an extra limb, wealth; and by one with a missing limb, one's offspring. (p. 48)
He struck the amorous woman with the breaking of his horn, and likewise his brother with his one-eyed eye.
Death occurs through a bell, and there is an obstacle if it is on the head;
a friend is killed if it has a copper-colored back, and one's fortune is lost due to the absence of a tail.
In the Muṇḍamālātantra:
"O auspicious lady, as long as one relies upon the Māyā of the Mother, he is called a 'child' (śiśu).
Even by the killing of such a person, O Bhadrā, one's own son perishes. (21)
One should never cause the destruction of the body that consists of the immutable; however,
when a transformation involving the production of semen has occurred, its destruction is prescribed by the ritual injunctions.
For even when the semen is diminished, the killing of an elder is indeed a "killing of a guru" because of the gravity of the act. || 22 ||
Now, the *tāmasika* offering:

O Dear One, the *tāmasa* [devotee], possessed of the qualities of *tamas* such as indolence and the like, does not offer an oblation with faith, nor likewise in worship and other rites, O Dear One. (23)
O Goddess, for practitioners, that is not merely a matter of name alone;
the offering of a bali sacrifice is in vain for him, being nothing but the slaughter of a living being.
O Goddess, a practitioner who is dominated by tamas never, never at all [attains success];
because he is fallen due to being devoid of worship, he is a practitioner in name only. (25)
The offering of the bali should be given by whomever and in whatever manner it is performed;
no formal ritual procedure need be observed, for the bali-offering is indeed merely a matter of measure.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
Fifteenth Chapter:
When a Vaiṣṇava, a devotee of Viṣṇu, becomes one whose very self is the soul of Viṣṇu, then he should always perform meditation upon the supreme, auspicious Goddess Vaiṣṇavī. (1)
That which remains of the conduct of the bound (paśu) and precedes the conduct of the Śaktas is declared to be the Śaiva conduct; one should worship by means of the conduct of the bound.
O Maheśvarī, O Śaṅkarī, one should worship Prasāda, Cyambaka, and other Tantric deities according to the Vīrācāra practice by means of the five elements (pañcatattva).
Now, regarding the conduct of a Śaiva: in the *Samayācāra-tantra* it is said—
“Endowed with the eightfold yoga, one should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rule.”
As long as knowledge remains in meditative absorption, so long is it declared to be Śaiva.

Now, the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*). In the *Kālikākulasarasvatī*: restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*).
The eight limbs of yoga, O Pārvatī. || 5 ||
First is the definition of *yama*:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, uprightness, forbearance, fortitude, contentment, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten *yamas*.
The characteristic of restraint (yama), which is a limb of yoga, has been declared to be tenfold.
(p. 50) Now, the definition of the observances (niyama):
austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Deity, listening to the established doctrine, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings.
And the tenfold restraint of the limbs of yoga has been declared, O Pārvatī.
Now, concerning the seat: 1. Padmāsana, that called Svastika, Bhadra, Vajrāsana, and likewise Vīrāsana—these are declared to be the five seats in their proper order. || 8 ||
Having taken hold of the left foot, one should place it upon the right thigh;
likewise, one should place the right foot upon the left, seated according to the prescribed rule.
O Dear One, this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana) for recitation, worship, and other such practices.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees, with the body straight, the practitioner of mantra should enter; that they call the *svastika* posture. 10.
One should place the two ankles firmly on either side of the perineum;
with the feet positioned below the scrotum, one should support them with both hands.
This is declared to be the Bhadrāsana, devised by the yogis.
Having placed the feet wide apart and turned the fingers inward, one should restrain the hands; this is declared and described as the Vajrāsana posture.
Placing one foot below and likewise resting the other upon the thigh, with the body held straight, the practitioner of mantra should enter [the posture]; this is declared to be the vīrāsana.
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma):
O Goddess, without breath control there is no fitness for worship.
Both breath control and the postures (āsana) are approved for every form of conduct. (14)
In the *Tripurāsāra-tantra*:
"O beautiful one, when Kuṇḍalinī is sleeping by herself in the Mūlādhāra, then no ritual action whatsoever should be performed. (15)
O Supreme Goddess, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), that Goddess and that Supreme Lord, having abandoned sleep, assume their own desired forms. 16.
Now, the fruit of *prāṇāyāma*:
One should perform *prāṇāyāma* with the root-seed syllable as the seed-syllable.
Indeed, *prāṇāyāma* is declared to be the very nature of the deity. (17)
O God, when the true nature is described, O Śiva, there is the vision of that true nature;
from the vision of the true nature, one's own true nature quickly becomes manifest of itself. (18)
He states another means of valid knowledge in the *Gurugītā*:

"O Pārvatī, O lady of excellent hips, just as a worm becomes a bee [by the power of its past impressions], so too does an embodied being constantly become one with Brahman through meditation on the Guru. (19)
In the *Tripurāsāra*: "Brahmā is devoted to breath-control; Hari is devoted to breath-control;
even Śaṅkara is breath-control itself, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (20)
Pūraka is Brahmā, Kumbhaka is Hari himself, and Recaka is Rudra himself; thus Prāṇāyāma consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
The retention of the nostrils by means of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be understood as *prāṇāyāma*. (22)
Inhalation (pūraka) is performed through the left channel with sixteen recitations;
retention (kumbhaka) is performed through the middle channel with sixty-four recitations;
and exhalation (recana) is performed through the right channel with half that number of recitations. || 23 ||
In another tantra: "One should fill the breath with sixteen [counts] and retain it for four times that."
One should recite it for half a *kumbhaka*; if unable, for a fourth part.
Thus, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) consists of *kumbhaka*, *pūraka*, and *recaka*—or, in case of inability, simply the fourfold cycle.
One should fill the breath through the iḍā and hold it with the right nostril.
One should perform retention (kumbhaka) in the suṣumnā while holding the nostril,
and one should exhale (recaka) through the piṅgalā by means of retention while holding the left nostril.
In the *Niruttara*:
"Prāṇāyāma is proclaimed [to consist of] twelve [cycles]; pratyāhāra is said to be twice that. One should know that the auspicious dhāraṇā is twice the number of pratyāhāra. (27)
Retention (dhāraṇā) is declared as the twelfth, and meditation (dhyāna) belongs to one skilled in meditation.
By means of these twelve meditations alone, concentration (samādhi) is designated.
Then, through concentration, one either performs actions or does not perform them.
O Goddess, why should one not attain success on this earth through *kumbhaka* alone?
Through it, one attains the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) and the state of meditative absorption (*samādhitva*), and death at its appointed time is destroyed. (29)
In the *Tripurāsāra*, regarding Samādhi: The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Devas, O Lord of the Life-force, you who are the eternal bestower of reality!"
Now I wish to hear the characteristics of one who is established in samādhi. || 30 ||
The illustrious Śiva said:
Even one who is a devotee of Śiva and whose very self has become the self of Śiva must always perform meditation upon Śiva—the peaceful one who pervades the universe. (31)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Sixteenth Chapter.
Now, the definition of the sacrificial animal (paśu) as the determinative factor (vibhāva):
The practitioner (sādhaka) should worship the Goddess with secondary substitutes according to the Vedic path.
O Śivā, this practice of the beasts has been proclaimed as the doctrine of Vibhava; O beloved one.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
Now, the substitute for wine (*madyānukalpa*):
O Dear One, cow’s milk should be boiled with fire, along with the juice of the *karjūra* fruit.
For him, molasses is equal to liquor, and betel-leaf mixed with lime-powder is likewise. || 2 ||
Seasoning mixed with salt, raw rice combined with ghee,
the juice of dates, and sugar mixed with cow's products—
O Supreme Goddess.
The great arising is considered by Vibhāvasu to be equal to wine for the animal [without the rock salt]. || 3 ||
Now, regarding the substitutes for meat:
wheat, red raw sesame, white [sesame], O Maheśvarī;
and autumn-harvested rice, as well as red rice, O Śivā.
[A fragment from Gh: "A piece of meat is proclaimed to be equal to wine; the *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruit is likewise celebrated.
The *kuṣmāṇḍa* should be known as being like meat; this is the opinion of Vibhāvasu regarding the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). Now follows the substitute for fish.
O Supreme Goddess, if coconut, wood-apple, myrobalan, and yellow myrobalan are burnt, it is indeed the ritual preparation of animal flesh and fish.

(55) Regarding the substitute for the *mudrā* offering: O Śivā, parched rice without salt or water is considered the substitute for the *mudrā* by the supreme Vibhava for the sake of the bound soul (*paśu*).
Now, the secondary rite for sexual union: [In this regard, the reading from manuscript (gha) is as follows:
"O Goddess, the sexual union of animals is the application of the *yantra* in one's own hand;
having carefully extracted the essential reality (*tattva*), it is auspicious even without [avoiding] festival days and the like."
O Śivā, one should consume that supreme substance with the root mantra;
O Goddess, without the five principles (pañcatattva), the mantra of the Goddess becomes futile.
This substance is indeed not a deity, nor is it ever to be drunk, O Śivā;
one should worship the deity according to what is declared in the Vedas, for the doctrine of the animal (paśu) is that of the fire-god (vibhāvasu).
For animals there is no sexual union, nor is any such thought conceived.
In the great thousand-petaled lotus, [he is] endowed with Śiva and Śakti.
With that nectar, one should thoroughly satisfy the supreme Goddess;
when she is pleased, the Blessed Lady reveals the reflection of her own self.
O Goddess, without the five principles (pañcatattva), the worship of the Goddess becomes fruitless;
one should worship the God according to the Vedic injunctions, for the view of the Paśu is that [the deity] is merely fire.
Now, the definition of the Hero of Dissolution (vibhāvavīra).
In the Picchilā, the Śrīdevī said:
"O Mahādeva, O Great Yogin, [you whose] body consists of the knowledge of reality."
Having discerned the conduct of heroes, reveal it in my stead, O Lord.
Śrī Śiva said:
"In recounting the conduct of the heroes (vīrācāra), a doubt arose in my mind:
'This must never be spoken to a heretic or an atheist.'"
O Mistress of the Family, the state of a hero is my very life-force and all-in-all.
O Goddess, without the state of a hero, the worship of the Goddess would be in vain. (12)

Now, regarding the *vibhāva-vīra*: O Great Goddess, because there is doubt concerning the practice of the natural state (*prakṛti*), one should worship with the five principles (*pañcatattva*) through the single mental manifestation (*mānasaikavibhāva*). || 13 ||
Alternatively, one may worship the Supreme Goddess with secondary rites (*anukalpa*). One should worship the Goddess with secondary rites according to the path of the Tantras.
This is declared to be the *Vīrācāra*; O Śivā, this is the doctrine of Vibhāva concerning the Śāktas.
bestowing happiness and liberation. || 14 ||
One should perform worship with the five mental principles (tattvas) through the mind;
or, one should worship the Goddess externally using substitutes for the five principles.
Now, the authority regarding the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
In the *Vīra-tantra*:
"Liquor, meat, fish, ritual gestures (*mudrā*), and sexual union."
This is declared to be the fivefold reality (pañcatattva), which bestows both happiness and liberation upon the Śāktas.
Now, the substitutes for liquor:
in the case of *picchilā*, coconut water; in a bronze vessel, buttermilk mixed with jaggery.
Ginger combined with jaggery, prepared food, and burnt milk—O Supreme One! these are substitutes for liquor that bestow the fruits of the four aims of life. || 17 ||
In the *Niruttara*:
"A Brāhmaṇa, having drunk liquor with a heroic spirit (*vīrabhāva*), should mutter the mantra.
Even in its absence, a twice-born man should offer cow's milk in every age. (18)
Betel, copper filings, Tvaritā, Tāḍitā, ahiphena,
date-palm juice, dhūstūra, and likewise samvidā—
these eight are declared to be the divine liquors (surās) that bestow bliss upon the practitioners. || 19 ||
Now, regarding the substitutes for meat:
salt, fresh ginger, pināka, sesame, wheat, māsa beans, and garlic, O Maheśānī, are remembered as substitutes for meat. (20)
Now follows the substitute for fish. In the absence of fish, burnt substances serve as the substitute in every age.
Even in the absence of the *mudrā*, O Supreme Goddess, roasted *kṣaṇaka* [grain] may be used. (21)
Thus is the secondary ritual for the mudrās. Now, the fifth secondary ritual, as stated in the Vṛhadyonitantra:
If a practitioner devoted to the Kula does not worship the Yoni,
the Goddess becomes angry with him, and his recitation and worship become fruitless.
O Maheśānī, in the absence of a physical vulva, the most excellent practitioner should worship Aparājitā in the form of a vulva in order to obtain the fruit of vulva-worship. 23.
The Goddess said:
"O God, it was previously stated that the Yoni bestows both worldly happiness and liberation upon everyone.
In its absence, O God, how can there be the Anukalpa and Aparājita?"
From what was this flower born, or by whom was it offered as worship?
Tell me, O Lord of Gods; by whom is sexual union [ordained], and tell me, O Master, the truth of this. (25)
In the Vṛhadyonitantra, the illustrious Śiva said:
"O Supreme Goddess, when Prakṛti established the Yoni within the tail of the peacock and became black, then Aparājitā was born."
(58) Having emerged from the tip of the flame, she was born upon the surface of the earth from the womb;
O Goddess, the mark of the womb remains there, consisting of the essence of the Kāmakalā. || 27 ||
Having reached the Viṣṇukrānta plant, Hara assumed the form of a creeper;
that flower, which is the very nature of the female organ (yoni), was supremely pleasing to the Goddess.
O Supreme Goddess, one who possesses the state of a hero (vīrabhāvī) should worship that flower anointed with red sandalwood; he shall obtain the fruit of the worship of the yoni.
O Pārvatī, O beautiful one, through the Śiva-liṅga situated within the interior of the Hayāripu flower,
sexual union occurs even in the absence of a physical power (śakti).
One should scatter fragrance upon another flower, and then cast that flower upon yet another;
having extracted the essential reality from that, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
If one performs libation upon one's own head and drinks [the nectar], one becomes a partaker of bliss;
the greatness of Aparājitā cannot indeed be described.
This flower, which consists of a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), is difficult for all the gods to obtain.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having established his own *liṅga* among the *karavīra* flowers, the Supreme Person became Mahādeva as Rādhikā for the sake of the bliss of erotic love. (33)
O Maheśvarī, whatever is the characteristic of Prakṛti in the peacock's tail,
having known this source of the self, Hari should bear it upon his own head.
In the Viśvasāra:
"As a substitute for semen and blood;
O Maheśānī, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with semen and blood."
And in the absence of those, one should perform with substitutes for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal of the practitioner. || 35 ||
O Dear One, in the absence of blood, red unguent is the substitute;
and in the absence of semen, fragrant sandalwood from Malaya is the substitute.

O Maheśānī, what on this earth cannot be accomplished through the union of both the primary rite (*anukalpa*) and the secondary rite (*anukalpa*), which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life? (37)
O auspicious lady, by wearing this charming flower—a substitute for the Mahāpuṣpa—for a kalpa upon the forehead, one becomes equal to Śiva; of this there is no doubt. (38)
In the Rādhātantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, whether one follows the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Vaiṣṇava path, by applying a tilaka on the forehead with [this] flower, one becomes truly endowed with beauty. (39)
O Goddess! By means of the primary *tilaka* marks, one attains union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva;
and by means of secondary *tilaka* marks, O beautiful one, one attains similarity in form (*sārūpya*).
Now, the measurement for the *tilaka*:
Brahmā consists of the left line, Sadāśiva the right line, and Viṣṇu resides in the middle space; one must never smear that spot.
In the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
"The great Viṣṇu is formless, yet he assumes form moment by moment;
when he takes on a formed appearance, he is two-armed and holds a flute. (42)
In the Rādhātantra:
"Kuṇḍalinī is in the form of sound (nāda), and her abode is always at its root;
above that, she is in the form of the point (bindu), the primordial Tripurasundarī. (43)
One should apply even a mere drop of blood at the base of Kuṇḍalinī as a triple-layered tilaka.
O Maheśvarī, on the right, the left, and likewise in the middle of the tilaka,
Jāhnavī, Yamunādevī, and Vāgdevī are ever present.
A devotee of Śiva should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and a devotee of Śakti a circular mark, O Śivā;
a follower of Gaṇapati should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); this is also the characteristic of a spiritual aspirant (sādhaka).
In the *Jñānadvīpa*:
"O Goddess of gods, the practitioner should perform the ritual in this sequence: first by means of substitutes (*anukalpa*), and secondly by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (47)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Seventeenth Chapter: Now, the dimensions of the Yantra.
In the Varadā Tantra, the Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, by your grace I have heard the doctrine of Vibhāvasu;
now I desire to hear the excellent exposition on the Yantras.

Tell me, O Lord, of the machine for a beast that possesses both its own nature (*sabhāva*) and differentiated states (*vibhāva*), which is dear to a hero who likewise possesses both his own nature and differentiated states. (2)
Śrī Śiva said:
O Sovereign of the Gods, the gross form of the body is the machine of the bound soul (paśu);
it is an artificial machine created by itself, fashioned as a likeness of the Supreme Light.
Even for the hero Vibhāvasu, there is a *yantra* fashioned from flowers and other materials;
the *yantra* of the hero is to be known as the *yoni-yantra*, which has been revealed.
O Maheśānī, without a yantra there is no fitness for worship;
therefore, O Maheśānī, one should perform the ritual preparation of a yantra. (5)
O Dear One, two diagrams (yantra) should not be made, nor likewise two images (mūrti);
practitioners seeking the cause of accomplishment should not prepare two jars (ghaṭa).
In another tantra: "Even in a single worship, one should worship a single deity once;
a single yantra is to be envisioned, and in the case of two deities, there is dual worship. (7)
In the *Mātṛkābheda*:
"If the practitioner should construct a great yantra as a place of birth, he must never, out of delusion, fashion an image there. [g, ṅ: "out of delusion"]. Therefore...
However, this additional reading is seen in manuscript "ka": "If one should perform the *mūri*, one should not cause the *tantra* and *yantra* to be made. || 8 ||
But if, out of delusion, one should perform it, O beloved, one should sacrifice twice;
then the offering of the bali should be twofold, and likewise the worship.
One should recite the mantra twice as many times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) twice as much;
otherwise, the worship is fruitless and the offering of the bali-oblation is fruitless.
Since everything indeed becomes fruitless because of this [defect], one should therefore not cause the yantra to be made [in such a way]. || 10 ||
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, supreme bliss, bestower of knowledge and realization! O Master, tell me the names of the worship, the salutation, and the hymn of praise, as well as the name of the yantra.
Śrī Śiva said:
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the entire conceptualization is merely a machine;
out of affection for you, I shall speak of that which distinguishes the distinction.
(p. 62) Now follows the description of the various specialized yantras:
in a śālagrāma, in the mental yantra, in an image, in a jar, in water, in a book, in the Gaṅgā, in a Śiva-liṅga, and in a flower. (13)
Now, regarding the fruit of worship at the yantra:
one obtains a hundredfold merit at a Śālagrāma stone and a hundred-thousandfold merit at a Maṇi;
O fair-eyed one, the merit at a yantra is a hundred-thousandfold, and at an image it is likewise a hundred-thousandfold.
O beloved, there is one unit of merit in a water-pot and one unit of merit in the water;
however, in a manuscript it is a thousandfold, and the fruit is equal to that at the Ganges.
O Maheśānī, by worshipping in a stone liṅga, or even without a stone liṅga, or in a flower-yantra, one indeed attains infinite [merit] and possesses all siddhis. (16)

O Maheśānī, one should not draw the supreme yantra upon a śālagrāma stone during worship; when the mantra is present, one should not draw the supreme yantra; and during the worship of Pramā, one should not draw the supreme yantra. || 17 ||
In another tantra it is said:
"O auspicious one, once a *likhya* yantra has been made, one should not fashion another yantra;
O Great Goddess, once a yantra has been made, one should not fashion a *likhya* yantra. (18)
The place of birth is the great yantra, which distinguishes the various forms of the deity;
even in a single worship there is a single yantra, and even in a yantra, single-worship is auspicious.
In the *Jñānadvīpa*,
the venerable Goddess said:
"One should then worship the great yantra, which is the support of worship, as well as the retinue."
O Maheśāna, in the absence of the yantra, from where could one worship the retinue?
The illustrious Śiva said:
Having carefully placed a water-pot before the image, one should worship the attendants there in that pot, O Supreme Goddess. (21)
One should worship the presiding deities of the machine at the mouth of the jar;
one should conceive of the jar as the embodiment of all the deities.
One should contemplate this jar as being of the very nature of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (suradruma). || 22 ||
In the Kulārṇava:
"One should arrange only the mere vessel among the reflected images;
one should place a leaf, a flower, a fruit, dūrvā grass, and a vessel filled with water. (23)
In the *Varadātantra*:
"O Goddess, whenever one prepares a jar for the sake of auspiciousness, worship must not be performed there without the ritual construction of a yantra. (24)
Now, the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and its substitute (*anukalpa*).
In the *Nigamānanda*, the venerable Goddess said:
"When the direct perception is established in the yantra, one should not employ a substitute."
When the secondary ritual procedure (anukalpa) is established, one may even perform it as a direct perception within the yantra.
Where one is personally capable of performing an action, there is no conceptualization of another agent;
likewise, even when a machine is visibly present, one should abandon the notion of a [separate] doer.

If the secondary alternative (anukalpa) exists, one should employ the secondary alternative; if it does not exist anywhere, one should not employ the primary alternative (pratyakṣa) when the primary alternative is present. || 27 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśvarī, tell me of the direct form and the secondary form;
O Dear One, who else but you could speak of this eternal Vidyā consisting of the primordial seed-syllables?
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Mahādeva! Having realized that supreme substance in which delusive knowledge arises regarding material objects, one should perform the ritual substitution for that substance. (29)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa*, composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Eighteenth Chapter:
Now, the Śākta Conduct.
In the Niruttara:
One who is endowed with power (śakti) should be devoted to the worship of Śakti;
O Goddess, without the goddess Śakti, one should not contemplate any other deity.
One should worship Śakti with the fifth [tattva] and perform the worship with the five principles (pañcatattva).
This is to be known as the Śākta conduct (śāktācāra), which is esteemed above all other modes of conduct. || 2 ||
O Goddess, without the practice of Śākta, any other practice is like a corpse;
therefore, O Supreme Mistress, the practice of Śākta is indeed the seed.
(95) You are liberated from the bond of desire (or: the bond of karma), yet you bestow bondage upon the one who is already liberated.
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, the practice of Śakti (śāktācāra) is indeed the seed. || 4 ||
Having diligently abandoned the company of one who reviles the Śākta conduct, one should perform the Kula rites according to the very path taught by me. (5)
Now, regarding the abandonment of association:
O beloved, one should always avoid association with physicians, Brahmins who cause estrangement, women who cause separation, and astrologers.
One should always avoid the company of a rogue who is a lecher,
as well as the company of cattle, of heroes whose minds are deluded,
and of lustful men. (7)

Truly, truly, and again truly, one should avoid association with those who behave according to their own whims, with those who are slanderous, with those devoid of devotion to the Guru, and with those who harbor hatred toward the Śakti.
[This half-verse is found in the Cha and Ja manuscripts, but not elsewhere. "One should perform the rites of the *kula* by the very path taught by me;
having abandoned association with the *paśu*, one should resort to association with the *vīra*."
And the Śākta, O Goddess, is of two kinds, distinguished by the divisions of Vāma and Dakṣiṇa.
Now, the characteristics of the Right-hand Śākta practice (*dakṣiṇācāra-śākta-lakṣaṇa*). In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"Being devoted to one's own duty, one should perform worship with the five principles (*pañcatattva*)."
That very one, following the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra), having become Śiva, should worship the Supreme.
(p. 66) Now, the definition of one’s own duty (*svadharma*).
In the *Bhairavatantra*:
"O Maheśvarī, whatever conduct belongs to whichever caste..."
One should understand that as one's own duty (svadharma), which is proclaimed and declared in the Śruti.
In the *Niruttara*:
"For all twice-born castes, the ritual procedure here is said to be twofold: the *pāśava* rite by day, and the *kīlika* rite by night. (12)
Rituals such as the *puraścaryā* are of two kinds, distinguished by their underlying disposition (*bhāva*).
One should always perform worship at night, and during the day one should perform that which is Vedic.
One should worship the Goddess both by day and by night, so that it may yield the results as described.
Worship performed at night in a secluded, auspicious place yields a hundred thousandfold merit.
Worship during the day yields a hundredfold merit, at night a thousandfold, and at midnight it is multiplied a hundred-thousandfold; one should perform the worship while maintaining secrecy.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"Worship during the day is indeed for the bound souls (paśus), while worship at night is for the heroes (vīras).
One should worship at midnight with the fifth [tattva] or with the five principles (pañcatattva). (17)
Now, the characteristics of a hero (vīra):
O Dear One, liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—this is declared to be the conduct of a hero, the very seed of the practitioner. 18.
Having worshipped oneself as the deity Śiva by means of the five principles (pañcatattva), one should be united with the fifth bliss and intent upon the five principles. (19)
One should worship the Mother of the World with the fivefold reality on the fifth [tithi];
this is declared to be the Vīrācāra, the seed-syllable for the practitioner as well. (20)
Now, regarding the concealment of the conduct of heroes: in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi it is said—
"One should worship the Goddess during the daytime in accordance with the ways of worldly conduct."
O Goddess, without following worldly conduct, secrecy cannot be maintained;
through secrecy, the accomplishment of the task occurs, and through disclosure, it becomes a giver of success. (21)
In the Haṃsamāheśvara:
"From manifestation there would be a loss of accomplishment, and from manifestation there is poverty.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, one should never cause manifestation. (22)
O Pārvatī, it should be guarded with great effort like one's own private parts; one should conceal it from the sight of the uninitiated (paśu), but one should never conceal it before a hero (vīra).
In the Kulārṇava:
"Having made the secret manifest, the practitioners move about."
From public disclosure there would be a loss of accomplishment; from secrecy, accomplishment follows without a doubt. || 24 ||
One must never conceal [this] among one's own practitioners;
for even if it is kept secret, there would be a loss of accomplishment, whereas through its disclosure, one becomes possessed of accomplishment. || 25 ||
O Śivā, this bestows the fruit of even divine heroes through secrecy;
O Goddess, by failing to keep it secret from the foremost of heroes, one goes to the Raurava hell. (26)
By keeping it secret from the uninitiated (paśu), the practitioner attains success;
by keeping it secret from the heroes (vīra), everything becomes fruitless—of this there is no doubt. (27)
One should not do so in the abode of a paśu, nor within the range of a paśu’s vision;
nor even in the presence of a paśu, nor should one show it to a paśu at all. 28.
If the materials for worship or the substances for drink are gazed upon by a sacrificial animal (paśu),
those materials should be cast into water, and one should recite the great mantra of the Goddess. —
As stated in the Jñānārṇava:
One should not offer a substance that has been looked upon by a *paśu* to the Goddess.
The worship of the Kula, the Kula substances, and union with a Kula woman must be kept secret; if revealed before a *paśu*, death shall ensue. (30)
The Goddess said:
"It must be guarded, guarded, guarded with great effort!
O Lord, in what form does the characteristic of a bound soul (paśu) or a hero (vīra) appear?"
"O Lord, reveal the characteristics of these two in my place;
O Lord, this is what I request from you, if you have favor toward me. (32)
Now, the characteristics of the animal-hero (paśuvīra):
Śrī Śiva said—animals are said to be of five kinds; hear this classification of them, O Dear One.
O Śivā, [one should avoid] a rogue, a deceitful person, a lecher, a chatterer, and a hypocrite.
These are declared to be the sacrificial animals, O beloved one; I shall likewise explain that by which one does not become engaged in other practices, nor performs other practices, O fair-faced one.
One who has fallen from either the Vedic or the Tantric path is certainly cooked in hell;
or rather, he who has fallen from the [proper] drinking [of the sacramental substances] possesses the characteristics of a mere beast (paśu).
By the mere knowledge of these [truths], the ritual action of the Kaulika reaches its consummation. (35)
In another Tantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, he who acts according to his own whims, transgressing the injunctions of the scripture, is a bound soul (paśu) and is certainly cooked in hell. (36)
In the Kumārī Tantra:
"O Śivā, the practice of the Kula rites must never be performed in the presence of the bound souls (paśus), just as the recitation of the Vedas is not for a Śūdra. (37)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Nineteenth Chapter.
Now, the characteristics of the practitioner (sādhaka).
In the Kulārṇava, the Goddess said:
O Śiva, what is the characteristic of the state of a hero, or what is its conduct?
Having been made known, O Supreme Bliss, reveal it in my presence. (1)
One may also know the characteristics of the practitioner by means of drinking liquor;
that drinking is said to be threefold, according to the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu). (2)
The divine [drinking] is from the goddess; the fierce [drinking] is from the drink; the heroic [drinking] is after the dismissal [of the deities], [provided it is accompanied by the mudrās].
Even by one's own will, drinking [the wine] is declared to be the "drinking" of the bound soul (paśu). || 3 ||

Listen now to the fruit of drinking [the wine]: it bestows devotion and liberation, it is divine, heroic, and endowed with devotion; it is the drinker of the Lord (Paśupāna) and the destroyer of hell. || 4 ||

O Mistress of the Kula, even if one possesses divine status or heroic character, and even at the cost of one's life, the drinking of wine by a *paśu* is forbidden; however, one who is devoted to the Śakti may drink.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, reveal to me the drinking of one’s own desire in my own abode;
or by what form, O Deva, does a man become a partaker of the drink in the presence of the Goddess?
Śrī Mahādeva said:
One should practice drinking when the wheel is broken; this is proclaimed as "drinking by one's own will" (svecchā-pāna).
That "will" is to be known as twofold, according to the distinction between the ignorant and the wise.
The ignorant person drinks intoxicating liquor for his own pleasure;
even the wise, having formed a circle (cakra), may drink wine, for the circle is indeed joined with power (śakti).
Now, regarding the characteristics of the *cakra*:
the venerable Goddess said:
"Reveal to me, in my presence, some of the characteristics of the *cakra*."
O Lord of the Mistress of Life, tell me what is the fruit for the sake of attaining perfection. || 9 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Dear One, for one who partakes of wine within the Śrīcakra, what on this earth is not accomplished?
Longevity, strength, wealth, fame, prosperity, and the mastery of the six rites—[all these are attained]. O Beloved!
And the accomplishment of the six rites; [also the accomplishment] of the six rites. || 10 ||
One obtains liberation, wealth, as well as nourishment from the Śrīcakra; moreover, through enjoyment one attains liberation and accomplishment by means of serving the Śrīcakra. (11)
O Great Goddess, whoever recites the root mantra within the center of the wheel obtains the fruit of reciting it a hundred thousand times by reciting it just once.

O Maheśvarī, the enjoyment of what is to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk should be performed within the Cakra; it is said to yield infinite fruit. O Śivā, the Cakra is declared to be of two kinds: the Divine (divya) and the Heroic (vīra).
Now, the measurement of the divine wheel:
The divine wheel is joined with the Goddess and is free from fear and shame;
through seeing it, there is the accomplishment of desire, and through touching it, one becomes a hero. 14
And from such service, liberation arises according to the established doctrine and conduct;
this has been declared as the Divine Wheel (Divya-cakra). Now hear of the Heroic Wheel (Vīra-cakra). || 15 ||
The wheel resides within the body of Śakti; without Śakti, there is no possessor of the wheel.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should drink the honey while united with Śakti.
In the *Nigamakalpa*, the illustrious Mahādeva said:
One should worship the divine power (*divya-śakti*) within the divine circle (*divya-cakra*) through amorous play;
or one may delight the power in the hero-circle (*vīra-cakra*) even with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
This divine wheel, which is liberated from passion and hatred and exists solely for the sake of one's own self, has been proclaimed; now hear of the Vīracakra.
O Pārvatī, one should worship one's own chosen deity there with the fivefold principle (pañcatattva);
the fifth [wheel] is that wheel proclaimed by the heroes (vīra) through the fivefold principle.
In the *Kulārṇava*:
"Where there is enjoyment, there is no liberation."
Where there is liberation but no enjoyment, [there is no fulfillment];
but for those who worship the pair of feet of Śiva, both enjoyment and liberation are held right in the palm of their hand. (20)
There is no twice-born man whatsoever who drinks liquor, nor would any Brahmin who has been so described ever drink it;
for those who worship the pair of lotus-feet of Śiva—
Through enjoyment and intoxication, liberation is held in the palm of one's hand. || 21 ||
O Goddess, he who is not of the path of duality is a Śākta; for one who is Śākta, there is no duality anywhere.
[This applies] to those who worship the pair of lotus-feet of Śiva.
For even in the case of difference, non-difference is indeed established as being within the palm of one's hand.
If the Śākta is endowed with the five [powers] and possesses knowledge in the fifth,
then, O Great Goddess, he may drink wine and delight in a woman within the Cakra.
O Maheśvarī, one should drink wine accompanied by a Śakti even within the Śrīcakra; for the knowledge of the Śakti is most excellent and is the first sprout of Nirvāṇa.
Now, the characteristics of the *vīracakra*:
In the *Kukkuṭatantra*— the *vīracakra* is to be known as threefold, and fourfold when including the *paśu*.
It should be known as superior, middling, inferior, and even the most inferior of the inferior. || 25 ||
O Goddess, where there is but one Śakti and only one practitioner, this should be known as the Cakrodaya; she is Kālī and he is Śaṅkara. || 26 ||
This reading is seen in the two manuscripts, but not elsewhere] "Listen, O wise one, to the Path of Accomplishment (Siddhivartman), by practicing which one shall attain perfection."
Having brought forth a single power, each practitioner should always [do so]. (27)

The Kaulika should worship with great effort by means of the five principles (pañcatattva). By doing so, he shall attain accomplishment (siddhi), which does not fall within the range of vision of anyone else. 28.
O Goddess, when the one belonging to the three powers resides there, and the triple practitioner is present,
that should be known as the middle wheel; he is the Hero and she is Bhairavī.
O Dear One, that wheel in which there are six practitioners and six powers abides is to be known as the lowest wheel; she is the one to be accomplished (sādhya), and he is the practitioner (sādhaka).
O Śivā, this wheel of the animal (paśu) which is distinct from this [divine wheel] is censured and devoid of power;
for a wheel that lacks power is merely intoxication.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "The practitioner should place the Śakti as calculated by the [number of] Sādhakas within the Great Wheel;
nine Śaktis in the middle [wheel], and even in the lowest [wheel], at least one Śakti. (32)
O Maheśvarī, when a circle is devoid of power— that is, a circle of bound souls (paśu)—
the practitioner should never enter that circle at any time.
One should not practice intoxicants, meat, and sexual intercourse within the Śrīcakra;
however, O auspicious one, by practicing sexual intercourse within the Śrīcakra, the adept attains the state of Śiva. (34)
And because of delighting within the circle (cakra), O Maheśvarī, the practitioner became [successful];
this is called the Vīracakra; now hear of the Devacakra from that. 35.
74) Now, the characteristics of the circle of the goddesses (*devacakralakṣaṇa*):
O Śivā, [the offerings are] drink, wine, the flesh of the body, and fish born in water.
O Supreme Goddess, the *mudrā* as well as other substances, their union consisting of the five elements, and the Great Wheel in the form of emanation— this is the Śrīcakra.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twenty-first Chapter: Now, the description of the locations of the Śrīcakra.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from disturbances,
one should practice the *cakra* in that location where there is a temple of the deity.
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, one should diligently prepare a place at sacred fords and other such sites, or at the roots of trees dedicated to the deities, in the stead of the deity itself.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O auspicious lady, the abode of Śakti, one's own home, a brothel, and the house of a practitioner—these are the supreme locations for the Śrīcakra. (3)
Having understood the position of the Guru and his command, one should arrange the place;
or else, one should arrange it according to the command of whichever [deity] occupies that place. || 4 ||
If there should be agitation where the wheel moves by whose command,
whatever sin belongs to that agitation, that sin goes to him.
(p. 75) Now, the measurement of the seat of the Śrīcakra.
In the Jñānārṇava:
O Goddess, one should not perform the rite of the hero (vīrakārya) without the corpse-seat (śavāsana);
entering the house of creepers is to be known as superior even to the corpse-seat.
O Maheśānī, in the absence of a corpse, one should imagine a seat; O Maheśānī, in the absence of a vulva, a triangle is an auspicious seat.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"O Goddess, one should not perform the rite of the Hero (*vīrakārya*) without a corpse-seat (*śavāsana*).
In the absence of a corpse, a seat of grass (*viṣṭara*) is indeed declared to be the Hero’s Seat (*vīrāsana*). (8)
O Maheśvarī, when joined with Śakti, one should perform the rite of Śakti upon a corpse-seat;
O auspicious lady, a single corpse is the seat, while a pair is the spread-mat seat.
One should not make a pair of corpses, even if one exists as a pair; for this very reason, O Maheśānī, the seat is conceived as a pair.
Another seat is conceived as either four-cornered or triangular.
In another tantra: "For the sake of desired objects, one uses a blanket; for liberation, a red blanket.
On black antelope skin there is the attainment of knowledge, and on tiger skin, liberation. (11)
Success in mantra comes from sitting on a seat of *kuśa* grass; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Any other seat, however, should be provided with various beautiful coverings and the like.

O auspicious lady, a beautiful triangular seat made of red cloth, joined with various colors and thus variegated, is indeed most pleasing; having firmly established there a seat fashioned according to one's capacity, one should sit upon it.
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"In a secluded, solitary, and delightful place, free from disturbances..."
On a praiseworthy seat, whether red, variegated, or captivating to the mind. || 14 ||
Seated comfortably on an easy seat, facing either the east or the north,
one should assume the vīrāsana posture for the sake of satisfying the deities, O Śivā.

The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is prescribed for the heroes of the Right (Dakṣiṇa), while the posture of one's own choice (svecchāsana) is prescribed for the divine adepts of the Left (Vāma) tradition. || 16 ||

In the unsurpassed [tradition], O Dear One, what rule or even what prohibition is there for the Kaulas? For those of the Vāma, Siddhānta, and Divya [paths], no restrictive regulation has been conceived.
One should prepare a seat for others and, having performed purification, sit down in a secluded, solitary, and pleasant place that is free from disturbances. (18)
O Śivā, having established the seat there, one should accomplish the rite with the mantra;
O lady of excellent hips, one should draw a triangle on the seat with blood.
The seat is indeed four-cornered, while the triangular yoni-maṇḍala is the earth-circle seat; it should be known [to be honored] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth. || 20 ||
One should worship Ādhāraśakti, or else Kamalāsana;
O Śivā, one should worship Ādhāraśakti and [the seat] ending with the lotus in three ways.
In the *Nigamakalpalatā*, the venerable Śiva said:
"The supreme mantra of pure meaning has been revealed in many ways; yet, even in ten million lifetimes, it is not possible to fully comprehend that mantra. (22)
The Śrī Devī said:
O Maheśāna, without *bhāva* (sentiment/intention), nothing at all is manifested.
Even if it is exposed, the source (yoni) remains pure through the cleansing of that source;
O beloved, the seat upon the Śrīcakra should be neither too low nor too high.
Now follows the rule for the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara).
In the *Yāmala*: "One who is endowed with worship and consecration, and who knows the true reality of the meaning of the Kula scriptures..."
Even one who is devoted to the deity and the guru, endowed with power, and engaged in ritual action; || 24 ||
With his mouth filled with betel, fragrant with the scent of incense, and well-adorned with red unguents, perfumes, and fine garments, the Guru [appeared]. (25)
In the Jñānārṇava:
"Wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, smeared with white sandalwood paste, joined with red sandalwood, and adorned with red flowers. (26)
Even in the absence of Brāhmaṇas, a Kṣatriya may be the preceptor;
in his absence, a Vaiśya may be so, but a Śūdra shall never be one under any circumstances. (27)

Even a Śūdra may become an Ācārya if he has received the consecration (abhiṣeka), O Dear One; for other consecrations consist of the form of the deity. If the drinking from their hand takes place, O Dear One, that constitutes the consecration.
Now, the characteristics of entering into the center of the wheel are described in the *Gautamīya*:
"The Lord of the Wheel, being of heroic nature and accompanied by his consort, should prostrate himself upon the ground."
Having placed a vessel of liquor in his hand, he should cause him to sit upon a seat. || 29 ||
Having assumed the vīrāsana posture, the mantra-practitioner should gather the materials for worship [on a seat] that is neither too low nor too high, situated at a height of four finger-breadths.
There, on that seat, the mantra-practitioner should dwell, intent upon the meditation of the deity. (30)
Having held— and meditated upon— wine endowed with the qualities of heat and sharpness, free from foul odor,
and having first prostrated, one enters into the Śrīcakras.
In the left hand [he holds] a beautiful woman, and in the right, a vessel of wine;
the drinking-cup is in the hand of the Śakti, and there is entry into the Śrīcakras.
In whatever form the Lord of the Wheel causes [the disciple] to enter the center of the wheel,
in that same form the practitioner should cause everyone to enter the center of the wheel.
O beautiful-eyed one, holding the articles of worship and the drinking substances in her hands,
she holds the vessel for drinking in the hand of the Śakti, while the Śakti herself is held in her left [hand].

Regarding the reality of the *nigama*: O Supreme Lord, if the Śakti, joined with Vīrānanda, becomes the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), then that wheel is undoubtedly the Wheel of the Deity. (35)
In her left hand she holds a vessel of wine, and in her right, the supreme bliss of Śiva;
having entered the Śrīcakras, she is free from fear and shame. (36)
O Supreme Lord, one need not perform the purification of substances within that wheel;
for by the mere touch of it, the purification of substances occurs at that very moment.
O Great Lord, one should contemplate the *liṅga* within the *bhaga* of each vessel;
having taken a drop from the vessel, one should cast it into the circle of the womb (*yonimaṇḍala*). 38.
If Cakreśvarī, greatly delighted, reveals her vulva, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps for that specific purpose. || 39 ||
And then one should engage in dalliance, if she is possessed of passion;
at the end of the dalliance, O Great Lord, one should joyfully drink from the vulva. (40)
In its absence, water should be drunk together with the *kāra* and the *bindu*;
the water should be known as the *śakti-yantra*, since it awakens one from *māyā*. (41)
If that water is stained with blood, and if it is stained with semen, it possesses the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).
The water from the womb should be known as Brahmā, and Janārdana is its [the womb's] seed.
Mahādeva is her semen; in the absence of these, there is a substitute (*anukalpana*).
Kuśida, Bhagarakta, Śukra, and Malayodbhava, along with the water known as Bhagavārī— these, when combined with the three qualities (guṇas), constitute the three deities.
O Lord, if by good fortune one should obtain the Cakreśvarī within the Cakra, then that body, my body, and the body of the male [Sadāśiva] are all Śiva. 44.
O Maheśvara, the Śakti who resides in that wheel is my own form;
even though the practitioner is equal to you, he is within the beautiful circle of deities.
O Great Lord, in any other assembly, many obstacles arise;
in the Kali age, it is the assembly of the gods, the assembly of the gods, the assembly of the gods [that prevails]. (46)
The greatness of the divine wheel cannot be fully described;
there, singing, drinking, and sexual union are enjoyed at will according to one's pleasure. (47)
The great task of recitation and all else arises from the pleasure of one's own will;
for this very reason, O Maheśāna, the circle of deities [is established] in the Kali age. 48.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twenty-First Chapter:
Now, the non-differentiation of castes within the Śrīcakra.
In the Tārātantra:
At the beginning, in the Bhairavī-cakra, all castes were the best of the twice-born;
when the Bhairava-cakra had ceased, all castes became distinct from one another.
That deluded soul who creates distinctions of caste even within the Śrīcakra falls undoubtedly into a terrible and most difficult hell. || 2 ||
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra]:
"The deluded soul who creates distinctions of caste within the center of the Cakra shall be destroyed by the wrath of Caṇḍī; his luster, nourishment, strength, and fame will perish. (3)
One should not observe distinctions of caste regarding wine and sexual intercourse;
for wine and [the act of] sex, O beautiful one, are the seed of great bliss.
O Maheśvarī, what is the use of saying more? Within the center of the wheel, O beloved, all men are my form and all women are your form.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Just as many cows remain bound by a single rope, so too do men remain bound by the fetter of caste. (6)
Having severed the bond of caste through the sword of wine and by the word of Śakti,
one should drink wine even in the Śrīcakra, abandoning all distinctions of caste.
The Śrī Devī said:
"Jāti alone is subtle consciousness (sūkṣmabodha), while that which belongs to the genus (jātīya) is gross consciousness (sthūlabodha).
By what is the subtle destroyed, or by what does its manifestation occur once again? (8)
p. 81) Śrī Śiva said:
The entire universe is the Śrīcakra, which is manifested within his consciousness.
If there were no decrease or increase when Ramā was born, she would be like the Lord of the Night (the Moon). || 9 ||
In the wheel joined with the power of wine, there is decrease and increase moment by moment;
through the decrease and increase of the wheel, there is the decrease and increase of birth.
O Śivā, for a man bound by the fetters of caste, another's wife is like a mother;
O Śivā, for one fallen from his caste, even his own beloved wife is but a common courtesan.
O Maheśānī, one who drinks liquor should abandon his mistress and worship only his supreme mother; he should not engage in sexual union with her. 12.
Any other woman who is like a mother is the supreme beloved in the Śrīcakra;
one should worship and take pleasure in that Śakti, and she too [will do so] out of joy.
When caste has been destroyed, where will there be any fault for him?
O Supreme Goddess, one should cast off the bond of caste within the Śrīcakra.
O Great Goddess, if one who has taken refuge in the Wheel of the Cakra resorts to the fetter of caste, his drinking becomes in vain and serves only to destroy his caste-status. (15)
Now follows the description of the substances for the Śrīcakra.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"O Dear One, the cause [consists of] meat, milk-rice, curd, milk, and ghee."
O beloved, having carefully set out meat, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and rice accompanied by various side dishes; || 16 ||
O blessed one, O beloved, [he brought] oil-cake, garlic, sugar, honey, flour-paste, various foods, special delicacies, and diverse messengers' gifts. 17.
O Goddess, for the sake of satisfying the deity, one should place fish, meat, parched grain, and captivating heroic substances within the Śrīcakra. (18)
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*: "O auspicious one, O beloved, one should place saffron, pure vermilion, sandalwood, *rocanā*, *aguru*, camphor, and barley-meal upon the *śrīcakra*."
With various fragrant incenses, one should create a delightful aroma;
then, one should apply the incense leaves upon the Śrīcakra. || 20 ||
Chewable food, food to be sucked, as well as food to be licked and drunk, beautifully presented in bronze vessels—excellent rice-pudding, buttermilk, and fragrant water, O beloved. (21)
In the Vīra Tantra:
"O Dear One, one should set out many side dishes—pungent, sour, and bitter—as well as various meats seasoned with ghee. (22)
O Dear One, one should place the haṃsa-seed, milk, salt, oil-cake, garlic,
and ginger in the center of the Śrīcakra.
In the *Kālikākulasarvasva*:
"One should employ dried ginger, burnt fish, the powder of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), parched grain, and flattened rice within the *Śrīcakra*. (24)
Now, the placement of substances within the Śrīcakra:
having arranged various substances in the form of rows,
the supreme purified substance is placed in bronze vessels.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place it in the center of the wheel in the form of a row.
In the *Kulatattvasāra*:
"O Maheśvarī, the substance situated in a bell-metal vessel is to be eaten."
Having purified everything according to the prescribed rule, one should arrange it in the form of a row.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twenty-Second Chapter: Now, the Rule for the Śrīpātra.
In the Kālīkalpa:
O Dear One, for rites of subjugation and attraction, one should use a well-adorned golden vessel;
for rites of pacification and nourishment, one should cause a silver vessel to be used.
O Śivā, one should know that an iron vessel is used for the rites of killing and driving away;
O Mistress of the Kula, the Viśvāmitra [mantra] should be employed in all ritual activities.
A copper vessel, a bell-metal vessel, a vessel made of brass, a bilva-wood vessel, and a large vessel are all recommended for every ritual purpose.
Depending on the specific nature of the rite, one should employ different vessels; however, when there is no distinction in the rite, a single stationary vessel may be used.
The vessel established in non-duality. || 3 ||
Now, the characteristics of the installation of the Śrīpātra:
In the Tārā-tantra—
thereafter, one should draw a triangular mandala on the ground and then a quadrangular one.
Having established the support there, one should then place the Śrīpātra.
(p. 84) Now, the characteristics of the Śrīpātra support (dhāraka):
it is said to be of four kinds—the three-legged and the four-legged.
O Maheśānī, the six-petaled [lotus] and the eight-petaled [lotus] are proclaimed;
O Dear One, one should fashion the mandala according to the number of its parts and its corners.
Now follows the exposition of the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
In the *Nirvāṇatantra*, the Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Great God, O bestower of the principles, tell me the truth."
Now I desire to hear about the knowledge of reality; please explain that to me.
The illustrious Śiva said:
"If there is doubt in my mind regarding the narration of the knowledges of reality (tattvajñāna),"
By which grace of reality Viṣṇu, who is the refuge of the qualities of reality (or the quality of goodness), [is attained]. || 7 ||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak: Brahmā became the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), and through the grace of the knowledge of reality, Śambhu became the agent of dissolution.
And all others who are liberated, O Goddess, are so by the grace of Reality; for without the knowledge of Reality, liberation leads only to ridicule.
Without the knowledge of reality, O blessed lady, it is fruitless; there is no doubt about this.
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall proclaim the truth that is most difficult to attain. (10)
O Pārvatī, O Śivā, having heard this, one should carefully guard [these things] as if they were one's own womb:
liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual intercourse. (11)
O Daughter of the Mountain, this fivefold reality is declared to be the first sprout of liberation;
supreme sovereignty is joyfully attained through the drinking of wine.
By the mere eating of meat, a man shall become Nārāyaṇa himself;
by the mere eating of fish, Kālī becomes manifest before one’s eyes. (13)
Merely by practicing with the mudrā, one who assumes the form of Viṣṇu becomes worthy of worship by kings;
through sexual union, the great yogi becomes equal to me—of this there is no doubt.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the venerable Goddess said:
"By the first yoga alone, the practitioner becomes Bhairava;
and by the second reality (*tattva*), he attains the state of Mahābhairava. (15)
By the third principle, the practitioner assumes the form of Śiva;
by the fourth principle, he himself becomes the bearer of the form of Rudra; and by the supreme [principle], he attains supremacy—of this there is no doubt, for he becomes equal to you.
Now, the fruit of the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
In the *Nirvāṇatantra*, the Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me: by what means does that single principle become fivefold?"
What is its nature and its fruit; and how is it fivefold or even single?
Śrī Śiva said:
O Supreme Goddess, there is one single reality, yet it has five causes;
its effects are manifold, for indeed the cause itself possesses manifold forms.
The cause would become the effect, for the effect is indeed the cause;
just as iron is the cause of the weapon, the weapon is indeed the cause of the iron. || 19 ||
Thirst is the cause for water, and water is the cause for the thirsty one;
O Goddess, when there is a difference in the effect, one indeed conceives of a difference in the cause.

86) Wherever the five principles (pañcatattva) may meet in one place, there I go; those men are always equal to me.
[Those who always provide fish and meat. || 21 ||
O Goddess, those men who possess virtuous qualities and are devoted to the knowledge of reality are liberated while living; they are indeed Brāhmaṇas, and not otherwise.
Just as water dissolves into water, O Supreme Goddess,
even so, through the service of the principles (tattvas), one dissolves into the Supreme Self.
Thus, O beloved, I have told you this knowledge of reality which bestows liberation;
by the mere understanding of which, the attainment of liberation occurs without a doubt. (24)
O Maheśvarī, just as there is no stability without the earth, and just as there is no cause for the destruction of thirst without water; || 25 ||
Just as there is no dispeller of darkness without the sun, O beloved, and just as nothing is cooked without the application of fire, [so it is without this practice]. (26)
O Queen of the Gods, without the Moon, the rain of nectar does not arise;
O Beloved, without Mahodgara, birth indeed does not occur;
and likewise, O Goddess, without the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), liberation does not arise. (27)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twenty-third Chapter. In the *Kulārṇava*, the venerable Mahādevī said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of my life-breath, I bow at your lotus-feet."
Now I desire to hear the great definition of the primary reality.
87) Now, the definition of the primordial reality (ādyatattva).
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Supreme Goddess, that first reality is the seed-syllable (bīja) of all realities;
for without the seed-syllable, any other reality is like the east to one who is disoriented.
For this very reason, all the gods, for whom the cause was fashioned as if it were nectar,
fell into delusion when they attained enjoyment that was actually death.
That which is called the nectar (amṛta) in heaven is indeed the worldly liquor (surā);
and by attaining enjoyment through that liquor, the state of being a god (suratva) shall come to pass. || 4 ||

For this very reason, O Maheśānī, all the twice-born in every age are attached to wine; one should conceive of the seed of wine as the bliss of the tree [or, according to manuscripts gh and j, the bliss of Brahman].
O Śivā, the branch consists of dance and song; the leaf is mere speech;
the great power (Mahāśakti) is the form of the flower; and sexual union is the form of the fruit.
The emission of semen is the great seed; indeed, the mere act of creation is the cause.
If that substance, which has the nature of a tree, were endowed with power (śakti), [it would manifest]. (7)
In the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, through the drinking of wine, a Brahmin attains great liberation.
O Supreme Goddess, if a Brahmin should engage in drinking and so forth..."
At that very moment he became Śiva in form; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Priyambadā.
O Goddess, without the drinking of wine, the knowledge of reality is not obtained;
for this very reason, even a Brahmin should always practice the drinking of liquor.
O Daughter of the Mountain, a Brāhmaṇa is not such merely by the recitation of the Mother of the Vedas;
O Goddess, when one possesses the knowledge of Brahman, then he is called a Brāhmaṇa. (10)
Just as water is merged in water, or as that which is fiery is merged in the fiery;
just as when a jar is broken, the space within it is merged into the great space.
In that very same way, the Brahmin who eats at the proper time is absorbed into the Supreme Self.
In the Kulārṇava, the illustrious Mahādevī said: "O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, bestower of knowledge and ignorance!
O Sadāśiva, why has liquor—which is forbidden by the Veda—been spoken of [as permissible]? (12)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
The drinking of liquor is a great sin, as established in the Vedas and other scriptures;
therefore, those possessed of the power of action must renounce intoxicants in every age.
O Maheśvarī, those men who drink our flesh and blood, as well as wine,
without considering the dharma appropriate to their caste and stage of life,
become ghosts, spirits, and piśācas— brahmarākṣasas. (14)
The drinking of liquor is a great fault, as established in the Vedas and other scriptures;
nevertheless, a Brahmin partakes in liberation despite the drinking of liquor in age after age.
Indeed, it should neither be given nor drunk—this is the truth, the absolute truth, in age after age.
Nevertheless, all the brahmins were addicted to drinking liquor. || 16 ||
Now follows the rectification of the fault regarding the first reality.
In the *Jñānārṇava*, the venerable Śiva said:
"He who performs drinking in vain—that is called the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*)."
He is indeed a perpetrator of a great sin; such is the determination in the Vedas and other scriptures.
For this very reason, the lord of brahmins should never consume liquor in vain;
that drinking in vain is a great sin is the consensus of all the scriptures. (18)
Liquor is the cause of knowledge, yet liquor is the destroyer of knowledge; just as fire, though kindled by the wind, is extinguished by that same wind. (19)
If one should drink liquor for the sake of the deity, or if one should drink it for the sake of one's own bliss, that drinking is the causal drinking; any other is the consumption of poison.
By the very same piece of poison by which all living beings die,
the physician destroys the poison.
Wine is the cause of knowledge, and knowledge is the cause of liberation.
One who desires liberation may drink wine; anyone other than such a person becomes a sinner.
In the Haṃsamāheśvara [Tantra]:
"The water of the Gaṅgā is a cause, but liquor is the supreme cause;
if purified, it leads to heaven, but if unpurified, it bestows hell. (23)
O Supreme Goddess, at birth and other stages, drinking [the nectar] acquired through great merit is the cause for liberation; O Maheśvarī, it is also the cause for the sake of knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The twenty-fourth chapter.
In the *Kālikā-kalpa*:
"The Śrīcakra, joined with Ramanī, has been revealed by means of that cause."
If, in the absence of the cause, the Śrīcakra were not full of bliss anywhere at all; || 1 ||
The Śrīcakra devoid of a woman is [merely] a wheel;
it is joined with a woman when there is another substance in the Śrīcakra, according to the words of the Śakti. || 2 ||
In another tantra:
"Having known one's own home to be the Śrīcakra, one is oneself the Lord of the Cakra."
It may be so; having made a woman the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), one should perform the ritual activities. || 3 ||
O Pārvatī, what cannot be accomplished through the power of this knowledge?
For that reason, one should worship the Supreme Goddess even from her house;
however, if it is different from this, one should worship after performing purification for its cause.
Now, the explanation of the different substances. In the *Samayācāra-tantra*: "Substance (*dravya*) is said to be of three kinds, and meat (*māṃsa*) is also of three kinds."
O Śivā, it is proclaimed as being known as superior, middling, and inferior.
O Pārvatī, material originating from one’s own temple is indeed the best; that produced in the house of a liquor-distiller is proclaimed as middling;
and material arising from other castes is the lowest.
Thus it has been fully proclaimed.
The Śrī Devī said:
One should drink liquor for the sake of bliss—that bliss which bestows liberation. Tell me, by what [criteria] is it classified as superior, inferior, or middling? (7)
Śrī Śiva said:
There is no fault in Time at all; one who is liberated from action incurs no fault.
Likewise, there is no fault in the cause; the fault arises from that which is to be done.
The vaginal opening is the receptacle for semen, arising from the pleasure of the man;
O Śivā, as there is a defect when semen is emitted, so it is with the cause.
O Maheśvarī, for one who possesses the power of Śakti, there is no fault in drinking;
however, due to the difference in the practitioner’s actions, both [the drinker and the giver] become partakers of the fault. (10)
O Supreme Goddess, although water bestows all joy and is equally [beneficial] to all,
nevertheless, in the body of a sick person, that very water becomes a giver of suffering.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, liquor brings suffering even to an ignorant embodied being; yet it also bestows sālokya, sārūpya, and sāyujya. (12)
O Goddess, from the service of the lowest [liquor] comes a middling fruit, and from the service of the highest, the supreme fruit;
as for the claim that there is fault in liquors when one possesses power, that is merely the word of the ignorant. (13)
Therefore, all who possess knowledge may drink honey according to their own will;
for ignorance has action as its root, while action has purity as its root.

Purified wine that is delightful and bestows the fruits of the three aims of life may be drunk even at one's own will; such a knower shall partake in liberation. Furthermore, wine conjoined with Śakti bestows absolute isolation (kaivalya). || 15 ||
In the Tārā Tantra:
"The one who partakes of power (śakti) is attached to sexual union; the one who partakes of knowledge (jñāna) desires liberation;
the one who partakes of knowledge is attached to the causal [means]. Therefore, one should drink wine with joy. (16)
Both types of liquor that arise from a womb, if unrefined, cause great sin;
yet if refined, those same two types of liquor destroy all sins.
And liquor is the cause of the womb, while the womb is the cause of liquor;
O Great Goddess, when the mind is pure,
everything is pure— even in the absence of purity, it is pure.
Even in the absence of purity, there is impurity. || 18 ||
If one drinks unrefined liquor or engages in sexual union with an unrefined woman, through such drinking one goes to hell, and from such union death shall result. (19)
In the *Tripurāsāra*, regarding the purification of the power (*śaktiśuddhi*):
"First one should perform the purification of the power, and thereafter the [purification of the] cause."
O Maheśānī, without Śakti, the cause is equal to death;
therefore, one should purify both the knowledge of Śakti and Śakti itself by means of the Cause (Kāraṇa).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"First one should perform the purification of Śakti, and immediately after that, the Cause (*kāraṇa*)."
Having given [the offering] to Śakti, one should drink the liquor and perform purification in the proper sequence.
First, one should practice the purification of Śakti, who empowers both the Paśu and the Sādhaka;
the purifier, moreover, should cause that Śakti to enter into the Śrīcakras.
Now, the definition of the power of the animal (paśu-śakti).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, the Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the Life-force, O Eternal One among all beings!"
And reveal to me which power of the bound soul (paśuśakti) has been proclaimed as residing in my own station. || 23 ||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
The power of a bound soul (paśu) is devoid of flowers, while that of a hero (vīra) is joined with flowers;
in the first case it is a woman in her menses, and in both cases the supreme [power] is worshipped.
With whatever disposition one should worship a woman in her first menses,
by that disposition the Śakti becomes permeated for the sake of the practitioner’s success. (25)
The Śaktis were created for the purpose of delight; delight is the characteristic of a hero.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, they are worshipped by heroes along with flowers. (26)
A flowerless [plant] is to be worshipped by the Paśu; a flowering one is to be worshipped by the Vīra.
Even a flowering one may be worshipped by the Paśu, if he so desires. || 27 ||
In worship, the power of purification is the consensus of all conduct (or, according to manuscript *g*, of all scriptures).
In the form of Śakti, she dwells in the house for the sake of sport within the Great Śakti. || 28 ||
When the passionate woman (kāminī) has been purified by the worship of that [deity], she is then satisfied; likewise,
if the wine and the Śakti are impure, one should purify them during that worship, O Śivā.
Now follows the purification of the power (*śakti*) for both the animal (*paśu*) and the hero (*vīra*).
One should never at any time transgress the unpurified mechanism of power;
having resorted to the purified womb (*yoni*), the hero may then enjoy [it] to the end. (30)
One should perform the purification of the sacrificial animals (paśus) with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
for the heroes (vīras), it should be performed with the five elements (pañcatattva) or with semen alone.
In the Nirvāṇatantra:
"Semen is the supreme purifier, the cause of liberation for Śakti.
Furthermore, that woman who is devoid of worship and devoid of japa [is likewise]. (32)
If one desires liberation, one must not entertain any doubt regarding that woman, for she herself is Kālikā, the consort of the practitioner. (33)
That woman who is endowed with devotion, having made the practitioner Śiva within the body of Kālikā, satisfies him through the reverse act, knowing the welfare of the practitioner. || 34 ||
In the *Nigamānanda*:
"Having omitted three days, on the sixteenth day, one should perform purification with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and thereafter engage in sexual union. (35)
O Lord, when one sees a flower, then one should worship it in its true essence;
one should worship the chosen deity with blood smeared with semen.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Twenty-fifth Chapter:
Now, the description of the defects of impure liquor. In the *Gautamīya*:
For wine that is unpurified is indeed the supreme cause of great sin;
that same wine, when purified, is the supreme destroyer of sin. (1)
O Supreme Goddess, that drinking which is performed without the prescribed rite is called "animal drinking" (paśupāna); such drinking yields nothing but suffering.
In the *Kulārṇava*, the Śrī Devī said:
"O beloved of my life, tell me what is the procedure for the drinking of wine?
The Śrī Śiva said:
Bound by my affection for you, I shall explain the procedure:
having purified it, one should drink the liquor with the intent of pleasing the deity. (3)
Now, the purification of liquor. In the *Kālikākulasarvasva*:
"Seated upon a pure seat, facing either east or north, the practitioner..."
Either in front [of him] or on the left side, there should be a square mandala.
There, one should place the water-pot with the aim of pleasing the deity;
on one's own left side, however, [one should draw] a hexagon containing a central bindu.
One should draw a square on the ground and worship it with fragrant flowers.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, beginning with Māyā and joined with the syllable *ṅe*, ending with *namaḥ*. (6)
The mantra, however, is:
Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.
There, having placed the water-pot (kumbha), O Śivā, one should worship it with the mantra:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ), followed by the word "ṄE" and "Vahnimaṇḍala," then giving the phrase "Daśakalā," and at the end, "Ātmane Namaḥ. (7)
The mantra is: *Oṃ raṃ* [or *maṃ*] *vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ*.
There, one should adorn the jar situated upon that support with red cloths.
The hero should worship the entire solar disc within the water-pot.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Om), and [the syllable] "Aṃ" for the solar orb,
one should give the word "dvādaśa" (twelve) and, at the end, "namas" to the self of the Kalās.
The mantra, however, is:
*Oṃ aṃ, salutation to the solar disc, whose self consists of twelve kalās*.
Then, one should likewise place the divine causal [liṅga] within the pitcher. || 10 ||
Wrapped in a red cloth and adorned with red flowers,
the practitioner of mantra, having mentally visualized the spheres of fire, sun, and moon within the mandala, the jar, and the ritual substances, should worship them with great effort. (11)
Now, regarding the measurement of the *kalaśa*:
in the *Toḍala-tantra*—
O auspicious lady, the mouth should be shaped like a womb (*yoni*), or circular and pleasing to the mind.
One should discard what is broken, cracked, shattered, or black in color.
Neither too short nor too long, made of gold or silver, O beloved.
It may be made of copper or even of earth, provided it is exclusively devoid of iron.
One should fill the jar with liquor while reciting the root mantra;
there, in the center, the hero should worship the entire lunar maṇḍala.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), and then "uṃ somamaṇḍalāya," one should give the word "ṣoḍaśa" and at the end, "namo 'kalātmane. (15)
The mantra is:
