(145) One should perform the drinking from the vessel after breath control (prāṇāyāma), and breath control immediately thereafter.
At the conclusion of that, one should engage in delight, accompanied by the recitation of the root mantra. || 19 ||
O Maheśvarī, this wheel joined with three vessels has been described;
O Pārvatī, now hear about the wheel joined with five vessels, known as Vandana.
The fourth salutation to the vessel:
Oṃ! Wine brings forth the essence of the Fish; it is served by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others;
it is intent upon the dharma of the ritual acts of mudrā and sexual union; it is the locus of the salty, sour, and bitter [tastes].
May the fourth vessel—purified by the flesh of Bhairava and the eight Siddhas of the Ācāryas, and accompanied by the reality of the five *makāras*—protect us; salutations! (21)
The fifth: the salutation to the vessel.
Upon the support, which is the circle of the earth encircled by the king of serpents, rests the vessel;
its wine is the water of the seven oceans and the flesh [of the world], and its eight [legs] are the elephants of the quarters.
Thus, worshipping Bhairava daily with hosts of stars for protection, and with the multitudes of gods and asuras headed by the Sun, acting as obedient servants and attendants; || 22 ||
Now, the salutation to the nine vessels (*navapātravandana*).
In the *Rudrayāmala*:
"O Dear One, the ninth [chapter] is called the 'Salutation to the Vessels' (*pātravandana*)."
Having performed this, the best of practitioners becomes equal to Śiva; of this there is no doubt. || 23 ||
It is drenched by the nectar of the moon shining from the crest of the glorious Bhairava, and it is fully revealed by the hosts of Kṣetrādhīśvara, Yoginīs, and Mahāsiddhas.
I always salute that vessel, the first of all worlds for their happiness, which is this ninefold ocean of bliss, the manifest nectar of the Three Sections (Trikhaṇḍa). 24.
It is the illuminator of the wonder of the multitude of arts that converge in all traditions;
it is served by Indra, Candra, Mahendra, and the moonbeams, as well as by Brahmā and the other gods.
Salutations to this second vessel, which always brings about the dissolution of that which has flowed forth from meditation itself, and which bestows the increase of virtue upon the worlds. 25.
Alcohol brings forth the essence of meat; it was practiced by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others;
it is auspicious through the ritual acts of *mudrā* and sexual union; it is the basis for the salty, sour, and bitter tastes;
and it is purified by the flesh of the eight perfected masters (*ācāryas*) and Bhairava.
May the third vessel, accompanied by the fivefold reality (pañcamakāratattva), protect [us]; obeisance! || 26 ||

One should always serve with the five offerings this Lord Viṣṇu, who bestows all happiness upon those of his own lineage among living beings, who is praised by Brahmā and the other gods, and who is united with Śiva and Śakti;
[offering] fish, goat, pigeon, excellent juices, and the vessel that is the Lord of All.
And that vessel, which bestows all merit and happiness, is the fourth vessel; salutations! (27)

This Yoga, which is the essence of all the traditions of logic, family lineages, and arts, spoken by the goddesses with their various faces, is the constant secret of the scriptures on the limbs of the Yoga and Bhoga families, endowed with hidden mysteries.

I worship the fivefold vessel [of the senses], which has drunk the essence of Brahman through the yoga of those Bhairavas—consisting of bliss, emergence, resonance, the drop, and the digit—and whose hands are ever-extended. 28.

Having worshipped the parasol, which resembles the seat of the *cāmara* and the *śakti*, one should always worship the *śakti*; on the left is the charming woman who brings pleasure, the source of curiosity and wonder.
I worship the sixth vessel: the delightful enjoyment of various pleasures and luxuries, attended by the damsels of desire, the gratification of beautiful women, and the liquid essence. 29.

Intent on contemplating the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, bestowing the witness-consciousness, possessing a luster like lightning, the sun, or a creeper, and pervaded by a digit of moonlight;

May she who dwells between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, who possesses three coils and resides within the *kuṇḍalinī*, protect me—she who is the vessel at the filling of the seventh, whose joy exceeds even the fear of worldly existence. (30)
The sword, the sandals, the unique collyrium, the pill of Sarasvatī, the oral transmission, the fierce averting of death, the remover of distress, and the delightful speech of the world—
And the bowl is the eighth, which always bestows the eight siddhis, being mature and serene.
[This is] the supreme Sadāśiva, whose singular essence is bliss; Nandikeśvara, the illuminator;
Sāmrāmbā, the bestower of happiness and the fulfiller of desires who destroys ignorance;
and that which increases longevity, luster, and fame, and removes the delusion of worldly existence.
The severance of delusion;
the vessel which, when joined with the power of the New Lord, bestows the accomplishment of all aims. || 32 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter of the Sarvollāsa, composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Thirty-Sixth Chapter.
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"Having taken up the divine cup, with a steady mind and composed, [one should proceed]."
No doubt should be entertained here; for if it is done, death will ensue. || 1 ||
Now, the rule for the drinking [of wine]. In the *Kulatattvasāra*:
"First, the vessel for the Śakti should be offered with the root mantra, or else with the *manunā*."
I shall now declare the great mantra being bestowed; listen, O beloved.
The mantra is as follows:
"O auspicious Goddess, this vessel of wine accompanied by meat is offered by me to you;
having accepted it, O Lady, grant me victory again and again. (3)
O Supreme Goddess, having brought the grace of power with effort,
one should drink it mixed with one's own vessel and the causal substance for the sake of bliss.
The vessel accompanied by the remnants of Śakti bestows absolute bliss;
the Great Goddess, whose form is Śakti, increases absolute bliss. || 5 ||
O Śivā, the Śakti who possesses a gross-bodied form is the sole recipient of liberation;
yet for the practitioner, she assumes a more radiant form within the bliss of ritual action.
Just as space, O Maheśānī, is the form of all forms,
so too is a woman the illuminator of every action for a man.
In the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
"The fivefold drink is proclaimed as being conjoined with the meditation on the Guru and so forth."
O Goddess, having first accepted the cause, one should subsequently accomplish the effects.
In the first [chapter], there is meditation on the Guru, followed by the description of Brahman;
in the third, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and in the fourth, one should perform the recitation (japa).
Having performed the fifth [rite] in the fifth [day], one should likewise practice the Ānanda [rite] in the sixth;
O Śivā, the characteristic of the Cakra is the fifth [element] together with the vessel.
Now follows the description of the ninth vessel:
meditation on the guru, breath control (prāṇāyāma), recitation of the mantra, circumambulation, prostration, hymn of praise, singing, and dancing.
O Supreme Goddess, one should practice sexual union as the tenth bliss.
Now, the meditation on the venerable Guru (Śrīgurudhyāna).
In the Viśvasāra:
"Brahman resides in the thousand-petaled lotus, accompanied by the male and female swans."
The sacred seat (pīṭha) consisting of Nāda and Bindu is revealed as a pair of swans.
One should meditate upon the Lord within the heart as Your own reflection, which illuminates like a pure lamp—two-armed and joined with Śakti. (13)
The authority for this is found in the *Gurugītā*:
"He whose divine form is seated upon a lion-throne, situated in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus..."
One should meditate upon the Guru, adorned with the crescent moon,
who bestows true consciousness, bliss, and the desired boons.
Clad in white garments and anointed with white unguents, his divine form was adorned with ornaments of pearls and gems.
Seated upon the lap of his left side is the divine Śakti;
he possesses a gentle smile and is a treasury of perfect compassion. || 15 ||
Blissful, the source of bliss, serene,
whose nature is knowledge and who is endowed with innate awakening— the Lord of Speech, worthy of praise, the physician for the disease of worldly existence.
I bow eternally to the glorious Guru. || 16 ||
In the *Gurutantro*: "Brahman resides in the thousand-petaled lotus; that very [Brahman] is called the Guru.
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, within the thousand-petaled lotus. (17)
Sometimes the Guru, who is always to be meditated upon through mantra, is within one's own thousand-spoked wheel;
sometimes he is in the lotus of the heart, and sometimes he is within the range of one's vision.
Even when [the Guru] is seen, one should not contemplate his form in the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra);
there is no contemplation in the heart; rather, one should contemplate within the reflections—within your own reflections—that knowledge is the object of contemplation. || 19 ||
In the *Haṃsamāheśvara*:
"The supreme Brahman is in the thousand-petaled [lotus]; its reflection is in the heart. Indeed, the original object of that reflection is that which illuminates the human body. (20)
Just as a form of fire, O Goddess, is more intense than the fire itself yet appears as a mere gross object,
so too the supreme image of the gross always shines within the fire.
In another tantra: "To perceive the guru as a mere human being, and to conceive of the mantra as merely a collection of syllables..."
One who applies the knowledge of carving stone to images shall go to hell.
151) Now follows the definition of Brahman.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
This is declared to be the six lotuses, with the five sounds and the sixth bindu situated in the center of the *suṣumṇā*,
the thousand-spoked abode of Śiva.
Śivapura 23.
The five wheels are the five principles (*tattva*), while the sixth is devoid of principles (*tattva*)—[O Śivā, it is beyond space].
That is the mind, O Supreme Goddess; it is beyond the mind and stainless (*nirañjana*). (24)
Stainless, formless, beyond the reach of speech and mind,
transcending words, it is the illuminator that makes known that which is to be expressed by speech.
Where there is no illumination by the moon, the sun, or fire, the world shines forth through that [supreme] light; it does not shine in the absence of that light.
This thousand-spoked [lotus] has been described as being like a dye upon crystal;
the Bindu, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, is the enchanting thousand-spoked one. (27)
In each petal of the thousand-spoked [lotus], there are a thousand nādas and bindus;
for every bindu, there is a pair of nādas, and for every nāda, a pair of bindus.
O Maheśānī, sound is existence and the point (bindu) is devoid of existence;
everything consists of sound and the point, as declared by the knowledge of Brahman. (29)
Nāda is the cause of knowledge, and Bindu is the destroyer of knowledge; O Dear One, know that Brahma-knowledge is the Bindu permeated by Nāda.
Now, concerning breath control (prāṇāyāma): At the mūlādhāra, the Kuṇḍalinī is coiled around the self-manifested liṅga;
endowed with great erotic passion, she bestows liberation upon the individual soul (jīvātman). || 31 ||
Having led her up by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should bathe that Goddess in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
having led her into the Maṇipura, one should adorn her with the Cintāmaṇi jewel.
Having brought that Mother of the World into the unstruck great lotus,
one should worship her with great effort through the various distinctions of the causal [deities] and so forth. (33)

Now, regarding recitation (*japa*): one should recite the *Śakti-mantra* in the *Vibhāva* [cakra], the *Śiva-mantra* in the *Sabhāva* [cakra], and the *mantra* called *Viśuddha* in the *Ājñā* [cakra]; its completion occurs there.
In another tantra [Ch, J: thus, within another mantra, the state of being; one should accomplish the rites of recitation according to that command]:
"In the Unstruck (anāhata), the Great Power (mahāśakti) is the radiance of the individual soul (jīvātman), like a lamp."
Even though Śiva is pure, she (Śakti), intoxicated and enveloped by the command of her lover,
resides [there]. In the fifth and fifth principle, within the great city of the thousand-spoked wheel,
one should contemplate the Bindu, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, as a single body.
Then again, O Goddess, in each and every petal of the established lotus,
there is a body consisting of Śiva and Śakti, [wherein] through Śakti, it consists of Śiva.
Having meditated upon the cause and the worthy recipient, one should offer oblations for the attainment of the desired goal,
using water cleansed by the *bhaga* within the triangle situated at the *mūlādhāra*.
O Śivā, one should fill the cavity of Kuṇḍalinī with the root mantra;
she is tormented by the passion of desire and thirsts for the water of love.
Having the appearance of a spider’s thread, O Śivā, immersed in the water of the causal source;
with one face [entering] even into the cavity of the *liṅga*, O Maheśvarī, by means of the other face,
the divine stages are established through the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
Thus, O beloved [O Goddess], I have explained to you the characteristics of drinking wine;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret again and again. || 41 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Thirty-Seventh Chapter.
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra, the Goddess said: "O Lord, I have heard about internal worship; now tell me about external worship—what is it like?"
O God, if the internal worship should cause the mind to rejoice,
then at its conclusion, the practitioner desires external worship as well.

The inner worship is complete only when there is a vision of the deity at its conclusion; only then should the external worship be performed, otherwise the senses have been in vain. Therefore, O Mahādeva, I desire to hear the characteristics [of this].
The illustrious Śiva said:
"O Mother of the worlds, listen; O beloved of my life-breath, listen to that which has been spoken for the sake of the attainment of perfection by people in supreme bliss. (3)
First is the meditation on the venerable Guru: O Great Goddess, for the sake of attaining the fruit of that task which one accomplishes by His command, one should contemplate that Guru.
One should reflect thus:
in the second [state] is the contemplation of form;
for bliss is the cause in Śiva, and the form of bliss is indeed the cause.
Wine accompanied by a second [element] is for the second; the contemplation of form is for the second.
(p. 154) In the third [chapter], breath control (prāṇāyāma) [is discussed]. [The fruit of breath control has been proclaimed in many ways in the Śaiva tradition.]
In the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should perform the purification of the limbs; in the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa), O Śivā,
one should place them from the tips of the fingers and finger-joints, together with the joints of the hand.
In the fourth [period], there is recitation (*japa*).
Having placed the hand upon the heart and extended the fingers crosswise,
covering both hands with a cloth, one should always recite with the right hand.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the life-force, I bow at your lotus feet.
Why is it said that this must be kept secret? And what is its fruit? Tell me, O Master.
Śrī Śiva said: O Śivā, the mantra is indeed secret, auspicious, and likewise brings about the fruit of recitation (jāpaka).
For the cause must be concealed in that manner, and sexual intercourse is likewise to be kept secret.
From bad association there would be a loss of fruit; through good association one becomes a partaker of the fruit.
O Maheśānī, one who desires liberation should perform ritual action after abandoning attachment.
In the fifth [house], there is sexual union.
One should place Śiva in the temple of Śiva, where the pair of thighs and the pair of feet are joined.
For him who [experiences] the emission of semen into the vaginal opening (the path), liberation stands within his grasp.

155) In the sixth [chapter], it is clockwise; according to the *Yāmala*:
One should perform one circumambulation for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka,
four for Keśava, and half a circumambulation for Śiva.
The sequence for the circumambulation of Śakti:
having gone from the south to the north-western [corner] of that [triangle],
and then from there to the south-eastern [corner] of that [same triangle], one should perform the salutation as in the case of the triangle.
The circumambulation of Śiva:
the bull, Caṇḍa, the bull, and likewise the Soma-thread (or Venus);
Caṇḍa, the Soma-thread (or Venus), and again Caṇḍa.
Again, the Bull. || 14 ||
On the back, on the right, and likewise on the left, one should place Vṛṣa, Caṇḍa, and Somaka;
following the sequence from left to right, one must not cross over the Soma-thread (or Śukra-thread).
O Maheśvarī, whatever the type and number of seats belonging to anyone,
one should perform circumambulation of that same type and in that same number, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
The fruit of this is as follows:
O Goddess of gods, by circumambulating [the shrine], one plants the deity upon its seat;
whoever performs this with a spirit of devotion, even he shall attain absorption (laya) into the Divine. (17)
In the seventh [chapter], there is a salutation.
One should become absorbed in that part where the salutation occurs.
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, you are the one worshipped by all the world.
[She who is] to be saluted. || 18 ||
In the *Nārāyaṇītantra*:
"One should bow to Viṣṇu on one's left and to Gaurī and Śaṅkara on the right."
One should bow to the guru in his presence; otherwise, it would be fruitless. || 19 ||
One should salute the god with eight limbs, O Maheśvarī, or with five limbs;
or else with the hand and the head, or even with the head alone.

Now, the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra): With the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the speech, and the mind—this is declared to be the eightfold prostration. (21)
O Goddess, by bowing with the five limbs—chest, head, speech, mind, and sight—one should prostrate before the Lord; thus the deity becomes one who attains absorption (laya).
Having meditated upon each respective form within the auspicious great thousand-petaled lotus, the abode of all the gods, one should bow to and worship all that is undesirable.
O Maheśvarī, having placed a *dukūla* cloth in the form of a *nāda* around his neck, the devoted practitioner should perform prostrations and recite hymns of praise. (24)
The eighth hymn.
In another Tantra:
"One may recite the hymn even mentally, or mutter the mantra with one's voice."
One should know that for both of them it is fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel. || 25 ||
In the *Vīratantra*, the Śrī Devī said:
"One should accomplish all one's desired tasks by worshipping one's own chosen deity. How could one perform the worship or recite the hymn of another? (26)
The venerable Śiva said:
"Even though the living being has an infinite disposition..."

The hunter is among those who are infinite in their actions; and Ananta is one who desires the fruit, therefore he is the end of the worship of the gods. [In some versions: "Ananta is indeed the god."]
Through single-minded meditation on a single form, one desires the Self as being of a single nature.
For by means of a hymn of praise to another deity, one becomes identical with that deity who is one's own chosen god.
Therefore, O Goddess, the practitioner should perform a hymn of praise to another who is his own chosen deity. (28)
In the ninth [chapter], there is singing;
in the ninth, O Śivā, there is singing, dancing, and the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga.
Through the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-bhāva), the deity becomes a partaker of delight in the dance. || 29 ||
Or one should perform singing that bestows devotion, which is a single voice expressing the qualities of the deity;
one should practice this singing within the *cakra*, for Bhairava is the leader of song. (30)
Merely by singing, there is the ninth [stage], the consumption of the vessel;
and thereafter, the embodied soul may attain dissolution even in the supreme tenth stage. || 31 ||
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "In the first [stage] there is indeed mere devotion; in the second, contemplation of the form;
in the third, horripilation; and in the fourth, the shedding of tears. (32)
In the fifth [state], his speech is stammering; in the sixth, it is filled with singing and the like;
in the seventh, he falls to the ground; and in the eighth, he is neither conscious nor unconscious.
In the ninth, devoid of knowledge, one releases the life-force from the body;
in the tenth, O Supreme Goddess, one is born as a singer and a drinker.
158) Regarding the reality of the *nigama*, the venerable Goddess said:
"The singing is that of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*; the dancing is the expression of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*)."
Dancing, instrumental music, and singing, which are to be understood as being possessed by deities; || 35 ||
When there is bliss in song and dance belonging to both Śakti and Śiva,
then that bliss which belongs to Śakti is Śiva, and she too is Śaṅkarī.
Śaṅkarī || 26 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Thirty-Eighth Chapter:
Now, the measure for the offering of honey into the vessel.
In the Viśvasāra-tantra:

In the first [dose] there should be five *tolakas*, in the second four, in the third three *tolakas*, and in the fourth two *tolakas*. In the fifth there should be one *tolaka*; thereafter, one should drink honey until full.
Now, regarding the measure for the offering of honey in the ninth vessel:
O Maheśvarī, whether it be the fifth, the seventh, or the ninth vessel, what rule could possibly suffice for drinking honey beyond that? (2)
O Maheśānī, in whichever cakra it is prepared using a vessel of such a number,
the weight in *tolakas* from the first limit is measured in reverse order.
At the edge of the wheel, indeed, there is a single balance; at its end is the full vessel (pūrṇapātra).
At its end, one should engage in sexual union and joyfully drink the water from the vulva (bhagavāri). || 4 ||
In the first [offering] there is salt; in the second, liquor; in the third, combined with meat;
and in the fourth, combined with fish.
In the fifth [chapter], one should invariably drink honey when combined with everything;
or else, in the ninth [chapter], one should have all vessels made of salt.
Chewable, suckable, lickable, and drinkable [substances] are to be taken according to the power of one's speech;
and the man of knowledge, O Supreme Goddess, may even drink wine according to his own will—
chewable, suckable, lickable, and drinkable, indeed according to his own desire.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, one may eat, lick, or drink according to one's own desire.
O Goddess, without relishing, it is merely the swallowing of poison; by whatever means possible, one should effect that relishing.
In the Śyāmārahasya:
"O Śivā, just as wine is [meaningless] without the power (śakti), so too is [the ritual] without the mudrā;
just as play is [meaningless] without semen, so too is semen [meaningless] without play."
And everything becomes fruitless, just like [blowing on] fire or like consuming wind.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the *Sarvāllāsa*, composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha.
The Forty-Ninth Chapter.
The Śrī Devī said: "O Supreme Lord, what is play? O Śaṅkara, tell me, what is semen?"
And tell me, O beloved of my life, what wonder is there in this play? || 1 ||
Śrī Śiva said: Even in play with the Śaktis, the semen born of passion has bliss as its fruit; it is to be known as the result of the union of both causes.
Now, regarding play (*krīḍā*): in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, it is said—having received the command of the Guru, one should perform only the ritual action (*kriyā*).
Otherwise, the ritual action that is prescribed is like salt in a vessel.
And so it is stated in the Viśvasāra:
"If one drinks liquor without the Guru, or engages in sexual union without the Śakti, the Supreme Deity Kuṇḍalinī will not accept that substance. (4)
In the absence of the guru, or if he lacks the capacity, one should give the vessel to a worthy recipient and drink the honey;
or else, having given the drink to his son, that [act] yields the same fruit.
O Goddess, without the grace of the Guru, everything indeed becomes fruitless;
it is as certain as placing a wick in a lamp without oil.
Having received the command of the Guru, and being intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine, he may, as if in play, together with the Śaktis, strike within the circle of the yoni.
(p. 161) Now, the characteristics of the ritual play (*krīḍā*). In the *Niruttara*:
"Having brought a beautiful, beloved woman who is devoted to the *kula* for the purpose of *kulārccana*..."
Having divided the wheel of power (śakticakra) into three parts, one should then draw the śakti on the forehead.
On the *picchilā* [line]:
"White, red, and mixed are auspicious within the circles of power (*śakticakra*).
Having divided [the pigment] into three parts, one should draw it on the forehead; one should apply the mixed [pigment] in the center. (9)
O Maheśvarī, one should draw a white being, reddened by passion (rajas) and mixed with darkness (tamas),
born from blackness and possessing all colors, in the center of the wheel.
O Maheśvarī, the corner of Brahmā and the corner of Viṣṇu are on the right and left;
the corner of Śiva is in the middle region, described as the three dots (trivindu) possessing a threefold nature.
One should visualize a single drop, black in color and radiant in its central hue;
red at the top, white at the bottom, and joined with a mixture of colors in the middle.
In that regard, the *kalābindu* of desire is manifested in the corner of Śiva;
there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) for Śakti, because she is of the very nature of the Goddess herself. (13)
The Kula practitioner should meditate upon that desired Vidyā as his own essential nature;
having worshipped her, he should enjoy the Śakti, and the dismissal occurs upon the emission of the seed-syllable (vīrya). 14.

One should worship Śivā within the Śrīcakra, before the deity, and during sexual union. Furthermore, during the act of enjoyment, by worshipping before the Goddess, the deity shall partake in the experience of bliss. || 15 ||
In the Haṃsamāheśvara:
"Having drunk the substance—[namely, wine]—again and again, one should mutter the mantra;
having meditated upon it repeatedly, one should perform worship; and having known the Śakti again and again, one should approach the woman."

If one should delight in the power (śakti) of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the center of the wheel before the practitioner, O Great Goddess, he too shall become full of bliss; such enjoyment is approved by me. (17)
By him who rejoices when the wheel is pierced in accordance with the Guru’s command, the equal task has been accomplished; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (18)
If, O Goddess of gods, by good fortune she should serve her Guru as her lover,
that woman is the very form of Kālikā, provided that the emission of semen occurs within her womb.
O Supreme Goddess, if a woman is endowed with devotion toward the Guru,
the Guru may, by her command, engage in sexual union within her womb. (20)
It must not be performed otherwise; once it is performed, success is certain, there is no doubt.
However, if one should perform the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) joined with power (śakti) out of delusion, then because of the dissolution of the state of the Guru, one should again employ the wheel.
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, even if the practitioner has no desire, he must never engage in sexual union with the woman to be won over; if he does so, he shall fall [from his spiritual state]. (22)
For sexual union has semen as its essence, and semen has sexual union as its essence.
Without the discharge of semen, wine should be avoided, as should sexual union;
indeed, everything performed in such a state is said to be fruitless, like a woman with sons who has a dead son.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having received the semen of the practitioner, that woman is Kālikā herself;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, she is the one who causes the power of the courtesan to blossom. (24)
The practitioner shall become free from sin upon seeing the yantra;
by touching it, people in the world shall partake in merit; and by striking it, one shall be endowed with the power of action. || 25 ||
Upon the emission of the semen, Śiva became [the male] and Kālī, the Supreme, became the female. He who, with a spirit of devotion, performs union within her womb—
With a purified soul, he becomes a partaker of merit, capable of performing sacred rites, and auspicious. || 26 ||
From worship comes merit, O Maheśānī; from merit, fitness for one's duties;
from fitness, the state of Śiva; and through union with Śiva, one becomes a partaker of Nirvāṇa. || 27 ||
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"On an auspicious lunar mansion, on an auspicious day, for an auspicious rite, and in an auspicious place, the wise one should perform the sexual union; otherwise, he shall go to hell. (28)
O Goddess of gods, sexual union performed without the prescribed rite leads to hell;
O lady of excellent hips, what on this earth cannot be accomplished when performed according to the rite? (29)
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha.
The Fortieth Chapter:
Now, the Procedure for Sexual Union (Maithuna-vidhāna). In the Jñānārṇava, the Goddess said:
O Lord of gods, O Lord of the masters of life, O bestower of knowledge upon the worlds!
I desire to hear about sexual union according to the rule and its ritual procedure.
Śrī Śiva said:
Having consumed intoxicating substances, one should engage in sexual union according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, without sexual union, every ritual act shall be in vain. || 2 ||

Even in the case of a Tantric rite, if one performs it according to the Vedic method—or even if it is performed otherwise—it is undoubtedly a "magnetizing" act; of this there is no doubt. (This verse is found in manuscript Ch, but not elsewhere.)
O Maheśānī, those who say that sexual union bestows hell—for that purpose, O Goddess, sexual union has indeed been declared as taught by the sacred injunctions. || 4 ||
O Goddess, there is no doubt that for them, attachment acts as a magnet;
having seen that, O Goddess, the practitioner should perform the smelling of the vulva.
O Goddess, by the touch of his limbs, one should behold the circle of the womb;
O Goddess, without the command of Śakti, one should engage in sexual union through force.
O Supreme Goddess, if that rogue, following the counsel of the Asura,
were to inflict suffering upon Śakti through sexual union, O Maheśānī,
that deceitful man and she, Śakti, would abandon him at that very moment.
O Goddess of gods, one who reveals the heart of Śakti through useless speech should be known as a chatterer; one should completely avoid his company.
O Supreme Goddess, one who brings forth power through hypocrisy should be known as a hypocrite; one must abandon even a word from him.
When one brings forth power toward Śivā even through deceit without effort,
association with him and his speech will bring destruction even to the practitioner.
O Maheśvarī, even for one who is a magnetizer, a rogue, a deceiver,
a talkative person, a hypocrite, or a lustful man— without this doctrine.
For one who has been purified by the state of a god (surabhāva), delight should indeed be cultivated. || 11 ||
In the *Varadātantra*:
"By virtue of the grace of the sexual union of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others..."
Bound there by affection, I shall now make my mind—which ought to be hidden—steady; it shall be revealed today, but never to be revealed again.
O Goddess, for the sake of sexual union I am always present within the bodies of men;
and for the sake of sexual union, O Goddess, you are always present within the bodies of women. (13)
What is the use of saying more? By the grace of sexual union, I have resorted to knowledge and assumed bodies among embodied beings.
Sexual union is the supreme knowledge; it is mere action, consisting of the entire universe.
O Pārvatī (or Śaṅkarī), it indeed exists within the gross, the subtle, the power of action, and the radiant light.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the venerable Goddess said:

"O Supreme Lord, that which is proclaimed as sexual union (*maithuna*) is [attained] through ritual action (*kriyā*). If one who performs the ritual is possessed of knowledge, then that sexual union is born of merit. (16)
Manifestation, concealment, and mere action are well-ascertained;
among these, the primordial seed is "action" (kriyā), which is characterized by sexual union.

O Mahādeva, even when the rite is subtle, it is said to be devoid of mental disposition (*bhāva*) when performed with the mouth; yet, even for the sake of a mental disposition, the rite must be accompanied by physical action when performed with the gross body.
O God, even one of steady intellect perishes through endless talk;
for this very reason, O Mahādeva, sexual union occurs within the bodies of Śaktis.
O Lord, sexual intercourse with a beloved woman brings forth pleasure in the male body;
O Lord, the pleasure of a man is found in sexual union with female bodies. (20)
(166) O Maheśvara, what more need I say with many words?
Both you and I have manifested in the forms of woman and man for the sake of pleasure. (21)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Forty-first Chapter:
Now begins the exposition of the Fifth Bliss.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*, Śrī Śiva said:
O lady of excellent hips, the five principles (pañcatattva) bestow exclusive bliss;
among them, there is nothing found that equals the great bliss of sexual union (rata). || 1 ||
O auspicious lady, when such certain bliss arises from recounting the greatness of Rati,
how could that same bliss be found in other principles?
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, by the grace of Rati, I am always pleased with you;
indeed, being Śakti by nature, I abide in every house. (3)
Changeless, without support, beyond all existence, supreme and great—
for the sake of delight, contentment, and enjoyment— you are Śiva and I am Śivā.
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
"O fortunate one, from the union of the two, sexual intercourse certainly arises;
I am you, and I abide in the forms of woman and man for the sake of manifestation. (5)
(167) She is of her own form and of the form of Brahman; he is of male form and the very embodiment of Brahman.
O lady of excellent hips, he is always present among even insects and other creatures for the sake of sexual union.
In whatever manner joy is surely produced,
in that very manner he wanders upon the surface of the earth.
O lady of excellent hips, stable knowledge does not arise in other forms of bliss;
stable bliss is found in the fifth [state], which is the fifth among the five and bestows liberation. (8)
O Goddess, in sexual bliss (maithuna) reside creation, maintenance, and dissolution upon the earth;
without bliss, an embodied being does not remain for even a single moment.
Therefore, sexual union is indeed the blissful Brahman, higher than the highest; and because the bliss of sexual union consists of the nature of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. || 10 ||
In the Lalitākhyatantra:
"O Goddess, when one possesses the knowledge of Brahman through the mere recitation of the Mother of the Vedas, even if not born of a Brahmin lineage, then he is called a Brahmin. (11)
Therefore, all the twice-born are indulged in wine and sexual union;
through the drinking of wine one becomes wise, and through sexual union one becomes a knower of reality.

In the *Jñānārṇava*, the Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, O Lord of the Life-force, O Supreme Bliss! Deluded regarding the supreme principles, tell me, O Joy of practitioners, the characteristics according to the distinctions of states (*bhāva*). (13)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
The practitioner (sādhaka) who seeks bliss through the path of ritual action (kriyāmārga) is traditionally held to be of two kinds.
Indeed, the characteristics of the one whose nature is action have been revealed in many ways. (14)
Now, O Goddess of the Gods, the characteristic of one capable of action has been briefly described by means of which path a man becomes a partaker of the fruit. (15)
168) Now, the characteristics of the practitioner on the path of ritual action (*kriyāmārga*):
one may drink liquor without [the presence of] Śakti, and engage in sexual union without liquor.
If one drinks liquor without the mudrā, it is fruitless; there is no doubt about this. || 16 ||
One should worship Śakti without fish, and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) without meat;
liquor [should be taken] without chewing—this is fruitless, of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||
One must not drink excessively, for that would cause one to transcend the state of being;
when one transcends the state of being, action is lost, and knowledge is lost, O Mistress of the Kula. (18)
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Excessive drinking leads to suffering and incurs public censure in the world;
therefore, one who follows the path of ritual action (*kriyāmārgī*) should not practice excessive drinking. (19)
O Maheśānī, through excessive drinking, recitation, worship, and so forth become fruitless;
therefore, one who follows the path of ritual action should never practice excessive drinking.
Ānanda is the cause; Ānanda is the giver of liberation.
By means of Ānanda alone is the characteristic of the practitioner to be known. (21)
O Goddess, without fragmentary bliss, full bliss does not arise;
O Goddess, without fragmentary knowledge, full knowledge [or full bliss] does not arise. || 22 ||
O Śivā, sexual union devoid of blood is the lowest bliss; that which is accompanied by the cause [of emission] is middling; and that which is entirely free from bliss is the highest, O Śivā. (23)
O Ānanda, it is taught that for the highest [level], even a single vessel may suffice; for the middling, three vessels;
and for the lowest, many vessels in certain cases.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Forty-second Chapter.
Now, regarding the characteristics of the practitioner seeking bliss,
the Goddess spoke in the Jñānārṇava:
The characteristics of a practitioner on the path of action have been heard by me in many ways; now, O Sādhakānanda, I wish to hear the characteristics [of the practitioner]. (1)
Śrī Śiva said:
One who follows the path of ritual action (kriyāmārgī) is empowered by action (kriyāśakta) and is greedy for the five elements;
one who follows the path of knowledge (jñānamārgī) is anointed with the three principles (tritatvākta) and consists of pure bliss (kevalānanda).
The hunter. || 2 ||
One who has transcended mental states follows the path of knowledge; indeed, sexual union transcends mental states.
Devoted to the welfare of all living beings, one should drink wine that transcends mental states. (3)
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
"One's own chosen Vidyā is the form of all, proclaimed through the knowledge of one's own Self;
when the living being perishes, the Self perishes, for the three principles are served by the knower. (4)
O Goddess of the Gods, since the fruit of the five principles (tattvas) is considered to be fivefold,
for this very reason each of the five principles bestows knowledge.
Liquor, the mudrā, and sexual union—these three principles, endowed with the three qualities, grant accomplishment through their practice; they are Kālī, Tārā, and Sundarī. (From the *Kālikākalpa*)

The state of a hero (vīrabhāva) is to be known as twofold: divine (daiva) and demonic (āsura). In the divine state, the supreme consists of three principles; in the auspicious demonic state, it consists of five principles.
(170) Liberation occurs among the Āsuras; among the Devas, a man becomes a partaker of liberation.
O Maheśvarī, hear from me how the distinction between these two is made.
The Paśvācāra, the Śaiva, the Vīra, and the Divya;
then there is the Siddhānta state, and the Kaula state which is devoid of [all] states. || 9 ||
Liberation occurs when one transcends mental constructs; through mental constructs, a person remains bound. For this is indeed the seed of the Kaula practice and the divine final doctrine.
Indeed, the divine state exists within the asura, and the established conclusion (siddhānta) resides within the deva;
the divine is the very form of the deva, and the established conclusion is the deva himself. || 11 ||
In the *Nigamānanda*, the venerable Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, the seeds of the divine and the Siddhānta are the Right-hand and the Left-hand paths.
If these two are to be practiced for the sake of Kaula knowledge—"
For the sake of knowledge. || 12 ||
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha.
The Forty-Third Chapter:
Now, the definition of Daivānanda.
In the *Yāmala*, the Goddess said:
What is the nature of the first unfolding (ullāsa), and likewise the second,
the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth?
Speak in due order, Ānanda, on behalf of me who am present in each vessel.
The venerable Śiva said:
Everything is ungrasped by the senses and devoid of those respective states of being.
Consisting of that, it is immovable and tranquil; it is described as being characterized by joy and other such states. || 2 ||
When the first *ullāsa* has been attained, one should recite that [mantra] within the heart;
one should not perform any further causes [of practice], such as ritual gestures (*mudrā*) or the chewing of offerings (*carvaṇa*).
It is perceived as equal, as oneness, devoid of mind and intellect; it is both the perceivable and the imperceptible, other than that, yet consisting of that, and secondless.

While performing the individual causal rites within the state consisting of the bliss of attainment (*prāptyānandamaya*), one should at times practice meditation, recitation, and so forth, and at other times perform the act of relishing (*carvaṇa*).
3. That wherein the conceit of the body has dissolved, which is devoid of objective perception, and wherein the latent impressions have come to rest—that is the third [state]. 6.
When the third chapter (ullāsaka) has been reached, one should employ the means as it was bestowed;
even while relishing that, one should likewise move about within another [teaching] or within one's own seat (śāsana).
He stands firm. || 7 ||
With the internal object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking and opening of the eyes,
being absorbed in that and having its form— that is declared to be the fourth bliss (caturthānanda).
Where one should drink the cause consisting of the bliss of the musical instruments along with Śakti by means of the power (śakti),
whatever has been offered to the Hero and Śakti— all that is to be grasped as the act of chewing (carvaṇa).
O lady of excellent hips, liberation while living, transcendence of the mind, and repose within the circle of the Guru—this is proclaimed as the fifth characteristic. (10)
For these were not given by the Hero into a vessel that was empty, nor were they offered into one that was already filled;
for whatever remains when offered by another is indeed a cause for happiness, even without a mouth.
p.

172) 6. Where there is the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), free from both existence and non-existence—even in that state of absorption—I am the deity, the self, the mantra of my own imperishable nature.
One should reflect upon it. || 12 ||

In the sixth chapter, O Goddess of Gods, the three worlds are indeed identical with That; then, in the Tantric circle, there is intoxication (or delight) according to one's pleasure. One should contemplate everything—both external and internal—as being of the nature of the Self.
One should contemplate non-duality and supreme bliss; O Dear One, this contemplation is the seventh.
In the seventh, there is equanimity in the wheel (*cakra*); in the *tantra*, there is a state of union. (14)
From what has been drunk, the remainder should be taken up again and offered to the Yoginī as the supreme [offering].
No bliss whatsoever is perceived, nor is there any distinction between cause and effect. 15.
For indeed, being alone, free from duality, consisting of consciousness and having consciousness as its essence—
whether as a vessel or as a drinking cup— she should perform dance and song with constant exultation, served by her own mouth alone, together with the Heroic Woman (vīrāṅganā). 16.

When the ninth chapter (ullāsa) is reached, that bliss which is beyond reproach, transcending action, transcending the creative powers (kalās), transcending the mind, and perfectly pure [is attained]. 17.
The couple consists of Śiva and Śakti; there is no distinction of castes there.
One should perform the attainment, the mouth, the womb, and so forth, exactly as they are assigned.
Whether seated in rest or not seated, it is exactly as it has been assigned.
O lady of excellent limbs, I do not know the bliss born of the tenth joy,
which transcends parts, transcends the mind, transcends action, transcends mental states, and is the supreme self.
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, playing, or closing his eyes again and again, he performs mere activity according to his own will, arising solely from the bliss of the Self. (20)
Having drunk again and again, and having drunk repeatedly as desired arising from sexual union, he rises up and drinks once more; drinking, drinking, yet again indulges in sexual union. (21)
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, one should not abandon sexual union. Sexual union, O Supreme Goddess, is the seed that is the cause of birth;
it should be known as the cause of destruction and likewise the cause of maintenance.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. Chapter Forty-four:
Now, on sexual union (*maithuna*).
In the Vīra-tantra, the Śrī-devī said: "O Lord of Kula, O Master of Prāṇa, O You whose form is the bliss of the universe!
Now I wish to hear the characteristics of sexual union."
Śrī Śiva said:
Out of favor toward the sexual union of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others,
and bound by my affection for you, I shall keep this secret firmly in my mind.
And today I shall make it manifest, never to be hidden again;
O Maheśvarī, upon a variegated seat that is neither too low nor too high.
Having brought his beautiful beloved, who was shameless and sweetly smiling,
along with wine, meat, fish, parched grain, and his dear companion for sexual union.
O Śivā, one should place the vessel filled with the causal [liquid] on one's own left side or on the thigh, having repeatedly applied it to the mouth while reciting the root mantra.
Afterwards, O Dear One, one should personally drink the substance— wine, meat, fish, and so forth.
Having offered everything into the mouth of the Goddess, one should afterwards unite it with oneself.
If sexual union is joined [with this practice], it is called the "Great Wheel" (mahācakra);
the majesty of that wheel cannot indeed be fully described.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having removed the garment at the base with the root mantra, one should gaze upon the vulva with the root mantra;
having performed the touching with the root mantra, one should enter the linga with the root mantra. (8)
O Goddess, there is kissing of the two cheeks, massaging of the pair of breasts, and the sucking of the tongue; after that comes sexual union.
Everything should be performed with the root mantra; during the emission of semen, one should cause the semen to fall.
Having meditated upon the Guru, one should enjoy the Śakti, and at the end of the emission, one should recite the mantra.
In this manner, one should recite the mantra ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or even ten thousand times;
for the sake of offering a fee to the guru, one should mutter the mantra eight times.
Then one should perform the emission of semen (śukrapāta); at its conclusion, one should recite a hymn of praise.
One should recite the hymn at both the beginning and the end, and contemplate the Śakti-vidyā.
Thinking "I am Śiva," sexual union is approved by me. || 12 ||
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*:
"O Lord, without the hymn to the Yoni, knowledge of the Yoni does not arise;
O Lord, without knowledge of the Yoni, sexual union does not bestow auspiciousness. (13)
One should recite the hymn of praise at the beginning and end of the worship of the Kulasambhava;
in the middle, one should worship the Goddess and perform singing, drinking, dancing, and recitation.
(175) Listen, O Goddess, best among the gods, you who are saluted by both gods and asuras!
Now I desire to hear the hymn that is indeed difficult for all to obtain.
By the awakening to which, the embodied soul within the body becomes composed of Brahman. || 15 ||
Śrī Pārvatī said:
Listen, O God, best of deities, to that which is approved as the seed of all [or: of the living soul].
This must never be spoken to a heretic or to an atheist man.
O Digambara! This hymn to the creeper is my very life and my all;
O Lord, by its recitation, one becomes liberated while living. (17)

Oṃ! May the Mother of the World, whose form is Bhaga, who is endowed with creation, preservation, and dissolution, whose essence is the nature of the ten Vidyās, and who is the Yoni, protect me at all times. 18.
O Goddess, endowed with three corners, free from praise and blame, the source of the world’s bliss—may that Yoni protect me at all times. 19.
The Mother of the World, red in form, eternally established in the center of the womb;
may the Womb, which is the life-breath of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, protect me at all times. (20)
The *kārttikī*, the tresses, the form beautifully adorned above the womb—the womb that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; may the womb protect me at all times. 21.
Vīrayarūpā, daughter of the mountain, resplendent in the central place—
may she, the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, protect me at all times. (22)
In the center of the womb is Mahākālī, beautiful in the form of the aperture;
may that womb, the abode of passion and the giver of happiness, protect me at all times. 23.
May the goddess Kālyā and the other Yoginīs, who reside eternally within the corners of the womb, and may Manoharā, who is difficult to attain, protect my womb at all times. (24)
p.

176) 8. May the womb, which is eternally Śiva, shaped like Mount Meru, and which always dwells within the center of the womb, bestowing liberation when joined with desire—may that womb protect me at all times.
O you who are praised by all the gods, the source [of all], worshipped by all the gods;
you, the progenitor of all, may you protect me always. 26.
The womb that consists of all sacred fords, which destroys all sins, and which resides in every body—may that womb protect me at all times. 27.
O Hero, she who bestows liberation, wealth, happiness, and fame, as well as health—she who delights in these five principles is ever united with them. (28)
This hymn to the Yoni has been proclaimed; for whoever recites it in the presence of the Yoni, the Great Goddess in the form of Śakti shall always remain steadfast in his home.
For him, there is no wandering to sacred fords (tīrthas), no worship or libations (tarpaṇa), and indeed no preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
his liberation is unimpeded. || 30 ||
Merely through sexual union, one becomes equal to Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Truth, truth, and again truth: my word is never in vain.
O Digambara! If I have falsely spoken of your murder, O great sinner, you should recite this hymn with your palms joined in reverence. (32)
Whatever merit that practitioner obtains at all sacred fords (tīrthas),
including the ten Vidyās such as Kālī and the millions of sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā—
all these are truly present before him merely by the sight of the Yoni; of this there is no doubt.
[Ch, J: or otherwise] || 33 ||
One should recite this at the beginning and at the end of the worship performed according to one's lineage;
otherwise, O God, instead of enjoyment through worship, there will be death. (34)
One who recites this hymn with undistracted mind at one twilight or at all three twilights, standing before Śakti during the night, is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. (35)
Thus ends the *Yoni-stotra*.
At the conclusion of the hymn, O Supreme Lord, the Cause has been filled with praise.
It should be placed in the left hand, preceded by the secret mantra. || 36 ||
Now, the majesty of the water used for washing the feet of the Śrīcakra:
(This verse is not found in manuscripts *gh*, *ch*, and *j*). [The merit gained from bathing in] the Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Narmadā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Gautamī—

The water that has washed the feet of the Śrī-cakra bestows the fruit of millions of crores of holy baths at sacred fords within the vessel of the universe—at Gaṅgādvāra, Gayā, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, and the Sindhu; at the R̥ṣikulyā, Setu, Sarasvatī, and so forth. (37)
Then,
with water used for washing the *bhaga*, with water used for washing the vessel,
and with water used for washing the *liṅga*, one should sprinkle drops [of these waters] drop by drop.
One should place the hand upon the vulva, the hymn in the mouth, the ritual vessel in the hand, and cool, fragrant water, while applying the *tattvamudrā*. (39)
In another tantra:
"One should make the vessel very cool according to the sequence of the Śrīpātra and so forth—from the Guru’s vessel, from the Deity’s vessel, and from the Self’s vessel, O Maheśvarī. (40)
Water should also be sprinkled from the vessel of the practitioner onto the ground; having formed a paste with that water, one should apply a tilaka mark upon the forehead.
O Maheśvarī, if the vessel of the Śakti is distinct from the vessel of the Guru,
then water poured from that Śakti-vessel into any other vessel [only] reaches the ground.
In the *Kulatattvasāra*:
"From the vulva, from the linga, and likewise from the vessel, the cool [nectar] resides in the Śrīpātra."
One should sprinkle water on one's own head and other parts, drop by drop, using the *tattvamudrā*.
Whomever I touch with my foot, whomever I behold with my eye, that very person falls into servitude—even if he were equal to Śakra himself. (44)
O Goddess of gods, with this mantra or again with the root mantra (mūlamantra),
O Goddess, one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) on the mud with the remaining water.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha.
The Forty-Fifth Chapter:
O Supreme Goddess, at the conclusion of the cycle, one should joyfully recite the Śānti hymn.
Now, O Ānanda, the hymn of praise.
In the *Kulārṇava* [1]: [k, kh, g, c: O Mangala of the mind-born one, whose essence is auspiciousness, the Fortune of Beauty...]
Salutations to the Guru, the auspicious root-gesture;
to the Goddess of Beauty, the victory-banner on earth;
to Śrī Sundarī, adorned with the crescent moon.
With joy, I meditate upon her who consists of bliss. || 2 ||
2) [The worship] of Śrīsundarī and those who are her attendants,
whose eyes are red with the intoxication of wine.
May the days pass for us, whose minds are delighted and who are devoted to Maheśvara. || 3 ||
Having established a stream of nectar in their mouths and having worshipped the Śrīcakra according to the Kula tradition,
they tasted the flesh of the deer-eyed woman.
Embracing liberation, the wise proceed;
day by day, let the jar be filled with perfection, and day by day, let there be libation for the Goddess.
May there be a meeting with the Saṅgha day by day;
may there be a meeting with practitioners day by day. || 5 ||
Tasting morsels of flesh,
we drink wine until our throats are full.
Bestowing union with the Left-Eyed One (Vāmeṣaṇā), we attain both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation. || 6 ||
6. (This verse is found in manuscripts *gh* and *j*) There is no gain so sweet as that of flesh, nor is there any full delight like that of the five-syllable mantra.
I consider every day on which there is no attachment to her whose eyes are like those of a deer to be nothing but a foul, rainy day. || 7 ||
Then, thousands of prosperities come to the home of those who promote [the practice], while misfortune gradually approaches those who revile the practitioner, O Śrīsundarī.
In this world, life-breaths and wealth go to their destruction; life itself comes to an end in that very instant. || 8 ||
(180) 8. Leprosy and other diseases in the limbs, misfortune in the home, muteness in the mouth, and residence in a cremation ground;
The life-force of those who revile the practitioner of Śrīsundarī perishes at that very moment, for they go to their destruction. || 9 ||
9. Just as the common folk, along with sons, wives, and friends, direct their censure toward the preeminent practitioners of Śrīsundarī, so too [does it proceed].
In that same way, it quickly goes to destruction. || 10 ||
10. Drinking liquor in the initiation-halls,
sleeping at night in the houses of courtesans,
and eating in every house— [this is the life of the one who has been initiated].
The Kaulika practitioner becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin). || 11 ||
And subsequently, by the power of time, I shall fall into delusion; yet I shall remain as I am, for I have no sorrow.
In birth after birth, I shall [behold] you.
That I, Bhairava, remember my mother. || 12 ||
These wretched beings, wandering near the edge of the thicket of conceptual constructions,
enter the bottomless ocean of delusion.
They wander, having not tasted the path of the Kaulas. || 13 ||
The uprooting of the trees of sin and the blossoming of the curiosities of the mind.
We practice the attraction of those with lotus-like eyes and the drinking of intoxicating liquor as an offering. || 14 ||
Vārāṇasī, the daughter of Jahnu (the Gaṅgā), Prayāga, and the holy sites of Godāvarī and Kedāra have been visited; the sacred fords along the Godāvarī have been beheld.
I believe that by him alone were the worlds created— he whose very thought is Śrīsundarī.
This great effort of mine has been exerted within the ocean of existence through repeated births;
for the sake of liberation, by the grace of the Lord’s feet—
Now, the Kaula path has been accepted. || 16 ||
I behold no other, nor do I desire another; remembering none other, I take refuge in none other.
Never shall I [forsake] her who is the form of the Supreme Self.
I forget Śrīsundarī in my heart. || 17 ||
Having beheld the Śrīcakrarāja made of vermilion with white plaster, they fashioned it at night;
meditating upon Śrīsundarī in their hearts, they offered libations.
With playful glances, they bring the worlds under their sway. || 18 ||
Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation;
where there is liberation, there is no worldly enjoyment.
[For those who worship the pair of lotus feet of Śiva: the worship of Śrī Sundarī.
For those devoted to that, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are truly held in the palm of their hand.
In her left hand is a lute, she is skilled in dalliance; in her right hand is a drinking vessel,
in front of which is placed the warm flesh of a pig together with black pepper.
The lute upon the shoulder is graceful and auspicious; the discourse of true gurus is the Kaula Dharma, supremely profound and inaccessible even to yogis. || 20 ||
On the left is Candramukhī; in her mouth is a sweet vessel held in her lotus-hand;
on her head is the contemplation of the venerable Guru, who is the object of meditation in the mind.
With the tongue as the means for recitation, the transformation comes from the practice of the Kaula sequence.
He who, being tranquil, always drinks that nectar from the vessel [of the one seated upon the Kaula woman] shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 21 ||
21. With a single dry chickpea I drink from a jar; suddenly with a salted radish I drink from a pond.
If I taste a piece of cleaned meat, [I am satisfied].
I drink the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā together with the ocean.
The alms-bowl in my hand, the hymn of praise in my mouth, and bliss in the lotus of my heart;
with the lotus feet of the venerable Lord upon my head—what could be greater than this remembrance?
I am one devoted to the worship of union with women through the offering of meat; I am honored by the undertaking of the various dispositions of people [or: the undertaking of the path of the Kula].
I am devoted to the dust of the Guru’s feet; I have taken refuge in Bhairavī; I am turned away from the state of the bound soul (paśu); I am Bhairava; I am Śiva.
Thus ends the *Ānanda-stotra* as spoken in the *Kulārṇava*.
[This verse is found in manuscript J, but not elsewhere. Having drunk the liquor, one should recite it.
The practitioner, Kulabhairava, should perform the praise;
devoted to union with a woman of the Kula, he should carry out the Kula-activity.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha; [now begins] the forty-sixth chapter:
Now, the Consecration (Abhiṣeka).
In the *Uttaratantra*, the illustrious Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, without initiation (*abhiṣeka*), one should not perform the rites of the *kula*;
drinking [the sacramental substances] would be like drinking poison, and sexual union would bring about sin. (1)
He who exercises the office of an Ācārya without having received consecration—his four qualities, namely life-span, knowledge, fame, and power, perish. (2)
O Śaṅkarī, out of affection for you, I shall proclaim the consecration (abhiṣeka) which bestows all siddhis, though it is secret in all tantras. (3)
It bestows wealth, fame, strength, and longevity; it destroys the great sins (mahāpātaka); it fulfills all desires and eliminates all defects in mantras. || 4 ||
O Goddess, it accomplishes all aims, bestows the fruit of all sacred fords,
removes all malevolent magic, and destroys the defects caused by planetary influences.
O Goddess, it increases brilliance and is supreme for increasing strength;
it destroys the suffering caused by poison even for one bitten by Takṣaka. (6)
In the decline of vitality, the decline of strength, the decline of intellect, and the loss of wealth;
likewise, in faults committed through women, as well as in physical and mental ailments. (7)
In the case of a physical ailment, the wise preceptor should perform the consecration in the mind;
for women suffering from misfortune, the consecration is likewise to be carried out.
O Śaṅkarī, Dharma indeed removes all defects; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
[Whether performed] on a riverbank, on sacred ground, at the foot of a tree, or at a crossroads—|| 9 ||
One should also place an excellent jar— free from cracks, neither too short nor too long, made of clay or fashioned from gold— in a temple of the deities. (10)
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the seed-syllable of desire (klīṃ), one should purify it with the Vāgbhava syllable (aiṃ).
Having placed the jar with the Śakti syllable (hrīṃ), one should fill it with water using the Māyā syllable (hrīṃ).
Then, O Queen of the Gods, one should invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas) with this mantra: || 11 ||
Oṃ! All rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the oceans and lakes;
all the seas, rivers, lakes, clouds, and ponds. [In versions gh and j: "streams" (nadāḥ) instead of "clouds" (jaladāḥ). 12.
May all the sacred springs located in heaven, the netherworld, and on earth, and all holy pilgrimage sites, establish their presence within this jar. (13)
One should offer the leaves with the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrīṃ) recited;
the offering of fruit should be performed with the Kūrca mantra (Hrūṃ); and with the seed-syllables of Vadhū (Strī), the form becomes stable.
One should offer vermilion with the seed-syllable of fire and flowers with that of air;
and likewise, O Dear One, having offered vermilion and flowers with the seed-syllable of woman (*strīṃ*), one should offer them with the vowel-syllable (*phaṭ*).
Then, one should perform the sprinkling with dūrvā grass using the root mantra and the praṇavas.
One should perform the striking with *darbha* grass using the mantra "huṃ phaṭ svāhā"; having thus meditated upon the seat of the Goddess— [this reading is seen in manuscript J, not elsewhere].
Having invoked [the deity] there, one should worship it. || 16 ||
By means of the recitation of the mantra according to the procedure taught in one's own tantra,
the practitioner of mantra should install the jar— or, as some versions read, the practitioner of mantra should worship that jar.
With this mantra, the guide [should act]. || 17 ||
Oṃ! Arise, O Brahmakalaśa! O bestower of the desired accomplishments of the deities!
Filled with the waters of all sacred fords (tīrtha), fulfill our heart’s desire! [At the end of that:
Īśāna-indu-svara-kṣauṇī [the mantra is: ha-sa-ka-la-hrīḥ]. At the end of that...
With this mantra, "Bhuvaneśvarī," one should move the jar amidst the sounding of musical instruments. || 19 ||
The Guru, or the leader who is the instructor, should sprinkle the disciple;

in cases of fever, bodily affliction, or possession by spirits, he should sprinkle with *aśvattha* shoots; in the case of a gathering of spirits, with *udumbara* shoots; and in the case of defects in mantra, with *karavīra* shoots.
Fame, wealth, longevity, and splendor are attained through the leaves of the *śrīphala* tree as well. || 21 ||
[This reading is found in manuscript J: By those seeking the destruction of all sins, worship should be performed with *tulasī* blossoms;
for the attainment of the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), it should be performed by the Śāktas with *bilva* fruits. (From here onwards—)
In the manuscript, the reading "In the case of malevolent magic (abhicāra), consecration by means of the Nārasiṃha [mantras] is prescribed," and so forth, is observed. || 22 ||
One should perform the rite with *darbha* grass in all cases of defects caused by women, even when no *darbha* is available; likewise,
for the misfortune of women, there should be an ablution with *dūrvā* grass.
Alternatively, in all ritual acts, one should employ mango sprouts.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the Ṛṣi, Anuṣṭubh is the metre, Śakti is the deity;
the application is for the sake of accomplishing all intentions.
Oṃ! Rājarājeśvarī Śakti, Bhairavī, Rudrabhairavī, the goddess Śmaśānabhairavī, and Tripurānandabhairavī. (25)

The person (puruṣa), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the sixteen transformations (vikāra);
the qualities of the self (ātman), and those which are gross, subtle, and supreme.

The seed-syllable of the Vedas (*oṃ*),

The seed-syllable of the gods (devabīja), the seed-syllable of Ramā (śrī), the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrī), and the syllable of qualities (guṇākṣara).
The Cintāmaṇi (Gaṃ), the Great Seed (Mahābīja), Nārasiṃha (Kṣrau), Śāṅkara (Hau),

May Gāṇāpatya (glau), Vārāha (vlūṃ), and the seed-syllable of Kālī (krī)— which dispels fear—
consecrate these [limbs] with water purified by mantra. 60.
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī;

May the Karatoyā, Candrabhāgā, Śvetagaṅgā, Kauśikī,

The sky (or bowing) and the beloved (Svāhā) belong to Vahni; Vaṣaṭ and Kūrca (Huṃ) are considered his [mantras].
