Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
The Forty-Seventh Chapter:
Now, the disposition of the hero (vīra) of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra).
Devoted to his own duty, the hero, having become Śiva, should worship the Supreme Goddess.
That very practice of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra) is concealed in all the tantras. || 1 ||
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"Alcohol, meat, fish, ritual gestures (mudrā), and sexual union—endowed with these five principles (pañcatattva), the hero is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. (2)
Having realized "I am Śaṅkara," and being endowed with the greatness of the *kalā*,
one should meditate upon the *kalā* Kālī and worship her through union.
O Maheśvarī, the practitioner is Śaṅkara himself; there is not even the slightest difference.
He who, out of delusion, creates a distinction shall go to the Raurava hell.
"I do not dwell on Kailāsa, nor on Meru, nor upon the surface of the earth;
O noble lady, I abide wherever those who possess the knowledge of the lineage reside. (5)
Addicted to fish, meat, and liquor, and always lustful for women,
he should wander in the company of Śaktis while identifying himself as "I am Śiva. (6)
O Goddess, the outcaste (śvapaca) is the lowest of all castes; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, O Śivā, the outcaste who possesses knowledge of the lineage of Agni is even superior to a twice-born brahmin.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the *Sarvāllāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. The forty-eighth chapter: Now, the Vāmācāra (the Left-hand Path).
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"One should worship the women of the *kula* with one's own flowers and the five *tattvas*.
That is to be known as the left-hand practice (*vāmācāra*); having become *vāmā*, one should worship the Supreme [Śivā]. (1)
He states the measure for one's own flowers:
in the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the venerable Goddess said:
"One should worship Śivā with five flowers or seven flowers."

Having worshipped the Lover who rests upon Śakti at midnight—[along with the Śaktis]—one should worship the Supreme Goddess with the fivefold flowers: one’s own flower, the self-arisen, the vajra, the kuṇḍodbhava, O Śiva, and the golaka. || 2-3 ||
Having worshipped Śiva at midnight with *gopīcandana*, *puṣpa*, *vīrapuṣpa*, *maraṇa*, and the seven flowers, as well as with *ramaṇa*.
Having fashioned a yantra with a plucked flower, one should worship Śivā;
with an unplucked flower, one should worship Śivā through sexual union.
Having extracted and purified the flower, one should worship the Supreme Goddess; or,
if it is naturally pure water from the ocean that has not been extracted, one should likewise worship her.
As follows: || 6 ||
Through merit accumulated over a hundred births, one obtains flowers such as the *svayambhū*, which are difficult even for the gods to acquire. (7)
(p. 193) Now follows the description of the ritual arrangement of flowers, beginning with the *svayambhū* and other blossoms.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*:
"O Maheśāna, when the first menstrual period occurs for a maiden who has been married, that blood is proclaimed to be her own flower. (8)
O Mahādeva, O Lord, by touching the private parts of an unmarried maiden, she becomes menstruating;
and that substance, O Lord, is the Svayambhū flower.
If a flower arises from the beating of a married maiden or a man, that is designated as a *vajra*. And when a woman who is united with her husband engages with another man, [that too is a *vajra*].
One should extract blood from the vagina or from a difficult labor; know that to be born of a *kuṇḍa*. Listen, my dear, to that born of a *golā* [or, according to manuscript j:
born at the full time].
A woman who is without a husband and becomes menstruating through union with a paramour—her blood is to be known as *golaka*; now hear about that which arises at all times. (12)
And that blood which flows month after month from the circle of the womb— that blood, O Supreme Lord, arises at all times, my dear.
When a man is engaged in sexual union,
that blood mixed with semen which flows from the vulva is the substance known as *gopīcandana*.
O God, that flower which appears during sexual union with one's own wife—
Listen, O hero, to that flower, the Vīrapuṣpa, and the Svayambhūkusuma. || 15 ||
And month after month, for all women, there is the *svayambhū* flower and so forth.
Now, the specific distinction regarding the courtesan, and the specific distinction regarding the Cāṇḍālī woman—[according to versions gh and j: arising from the new moon]. || 16 ||
Now, the purification of one's own flowers and so forth [section kha]:
In the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*—
for whomever the self is impure, for that person everything is impure.
And for one whose self is purified, O Maheśvarī, everything becomes purified. || 17 ||
O Dear One, impurity is to be known as threefold, and purity is likewise to be known as threefold:
through family custom, through the Kaula tradition, or through the delusive scriptures, O Mistress of the Kula; yet everything is pure, for there is no lack of qualification for one's own duty. (18)
In another Tantra:
"O Maheśānī, in all matters everywhere—whether Vedic or non-Vedic—it is lack of faith alone that causes every ritual action to perish. (19)
O Maheśvarī, whether from a Kaula or even from a Kaulika, or from the worldly scriptures,
knowledge should be understood as entirely pure; for one possesses the authority to perform every rite.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha.
The Forty-Ninth Chapter (Ullāsa).
Now, the mantra for purifying one's own flowers and the like, as well as *svayambhū* (naturally occurring) flowers and the like,
is given in the *Nigamakalpadruma*:
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should extract the seed-syllable of Vahni (Fire), endowed with the fourteenth vowel and adorned with the Nāda and Bindu. || 1 ||
O beloved, having recited the syllable *kṣa*, conjoined with fire (*r*) and adorned with the left eye (*ī*),
one should purify the self-originated flower by reciting it ten times.

The mantra, however, is *hrīḥ rauḥ kṣrīḥ*. O beloved born from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍodbhava*), having first uttered the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava-bīja*), the seed-syllable of Desire (*kāma-bīja*) follows thereafter; at its end is the pure seed-syllable of Fire (*vahnibīja*). (3)
O dear one, having uttered the three seed-syllables of Māyā— *ai*, *klī*, and *ra*— within the mantras, one should purify the *golaka*.
O Maheśvara, having recited the mantra *hrīḥ hrīḥ hrīḥ*— the three seed-syllables of desire— and the *māyā*,
one should purify substances produced at any time with great effort. (5)
O Lord, having uttered the mantra *klīḥ klīḥ klīḥ hrīḥ*—
that is, the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū-bīja*) and the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*)— one should purify the *gopīcandana* with great effort, repeating each pair [of syllables] twice.
O God! The mantra is *strī*, *strī*, *klī*, *klī*. One should purify one's own flower, the Vajra-flower, with the root mantra;
then the practitioner should worship the Mistress of the Kula according to the Kula tradition. || 7 ||
O Dear One, one should purify all other collections of powers with the root mantra; one should worship the Goddess wherever the visualization occurs, for that very place leads to success.

One should worship the enclosure with water used for washing the *bhaga*, with water used for washing the *liṅga*, with urine-water, and with semen; for it is from these that the enclosure arises. (9)

One should wash and purify the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* for the sake of accomplishing the task; likewise, one should employ the seed-syllable of Kāma, the seed-syllable of Vadhū, the seed-syllable of Śabda, and *phaṭ*.
The mantra for urine, however, is *klīṃ*, *strīṃ*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*.
O beloved of life, listen to the mantra for the purification of urine:
it consists of the seed-syllable of sound (*śabda-bīja*), ending with *phaṭ*, followed by the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
O Mahādeva, this [mantra] ending with "namas" is prescribed for the purification of urine.
The mantra, however, is: *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ*.
O God, the purification of semen is performed with the chosen mantra, ending in *vauṣaṭ*, by means of *māyā*.
The mantra, however, is the chosen mantra *hrīḥ* (this additional reading is found in manuscript G);
the two *śukra*s should be purified and enclosed by *māyā*, followed by *vaṣaṭ*.
The seed-syllable of sound (Śa) is at its end; the mantra is said to conclude with "phaṭ. || 13 ||
The mantra, however, is: *hrīḥ vaṣaṭ hrīḥ huṃ phaṭ*.
O Mahādeva, one should thus perform the purification individually according to this sequence.
Having drawn a triangle on the ground with the water for the *arghya* offering using the left hand alone—[according to manuscripts *gh* and *j*: with the *bindu*].
Having sprinkled [the substance] once with pure water or with the causal [mantra], one should recite the root mantra and display the five mudrās;
that substance is generally pure, but its specific [purification] is declared by the mantra. (15)
Now, the dimensions of the five mudrās are given in the Kubjikā Tantra:
the Dhenu-mudrā, the Tatsya-mudrā, the Bhūti-mudrā, and likewise the Ākarṣiṇī-mudrā.
The Yonimudrā is supreme; thus the five mudrās are proclaimed. || 16 ||
The substance of nectar through the *dhenumudrā*, water filled by means of the *matsyamudrā*,
prosperity through the *pañcabhūtamudrā*, and attraction through the *milanamudrā*.
Having understood the *yonimudrā* as the seed of emanation, one should indeed purify the substance.
(17) Now, one should worship by means of the five principles (*pañcatattva*). The method of the five principles has been taught in the *dakṣiṇācāra*; now...
It has been stated concisely in the *Haṃsamāheśvara*:
"O Śivā, meat, fish, as well as ritual gestures (*mudrā*), liquor, and sexual union [constitute the five makāras]."
This is declared to be the fivefold reality (pañcatattva), which is certainly born from the fivefold reality.

When the reality arising from the five principles meets with a single principle at one time, then that reality becomes accomplishment; furthermore, the essence of that reality consists of the five principles. (19)
From the portion of earth, flesh arises; from the portion of water, the fish;
from the portion of fire, the mudrā; and from the portion of air, the cause.
In the void portion, sexual union is declared to be auspicious and consisting of the five elements;
for one should moisten the dry form of the earth element with the water element. (21)
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should dry that water even by means of the portion of the *mudrā*,
and likewise dry that supreme *mudrā* which assumes various forms, even by means of the portion of the wind.
O Goddess of the gods, everything is illuminated by means of the portion of sexual union; or else, one should worship Śivā through the five principles, with the fifth being the most important.
One should worship even with only the fifth heroic state (vīrabhāva);
by the command of Śakti one becomes a Śākta, or in some cases through the knowledge of Śakti.
198) Indeed, by his command, one should perform worship within the five principles or as the fifth;
one should contemplate Śakti within one's own body and find delight in Śiva within one's own body.
Having worshipped one's own body, which is united with Śakti, by means of the five principles (pañcatattva).
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Sarvāllāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. [Now begins] the fiftieth chapter:
Now, one should worship the women of the *kula*.
Now, regarding the characteristics of women of noble family (*kulayoṣit*),
the Śrī Devī said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of Life, O Bestower of the Five Principles (*pañcatattva*)."
O Lord of my life, I desire to hear the characteristics of women of noble family. || 1 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
O Śaṅkarī, that woman who is devoted to drinking liquor is indeed a woman of noble family;
yet, O Sanātanī, she who is incapable even of drinking liquor has fallen from her noble lineage.
Having protected the family abode, one should offer [the offering] exclusively in a secluded place;
the opposite regarding the family substances should be understood as the practice for women of the family (kulayoṣit).
Having partaken of wine and other offerings and having recognized the *kula*, one should establish the *kula*;
that woman, O Supreme Goddess, should be known as a woman of the *kula*.
O Supreme Goddess, that woman who, having given her family’s wealth to the Kula, serves the Kula as well, should be known as a Kulayoṣit. || 5 ||
O Supreme Goddess, if she brings the substances of the Kula and partakes of them within the Kula, that woman should be known as a true Kula-woman.
O Supreme Goddess, if one should worship the consort of another for the sake of serving one's own kinsman, that woman is to be known as a *kulayoṣit*. (7)
In another tantra:
"O Goddess, without one's own family (svakula), one's own family is not revealed.
It should be given to one belonging to a different [or extensive] family for the sake of the bliss of one's own family. (8)
O Supreme Goddess, that woman should be known as a Kula-woman;
among all women, she alone is to be recognized as a Kula-woman among the goddesses.
Among them, she who is distinguished and revealed in your place—
by worshipping her, one attains great bliss, and such a life is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, the Great Hero should never transgress against her.
Regarding the characteristics of the *kula* within the reality of the *nigama*,
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Mother Durgā, O highly fortunate one, I bow at your lotus feet."
And what is your lineage, O Great Goddess? Proclaim it in my presence.
The illustrious Great Goddess said: O Supreme Lord, a woman of noble family, deluded by the joys of the Kula,
always desires that the Kula-substance be given within the Kula-abode for the delight of the Kula.
Endowed with passion, joined with desire, afflicted by longing, and bestowing desire;
the form of the *parapuṣpa* is the place revealed as the house of the *kula*. (13)
O Maheśvara, the lineage is that of Varuṇa, the seed is Kuṇḍa, and the lunar [or Candramas] is the womb;
everything is indeed being led into or dissolved therein as Īśāna.
The western face. || 14 ||
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"O Śivā, the lunar [channel] situated within the watery [channel] is the abode of all the gods;
it is the aperture, auspicious, and vibrant, and when joined with meditation upon it, it bestows liberation."
This Kula seat should be known as the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
as is the action, so is the knowledge, and as is the knowledge, so is this object of knowledge.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"The Void situated in the center of the womb, and the Stainless within the Void—this is to be known as the station of Kula, the seed of all seeds. (17)
The Goddess said: O Supreme Lord, you have spoken of the Kula-seat as belonging to Varuṇa;
it is the Śambhu in the center, the seed-syllable of the Moon, which is the seed of the woman’s body.
O Great Goddess, what is that seed? Is it distinct from that, or how is it a woman? (18)

Śrī Śiva said: O Śivā, the Vāruṇa [letter *va*] ending with the seed-syllable of the Moon [*sa*], joined together, constitutes the Kula-sthāna; without this, the mere knowledge of Śakti does not arise. (19)
(201) Addicted to drink, intoxicated by passion, and always endowed with bliss;
her hips and loins are full, and the radiance of her vulva is like that of another flower. 20.

A woman of noble family is to be known as the best when she has no menses; she is middling when her menses are visible; and even an inferior one, O Supreme Goddess, is excellent when the menses are concealed within the middle. || 21 ||
When the supreme yantra is worshipped, a person becomes a partaker of liberation;
when the middling one is worshipped, even one devoid of devotion accomplishes their purpose.
O Goddess, without the knowledge of the flower, the knowledge of Śakti does not arise;
the Parājitā flower is her form, situated in the center of the Kula-abode.
Power is knowledge, the seed of all; for it, no seed exists.
O Śivā, [the world] is born in three ways: from eggs, from sweat, and from seeds.
The human body is proclaimed to be produced from semen and blood;
the semen is situated within the penis, and the blood is within the womb. (25)
This should be known as the seed of creation; of that, this is merely the seed.
No seed for that exists, nor can it even be described.
When wind predominates, there is birth from an egg; when water predominates, there is birth from sweat;
when fire predominates, there is birth from a seed; and when earth predominates, there is human birth. || 27 ||
O Maheśvarī, the body alone is produced from semen and blood;
it is permeated by subtle portions of other beings and is divided into various classes such as those born from eggs and so forth.
The greatness of the Kula-sthāna cannot indeed be described.
O Maheśānī, what is there on earth that is not accomplished for those who have ascended the Yoni?
Therein shall arise the yoga of action, the yoga of meditation, and the yoga of devotion. (29)
In the *Vṛhadyonitantra*: Now follows the description of the deity of the *kula*.
And in the triangles are the Great Lords;
she, whose form is triangular, is the abode of all the gods, O Dear One (or O Auspicious One). 30.
Kālikā and Tārā reside on the two sides; Bhuvanasundarī is above; Tripureśī is in the middle of the yoni; and Bhairavī dwells at the root.
Chinnamastā is in the cavity of the womb; Dhūmā has emerged at the edge;
Mahākālī is in the pores of the skin, and Mātaṅgī is in the girdle.
In the field of the womb (yonikṣetra) is Kamalā, the deity of the womb named Kāmākhyā;
at the root of the tree of the drop-flower (bindupuṣpa) is Kuṇḍalī, whose form is Brahman.
The drop (bindu) is Rudra himself, and Prakṛti has the form of the flower;
the seat (pīṭha) is the very nature of Kāma, O Supreme Goddess, and it is twofold.
Indeed, one should contemplate the nature of the manifest and the unmanifest—the secret which yields great fruit—as being in the form of the Praṇava and in the shape of a womb. (35)
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra, the Śrī Devī said:
"Reveal the characteristics of both the manifest and the hidden [forms]. (36)
Śrī Śiva said:
Residing manifestly in the body of a woman and existing in a subtle state within the body of a man,
O Goddess, by worshipping her in her manifest form, one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Even in secret worship, liberation shall occur if one is endowed with a spirit of devotion.
In the *Vṛhadyonitantra*:
"O Goddess, by worshipping this [center], one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand seats (*lakṣapīṭha*)."
O woman of excellent complexion, whatever fruit is obtained from the sight of the hundred thousand sacred seats (lakṣapīṭhas), [that is attained here]. || 38 ||
One obtains that fruit through devotion by beholding the Yonipīṭha;
by touching all the pīṭhas, the practitioner attains the fruit. (39)
O beautiful one, whatever sacred fords exist throughout the three worlds, those sacred fords abide within the yonis and pīṭhas, O beautiful one. (40)
The Yamunā always flows on the right side of the Yoni;
Sarasvatī flows through the middle part, and the supreme Jāhnavī flows on the left.
O Supreme Goddess, at the place of the flower is the Tīrtha in the form of a drop (bindu); in the cavities is Puṣkara; and all other Tīrthas reside within the field (kṣetra). 42.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*, the Śrī Devī said:
"O Mahādeva, by your grace, it has been understood that [this] belongs to a woman of the *kula*.
Now I wish to hear the characteristics of women of the *kula*. (43)

The illustrious Śiva said: A woman who is to be known as a Kula-woman should be understood by her characteristics; likewise, a practitioner (sādhaka) of a Kula-woman should be known by those same characteristics.
O Śivā, this is the characteristic of Kula: it is the gross form in the body of a woman, the subtle form in the body of a man, and for the wise, it is the very form of knowledge.
In another Tantra it is said:
"O Dear One (or Śivā), the *kula* of the male exists within female bodies, and the *kula* of the female likewise exists within the male;
this has been taught as having both gross and subtle forms, each distinct from the other."
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Fifty-First Chapter:
Now, the characteristics of sexual union.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the venerable Mahādeva said:
By what means should delight be produced, or what kind of delight is auspicious?
O Goddess, tell me that which brings you joy, so that we may be released from the bondage of worldly existence. || 1 ||
O Goddess, Mother of the entire world, supreme refuge of the Kaulikas!
Without the principle of the Yoni (yoni-tattva), one cannot be devoted to the Kula-dharma.
Whatever action has been performed by me through the grace of your womb,
O Great Goddess, that very same great *sādhana* has been forgotten.
If it has been forgotten, it may be spoken again; my oath [shall be repeated] again and again.
The Goddess said:
"O you of wicked mind and soul, you have become insane; you have forgotten the great means of accomplishment (sādhana).
This must not be spoken again, for I swear it to you repeatedly."
To be hidden, to be hidden, to be hidden again and again;
this has indeed been revealed once more for the sake of pleasure, contentment, and satisfaction.
Within another womb, the channel is threefold: Vāruṇī and likewise Raktikā.
And the Śukriyā, O auspicious one, which is radiant with the beauty of all lands. || 6 ||
Vāruṇī exudes water, Raktikā likewise blood, and Śukrikā generates semen; worship performed upon her yields great fruit. (7)

In the middle part, one should visualize Śukriṇī; on the right and left, one should visualize her radiant with *rajas* (Rajasvalā). Having meditated thus, one should always engage in union, causing the seed (*bīja*) to fall into the semen.
That substance, combined with saffron or else with vermilion,
or even with a single flower, should be offered after it has been purified.
In another tantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, O Mistress of the Kula, if the semen should be accompanied by blood, then it should be given as semen; this is the secondary alternative. (10)
Now listen, O beloved of my life, to the secondary alternative for red [sindūra];
even for that which is directly perceptible, its suitability resides within these secondary alternatives.
In the Gautamīya:
"That which is red is a substitute for blood, and that which is smeared with red is a substitute for semen;
a substance endowed with its own respective color is a substitute for that substance. (12)
One should join flower to flower among flowers born of flowers;
this applies both for the sake of the deity and for the sake of the hero, and sometimes even for the sake of the ignorant self.
Having meditated upon the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī in the middle portion, one should worship them, O Maheśānī; in the center, one should perform the pouring down of the semen.
p.
206) Now, its nature is as follows: having become the Left (vāmā), one should worship the Supreme (parā).
Ignorance resides within one's own body. In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"O Goddess, this entire world is known through the intellect (*buddhi*); it is the seed of the whole body, just as the earth is the strength of a tree, O Goddess."
Likewise, O beloved. || 15 ||
When joined with power, there is creation; power would exist when conjoined with creation.
They would be seeds for one another, just as wind and space are.
Mahādeva is the form of emanation, while Śakti is his own essential nature; Mahādeva is the form of the seed, while Śakti is his own essential nature. || 17 ||
The Great Goddess is the form of the seed, and Maheśvara is the form of the emanation; their mutual manifestation and disappearance are intended [to be understood] in this way. (18)
O Great Goddess, within the body composed of the five elements, which is the gross form of Maheśvara, Śakti resides there in a subtle form. 19.
The body, composed of the five elements, is solely of the nature of Śakti;
therein, Śivā, though one, appears in manifold forms in five ways.
In the *Kubjikā Tantra*: "The Power (*śakti*) possesses manifold forms, while the Person (*puruṣa*) has a single form;
just as, though manifold, the reflection in a mirror does not possess multiplicity."
If Śiva were also of the nature of Śakti, then Śakti would exist through union with Śiva;
for there is an inseparable relationship between these two alone.
The reality consists of the dyad of Śiva and Śakti; this reality is the cause of knowledge.
Śakti is to be understood through Śiva; that which is to be known—
Śaṅkara, empowered by Śakti. || 23 ||
The Puruṣa, when joined with Prakṛti, is the illuminator of all effects;
and when power is infused into the Puruṣas, it becomes the illuminator of everything.
O Goddess, without the knowledge of Śakti, the knowledge of Śiva never arises anywhere;
and without the knowledge of Śiva, no knowledge of Śakti is ever born. || 25 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Fifty-second Chapter:
Now, the Knowledge of Śakti. In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
O Goddess, without gross knowledge, subtle knowledge never arises;
therefore, it is only at the end of many births that the knowledge of Śakti is produced.
O Goddess, without the knowledge of Śakti, liberation leads only to ridicule;
that Śakti should be known as Vāmā, who bestows liberation even upon the Puruṣa.
O Kuleśvarī, the knowledge of Śakti is of two forms: concealed and manifest.
The concealed Śakti resides within one's own body, while the manifest bestows delight.
O auspicious lady, when manifest it is without knowledge; when hidden, knowledge does not arise.
If manifest it is satisfied by union, then when hidden it is satisfied by union. (4)
Now, the definition of the power of concealment (*guptāśakti*).
In the *Śāktakramacandrikā* [variant readings: *candrikāyām*]:
"Power is Brahmā; Śiva is power; Viṣṇu is power."
Vāsava said: "Furthermore, many other gods are proclaimed to have their root in Śakti;
therefore, O high-minded one, know that Śakti is indeed the most preeminent among them. (5)
In the Jñānadvīpa:
"O Goddess, whatever power is proclaimed for whichever object, she alone is the Sovereign of All, and he too is the Great Lord. (6)
In the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"O Maheśānī, the gross sense organs are Mahādeva, and Caṇḍikā is their presiding deity; what is to be done and what is not to be done belongs to her alone—of this there is no doubt. (7)

For the body exists for the sake of the senses, and the sense organ is endowed with power; through that power, there arises what is to be done and what is not to be done, while the Puruṣa remains untainted within Śiva.
From the power of will (icchā-śakti) arises desire; from the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), one becomes possessed of knowledge;
and from the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the effect arises for all the undertakings of living beings.
Ramaṇa, conjoined with Śakti, is to be known as Jaḍa-sadāśiva;
or else, Śiva is to be known as the embodied one whose seed is Śakti.

The body (deha) is to be understood as the physical frame, while the embodied one (dehin) is proclaimed to be Śiva; O Maheśānī, it consists of the knowledge of Vāmā, characterized by the gross and the subtle. 11.
209) Now, the definition of manifest incapacity.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the venerable Goddess said:
"Women are gods; women are life-breaths; women indeed are ornaments.
One should always remain attached to women, even toward one's own wife.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, you have spoken of the female form and the form of Brahman;
O Goddess Sadāśivā, how was it said that in the absence [of these], one's own wife [is to be resorted to]? (13)
The Goddess said: "O Maheśvara, women are of two kinds: those given by Brahmā and those given by Rudra.
A woman given by Brahmā is offered into the fire; but one given by Śiva is [united] according to desire. (14)
Śivā should be employed for the work of Śiva, and Parā should be employed for other rites;
no doubt whatsoever should be entertained regarding this, in accordance with my word. (15)
In the *Nigamānanda*:
"O Maheśānī, in the absence of a [physical] woman, one should joyfully satisfy one's own left-hand side (one's wife);
even for the sake of satisfying one's own wife, one should also satisfy another woman. (16)
One should joyfully contemplate one's own self as equal to another;
one should satisfy and delight the Śakti in accordance with her word and estimation.
O Supreme Goddess, one who has taken recourse to the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) should satisfy [the deity]. 18.
210) Now, the characteristics of the Vāmā worship are [given] in the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
One's own body and the body of a woman, one's own purpose joined with a lover, and the lover joined with power—these are the specific characteristics within one's own bodies. (19)
O Maheśānī, through sexual union one should perform the worship of Vāmā;
even for the sake of sporting with one's own Śakti, O Śivā, one may also sport with another Śakti.

One should take delight with the Śaktis, both within one's own body and in the bodies of others; having realized that one's own Śakti and the supreme Śakti are one, one should sport with the auspicious Śivā.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O beautiful lady, such pleasure as certainly arises for the face through sexual union is never produced by the body at any time. (22)
O lady of excellent hips, one should worship Goddess Ramā with delight;
by the mere act of worshipping Ramā, Ramā herself remains in his hand. (23)
O Maheśvarī, through sexual union (ramaṇa) there shall be heaven and liberation from suffering;
for this very reason, one who follows the Kula practice should possess devotion with his own mouth. 24.
If neither prohibition nor injunction exists anywhere in the Vāmācāra (or Svecchācāra),
then by his command, one should place the *liṅga* into the cavity of the *yoni* during the practice of Svecchācāra.
O Pārvatī, neither prohibition nor injunction applies to one who acts according to their own will;
if sexual union is joined with Śakti, it is solely by the command of Śakti.
The restriction applies to the man alone, and never to women;
by virtue of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he is undoubtedly qualified.
One should delight the Śakti within one’s own body, and never otherwise by any means;
like a fool who, having abandoned milk-rice in his own home, wanders about begging for alms. (28)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The fifty-third chapter: Now, the conduct of the Siddhānta. In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
Regarding oneself as the deity, one should worship the God according to the prescribed rite;
ever-blissful and ever-peaceful, such a one is said to follow the conduct of the Siddhānta. || 1 ||
(Here, the explanation of the verse beginning with "regarding oneself as the deity" should be understood.

Having regarded and known the deity as being within oneself, he who performs sacrifice according to this injunction is a practitioner of the Siddhānta; furthermore, what is his nature? He is eternally blissful and eternally peaceful.
Now, the nature of this Siddhāntācāra is as follows:
in the Śāktakramacandrikā,
those who consider themselves distinct [from the Self] are regarded as such.
[They do not see him] from the Supreme Lord; they do not see that God, for their exertion is in vain. || 2 ||
In the Gautamiya:
"If one, regarding oneself as the deity, should satisfy oneself,"
His conduct should be known according to the Siddhānta; his soul shall become Śiva.
And so it is stated in the Kulārṇava:
"Repugnance, shame, fear, sorrow, and disgust as the fifth;
family, conduct, and caste—these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters. (4)
The individual soul (jīva) is always bound by fetters; when freed from fetters, it is Sadāśiva.
Knowing this, O Maheśānī, if one should satisfy the Self, that soul, O Parameśānī, is indeed Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt. (5)
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*:
"By pleasing the Goddess, one pleases oneself; indeed, all the deities are pleased by the mere act of pleasing oneself."
Therefore, one who follows the family tradition should gladden himself with joy.
In the Kulārṇava:
"Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment."
For those who worship the pair of his lotus feet, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are indeed held in the palm of their hand. || 7 ||
O Maheśvarī, those who follow Viṣṇu, Śakti, Śiva, and others,
considering themselves to be the deity, should please [the deity] through amorous dalliance and other such acts.
Having abandoned the deity residing within oneself, one should contemplate an external god;
having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in one's own hand, one wanders about with the thirst for glass.

O Goddess of the Gods, having known the living being to be composed of the Divine through the five principles or again by following one's own will, one should satisfy it with food and other offerings. (10)
In the *Haṃsamāheśvara*:
"O Maheśvarī, whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) there may be, and whichever deities there may be—
O Sanātanī, all this has been made known as the body in the form of the living soul."
In the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi: "O Maheśvarī, the life-force (jīva) is to be known as the red [element] pervading the body."
O lady of excellent hips, blood does not remain at all in a dead body;
O Maheśvarī, [likewise] all things such as pleasure and pain belong to the *jīva* as well.
In the Jñānadvīpa:
"Indeed, there is only one Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) who exists in various forms for the purpose of deluding the worlds; therefore, one should remain even-minded. (13)
The Goddess should contemplate the oneness of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
for one whose mind possesses the sense of duality, liberation does not arise. (14)
In the *Kularahasya*:
"Now, as is Durgā, so is Viṣṇu; and as is Viṣṇu, so is Śiva.
For one whose mind possesses various dispositions, liberation does not arise."
Having understood that the entire body consists of the deity, one should know this body to be Śivā.

(214) O Goddess, if there is no knowledge of the body, there is nowhere any knowledge of the individual soul (jīva). O Goddess, if there is no knowledge of the individual soul, there is nowhere any knowledge of Śiva. || 16 ||
If a living being does not become Śiva even for a moment without the knowledge of Śiva, one should contemplate the deity as Brahman, having realized that the Self is Brahman. (17)
For him whose self is non-different from the deity, the individual soul (jīva) becomes Śiva.
O Mistress of the Kula, whatever body is pervaded, that should be known as the soul (or Śiva), O Kuleśvarī. 18.
Thus, for one whose [meditation] is very firm, the individual soul (jīva) becomes Śiva.
First, one should contemplate the body; then the soul; then the deity.
Thereafter, one should remember the soul as consisting of the deity, and the body as consisting of the soul. (19)
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The fifty-fourth chapter:
Now, the definition of the bliss of sexual union (*maithunānanda*).
In the *Nigamatattvasāra*, the venerable Śiva said:
O Great Goddess, the bliss of wine has been revealed in many ways;
now I desire to hear the characteristics of the bliss of sexual union. (1)
The Goddess said: "A doubt has arisen in my mind regarding the description of the bliss of sexual union;
having stationed Nandin at the door, depart for the chamber of Rati."
Out of affection for you, I shall explain the supreme and great means (*sādhana*),
by performing which the best of practitioners became Śiva, the Supreme Lord. (3)
O Lord, drinking intoxicants without sexual union indeed brings suffering;
O Lord, sexual union without drinking intoxicants brings about sin. (4)
After drinking, sexual union is auspicious; after sexual union, there is the cause for drinking.
Drinking conjoined with sexual union bestows liberation upon the living being.
O Mahādeva, in the bliss of fullness, sexual union does not arise at all;
everything is free from the senses, devoid of form, measurement, and so forth.
For this very reason, O Lord of Kula, the knower of the Kula may drink wine according to his pleasure;
for bliss, O Lord of Kula, is said to be twofold: fragmentary and complete.
Khaṇḍānandin, who follows the path of ritual action, [attains realization] from the sight of the yoni and the liṅga [or, according to *k*: from their friction].
One should not consume [wine] in excess, nor should one cause an unworthy vessel to receive it. 8.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess, if one should give many vessels when bliss has been generated, the passionate woman becomes angry when the ritual action is thus interrupted during its performance. (9)
Regarding the truth of the sacred precept (nigama-tattva):
Mahāmāyā, whose form is Śakti, resides within all houses;
when a woman is endowed with bliss, O Śiva, she is then my own body.
"I myself, in the form of the Goddess, create the body, the individual soul, as well as the vital breath, the mind, the intellect, and food; I perform eating and drinking. (11)
By the mere knowledge of bliss, I am revealed within the heart-lotus;
even upon that revelation, the Goddess herself becomes manifest to the practitioner.

(216) O Mahādeva, you are the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and I am the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*); there is no doubt in this. Having seen the practitioner in bliss (*ānanda*), as well as the one to be accomplished...
The auspicious one. || 13 ||
O Supreme Lord, liberation arises from seeing [Thee]; through the sight of Śiva, one attains *sālokya* (residence in the same world) with Thy beloved, whether she be one's own wife or another's. 14.
O Supreme Goddess, manifest in my abode that very sālokya, sārūpya, sāyujya,
and the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Now follows the exposition of the fourfold bliss of liberation. The Goddess said:
"O Beloved, that bliss which arises from the sight of a beloved woman in her sixteenth year,"
O God, that bliss is always found in the state of dwelling in the same world (sālokya); of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
O dear Lord, that pleasure which is felt upon touching a beloved woman in her sixteenth year is always present in the state of sā rūpya; of this there is no doubt. (17)
O Lord, that pleasure which is dear in union with a beloved woman in her sixteenth year is always present in *sāyujya*; of this there is no doubt. (18)
O Lord, that bliss which arises at the time of the emission of semen is indeed the bliss [of liberation] at all times; there is no doubt in this regarding nirvāṇa. (19)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
The Fifty-Fifth Chapter:
Now, the Majesty of Pūrṇānanda.
In the *Nigamatattvasāra*, Śrī Śiva said:
O Mother Durgā, O highly fortunate one, who are as dear to me as my own life-breath! Reveal the majesty of Pūrṇānanda in my abode.
The Śrī Devī said: Having known the embodied being to be composed of Brahman, one should contemplate everything as Brahman.
One never beholds the terrible fear consisting of birth and death. O God, as long as the embodied soul remains within the body, perfect bliss does not arise;
only when knowledge transcends all objective states does it become perfect bliss.
When existence is understood as consisting of that which transcends existence, and that which transcends existence as being existence itself,
then it should be known as full bliss within song and drink.
It is born. || 4 ||
Through song, O Śiva, drinking arises; and from drinking, singing.
Where is the sequence of bliss determined, and by what path? || 5 ||
What is duty and what is non-duty? What indeed cannot be described?
This discourse consists of that which transcends all states of being; this hymn consists of that which transcends all states of being.
Knowledge consists of that which transcends mental constructs; indeed, sexual union transcends mental constructs.

Drinking consists of that which transcends mental constructs; indeed, singing transcends mental constructs. Meditation consists of that which transcends mental constructs; indeed, [it] consists of that which transcends mental constructs.
Action consists of that which transcends existence.
In the *Guptasādhanatantra*, the venerable Śiva said:
"In some instances one should practice drinking, in some singing, and in others chewing."
In some cases one should practice meditation, recitation, and so forth; in other cases, one may engage in sexual union.
O Goddess, one should chew after drinking, and drink honey after chewing;
meat, accompanied by the *mudrā* and fish, is considered a drink that brings bliss.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever is to be chewed, sucked, licked, or drunk—whatever may be placed in the mouth that is considered a source of pleasure in eating—[should be offered]. 10.
In the *Nigamatattva*, the Śrī Devī said:
"O Mahādeva, in the state of full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), sexual union does not arise at all;
everything is devoid of the senses and free from any manifestor. (11)
O Śiva, if by fate the preeminent practitioner should become desirous of performing the rite, even though he has recognized the *yoni* everywhere, he should strike it again and again. (12)
In some place within the womb, in some place on the side, in some place on the back, O Maheśvara;
in some place on the face, in some place on the ear, and in some place on the head.
O Śiva, one should repeatedly perform the striking according to the sequence that transcends mental conception—
sometimes with the linga, sometimes with the hand, and sometimes with a finger.
In some places there was striking with the nostrils, in some with the eyes;
in some with the foot, the finger, or even the head and the tongue; and in some places there was the biting of teeth and the constant sucking of all the limbs.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the *Sarvāllāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha.
The fifty-sixth chapter begins: The Illustrious Śiva said:
O Mistress of the Kula, I wish to hear the definition of the bliss of power (śaktyānanda). || 1 ||
The Goddess said: O Mahādeva, the bliss of Śakti is revealed through great fortune;
when the bliss of love is revealed, O Maheśāna, it is equal to all bliss.
Just as the possessor of power (Śākta) has transcended all states of being, so too does the Great Lord (Maheśvara) transcend them;
likewise, there is equality even in bliss, and drinking and sporting are of that same nature. || 3 ||

Whether it be the Śakti or the Puruṣa [the practitioner], if he should fall upon the ground, he should immediately engage in sexual union, free from all disgust and shame. (Note: Two verses marked with symbols are found as additional in manuscript J.)
When the practitioner has fallen to the ground, the one to be accomplished (sādhya) should engage in dalliance;
when the one to be accomplished has also fallen to the ground, the practitioner should engage in dalliance. || 5 ||
It should not be performed without desire, nor should it be performed even by command;
otherwise it should not be performed either, for both would go to hell.
One who is devoted to Śakti should worship in the bliss of Śakti; one should worship Śivā in the bliss of Śiva.
O Lord, even a dog becomes auspicious when accompanied by Ānanda.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The fifty-seventh chapter. Now, the majesty of Śakti. In the Toḍalatantra:
O lady of excellent hips, this body remains insentient due to the power of the self;
it is not even able to bring itself under control, so what need be said of external power? (1)
O lady of excellent hips, if one’s own power is recognized as being external power,
one who is liberated from passion and aversion should satisfy it with great effort.
In the *Śāktakramacandrikā*:
"If another man should engage in dalliance with a married maiden [or wife], one must never inflict blows, insults, or deceit upon them. (3)
For marriage is defined as a conventional term for the purpose of ritual action, consisting of the capacity [for procreation];
Hara is the husband of a woman in general, and Śaṅkara is the husband of a man in general.
O lady of excellent hips, I am Śaṅkara; there is no doubt that knowledge belongs to Śakti.
The will of Śakti becomes will, and the action of Śakti becomes action.
From the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) arises knowledge, and from shame (lajjā) arises shame;
O lady of excellent hips, bondage and liberation arise from the power of will (icchā-śakti), without a doubt.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the power of the body is proclaimed;
it provides both worldly enjoyment and liberation more than any other philosophical systems.
Whom would he desire, if he were to become wealthy by means of wealth obtained merely in a dream? // 7 //
(221) Many deities are to be worshipped as you have described them, O lady of virtuous vows;
yet among them, Śakti alone is the primary object of worship, and she must be firmly established at the very beginning.
Firm in his vows. || 8 ||
Brahmā is Śakti, Śiva is Śakti, Viṣṇu is Śakti, and Vāsava is Śakti;
many other gods as well are proclaimed to have their root in Śakti. (9)
Since these are proclaimed to be incapable without power (śakti), therefore, O high-minded one, know that power is indeed the primary principle among them. (10)
O Pārvatī, just as an illusion arises like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell,
so too, through other philosophical views, one desires enjoyment and liberation. (11)
(These verses are seen as additional in manuscripts *gh* and *j*) Those who consider their own self to be distinct from the Supreme Lord do not behold that God; their exertion is in vain. || 12 ||
One should contemplate the Goddess as consisting of all the gods, the supreme one who consists of all the gods,
the Goddess whose nature is that of the Supreme Self.
In the Nirvāṇatantra:
With a disciplined mind, one should meditate upon the Goddess as one's own self;
one should constantly contemplate the oneness of one's own Guru, who is identical with the deity. (14)
One should contemplate oneself as the Goddess, whose essential nature is pure power (śakti). The man who contemplates [the Goddess] as non-different from himself attains identity with Her. || 15 ||
By constantly contemplating "I am He," one becomes absorbed in Him;
one should cultivate the realization: "I am the Divine, I am none other, I am liberated. (16)
Through the contemplation of Rudra one becomes Rudra; through the contemplation of Viṣṇu one becomes Viṣṇu;
and through the contemplation of Durgā one certainly becomes Durgā—of this there is no doubt. (17)
O Pārvatī, such a yoga of practice should be performed day after day.
One is liberated from the bonds of existence through [the cessation of] old age, death, suffering, and the like. || 18 ||
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha.
Chapter fifty-eight:
The Greatness of the Haṃsa Bīja.
In the *Mahānirvāṇa Tantra*, the Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Lord of Prāṇa, O Supreme Lord, you who consist of the three qualities within the three qualities;
O Beloved, tell me now the majesty of the seed-syllable *haṃsa*."
Śrī Śiva said: The greatness of the *haṃsa* seed-syllable cannot indeed be fully described;
bound by my affection for you, I have revealed its essence in brief.
O Śivā, the body is the temple; by means of the *haṃsa* mantra, the embodied soul always resides within the body, taking refuge in the seed-syllable *haṃsa*.
The letter *ha* is Śaṅkara himself, and the letter *sa* is declared to be Śakti; the mantra consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti is celebrated as the *ajapā*.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day and night,
the living soul constantly recites the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Śiva, the living soul always recites the mantra consisting of both Śakti and Śiva.
By what means should one recite the root mantra, and by what means should I, that very self, be contemplated? || 6 ||

Śrī Śiva said: The retention (kumbhaka) should be performed with the syllable *haṃ*, and the exhalation (recana) with the syllable *saḥ*. During the retentions, one should mutter the mantra, one syllable for each individual retention.
In another tantra:
"The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of Śiva, and the letter *sa* is the seed-syllable of Śakti;
the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is in the form of sound (*nāda*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is the point (*bindu*). (8)
The Visarga is the attachment to action; it is proclaimed as the seed-syllable Haṃsa.
O Maheśvarī, the two dots (bindus) constitute the Visarga, which is both creation and preservation.
O Goddess, one *bindu* is dissolution; two *bindus* have the form of creation;
three *bindus* have the form of maintenance; and again, one *bindu* is dissolution.
The individual soul (jīvātman) is the body composed of Śiva and Śakti, which takes the form of karma;
the supreme self (paramātman) is in the form of the *bindu*, as expressed by the seed-syllable *haṃsa*. || 11 ||
O beautiful-eyed one, the seed-syllable *haṃsa* is to be known as creation, sustenance, and dissolution.
O beloved, through the knowledge of *haṃsa*, there is creation; through the knowledge of *so'ham*, there is sustenance;
and through the knowledge of *nāham*, O Goddess, there is dissolution—this being the awakener of existence and non-existence.
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:

"By means of the *haṃsa* seed-syllable within one's own nature, through the dissolution of the body, one should contemplate [the Self] as 'I am He' (*so'ham*) in the Supreme; thus one should contemplate them as a single body. (13)
One should always perform worship with the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, and with the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, according to the distinction between the left and the right. (14)
In the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
"The seed-syllable of Śiva is the letter *ha*, which is the form of Śiva within the male body."
The seed-syllable of Śakti is indeed the letter *sa*; it is the male body, the very form of Śiva. (Note: This reading is seen as an addition in manuscript G.)
The seed-syllable of Śakti is indeed the letter *sa*; thus the body of Śakti is revealed.
Through meditation on "I am that" (*so 'ham*), which consists of Śakti, the meditation on light (*jyotirdhyāna*) is revealed. (16)

The subtle meditation is "I am Brahman," all-pervading and stainless. (This reading is seen as an addition in manuscript Ga. The gross meditation is the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, which is attained through the knowledge of differentiation.
Therefore, through knowledge, that most pure light-meditation which is to be attained shall arise for me.
I am not obtained through knowledge, nor through speech; I am beyond words, stainless, gross, radiant, and likewise subtle—meditation has these three characteristics.
The gross [meditation] is that which is associated with the senses and joined with the womb, the linga, and so forth;
for if one is endowed with the knowledge of "I am He," it is indeed the non-dual meditation on light.
The subtle [meditation], however, is eternal, formless, and purer even than the sky.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Fifty-ninth Chapter.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
Among the three types of meditation, by what means is that [Self] brought forth?

Śrī Śiva said: Gross meditation consists of the *haṃsa* seed-syllable and involves the distinction between the served and the server; subtle meditation, however, is indeed the distinction within the radiance itself, devoid of the distinction between the served and the server.
That meditation which is beyond all states of being—that, O Śivā, is my supreme knowledge.
Whatever power is proclaimed to belong to whatever object, that very power is the Goddess who is the sovereign of all, and that object is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself. (3)
In the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra:
"One should worship the Deity within one's own body, never in another's body;
having abandoned milk-rice in one's own home, the foolish person wanders for alms. (4)
O Mahādeva, from gross meditation one becomes Tejodhyāna; O Śaṅkara, from subtle meditation liberation arises; therein lies the origin of the syllable Oṃ.
[The breath-retention (kumbhaka). || 5 ||
The body of Śiva and Śakti is distinct, yet their meditation on light is non-dual;
consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti, subtle, and pervading the world as "Oṃ tat sat."
Three dots, two sounds, two dots, and one sound;
one dot and two sounds—this is the syllable Oṃ, the awakener of Brahman.
Kuṇḍalinī is shaped like a hook, and Sadāśiva is the form of the Bindu;
O Great Goddess, it is merely the mark that awakens Śiva and Śakti.
(226) O Goddess, without the two *bindus*, not even the slightest thing arises;
on the left is the Supreme Śakti, and on the right is Supreme Śiva. 9.
Brahman, whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti, is beyond speech and perfectly pure;
it should be known that the letter *ta* is Śaṅkara, and the letter *ta* is the embodiment of masculinity.
O Goddess, that sound consisting of the awakening of Brahman is hidden by power;
it is the pair of *bindus*, the single *nāda*, and the letter *ta*, which awakens one to Brahman. (11)
O Supreme Goddess, that sound is the indicator even of the syllable *oṃ*;
O Mistress of the Gods, a consonant does not exist at all without a vowel.
That entire consciousness, manifest in the form of being, is of that same color.
The letter *sa* is to be known as Śaṅkarī, and the letter *ta* has the nature of Nāda.
Knowledge consisting of Śakti and Brahman is the existent (sat) word that makes manifest the state of being;
the consonant is to be known as Puruṣa, and the vowel is to be known as Śaṅkarī.
Brahman, whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti, is expressed by the word *sat*;
moreover, O Supreme Goddess, it consists of the letter *sa* and the letter *ta*, which is the Puruṣa.
The knowledge of power is in the center, with the letter *a* elided, which makes all sounds known;
it has five sounds, seven points, and is the single limb, O Supreme Goddess. (16)

Indeed, that which is joined with these [letters] has the letter *sa* and the letter *va* revealed three times; and *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are likewise expressed by the three occurrences of the letter *va*. (17)
The fivefold sound, the five principles, the drop, adorned by heaven,
smeared with the three qualities, and the triangle, accompanied by three at each corner. || 18 ||
O Maheśvarī, there is a mere corner and a mere point, and in the center is the Nāda;
this entire sequence of phonemes is to be known as the limb situated above Śiva. (19)
O auspicious lady, without the two dots (bindus), the mere mark (aṅka) does not arise;
the syllable joined with the sound (nāda) and the dot (bindu) is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman. 20.
The word *tat* is that which is to be known; the word *sat* illuminates all existents. That which is both *tat* and *sat* is the seed of Brahman, revealed within the syllable *oṃ*. || 21 ||
Everything is born from the syllable Oṃ, and in the syllable Oṃ it is dissolved;
for Oṃ is the seed of creation and the seed of dissolution, O Three-eyed One.
O Maheśvarī, the state that has arisen from the seed-syllable *haṃsa* is eternal and transcends all states of being; it is the conclusion of both the right-hand and left-hand traditions.
I am that Haṃsa, yet I am not "I"; my nature consists of both difference and non-difference.
Indeed, for the divine Kaulas, it is absolute and transcends all states of being.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Pārvatī said: "O Lord, by what path has that which transcends all states of being been revealed?"
Even though it has been revealed, tell me that which distinguishes the divine Kaulas.
Śrī Śiva said: By whichever path one becomes a Kaula, by that very path one becomes divine;
through the state of oneness between both, one becomes composed of that which transcends all mental states.
The divine [tradition] belongs to those who are divine among the world; that of the Kaulas is devoid of divinity.
The divine one is generally like a god, while the hero (vīra) is one whose mind is arrogant.
The distinction between the divine and the hero is here explained.
In the *Nigamatattva*:
"O Śivā, for the Kaulas there is no restrictive rule; there is neither prohibition nor injunction."
The ritual procedure is Śiva;
likewise, it should be understood that for the divine beings, the only distinction is liberation alone.
Within the radiant state of divine energies, that which transcends existence is revealed;
that radiance is the atom, all-pervading and stainless.
And likewise for the Kaulas, it has been stated that in the absence [of external means], one should avoid existence;
today, as a consequence, I shall also describe the characteristic of the divine.
And so it is stated in the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"Whatever be the color of the deity, by that [color] its entire mass of splendor is filled."
Having visualized the entire world as consisting of light, one should conceive of the form.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Siddhāntācāra," in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the venerable Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The sixty-first chapter:
Now, the Kaula practice.
Having become free from dualities of mind and having realized the body as the digit of desire (kāmakalā), [one should proceed].
O Hero, O Goddess, this lineage is to be known as delightful and captivating. || 1 ||

"Becoming one whose mind is free from dualities, the state of non-existence (*asyabhāva*) is revealed in the *Yāmala*: 'O Śivā, he alone becomes transcendent of duality, and alone transcendent of existence.'"
The word *prakāśa* is free from dualities, singular, both short and long. || 2 ||
O Śivā, the world of moving and non-moving beings exists through the sequence of short and long [vowels]; it consists of heavy and light syllables, long vowels, and speech that transcends words. (3)
The entire world transcends existence; knowledge is Śiva, consisting of the object of knowledge.
(This half-verse exists in manuscripts *k* and *c*) This entire world is knowledge;
O Śivā, knowledge consists of the object of knowledge. 4.
O Maheśvarī, this entire world is knowledge that is to be known by the mind;
O Goddess, the mind is both the knower and the known, yet it is beyond all states of being and perfectly pure.
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Śivā, O Pārvatī, the gross, the subtle, and even the mind exist within the state beyond all states; from that which transcends all states, a state arises, just as a tree arises from a seed."
She shines eternally within the mind, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
therefore, O Great Goddess, She is beyond the mind and stainless.
Having understood that his state consists of the art of desire, it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"Through desire, the accomplishment of desires is attained; one who is free from desire attains liberation."
Therefore, O fair-eyed one, the entire world is of the nature of desire;
she, the eternal one in the form of a digit, always shines through desire.
Now, he states the measure of the *kalā*s;
in the *Nīlatantra*: "The *kulākula*, the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), the creeper (*latā*), the courtesan (*veśyā*), and the *vāruṇa*."
The *pīṭha* is called the hidden primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the womb (*yoni*). || 9 ||
In the *Niruttara*:
"The *kalā* and the *anukalā* are proclaimed to be merely a fraction (*kalāmātra*)."
And Kalā is said to be of two kinds, O Maheśvarī: the hidden and the manifest.
She is both hidden and manifest in her essential form, bestowing delight;
the heroes dwelling in the cremation ground always worship her as a single digit (kalā).
The heroes dwelling in the cremation ground should worship the secret vulva (*guptayoni*).
The hero should worship the manifest vulva (*vyaktayoni*) in the cemetery, O Śivā, in the secret place.
(This is the reading found in manuscripts K and G.)
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, the hero should worship the manifest source (vyaktāyoni) in the secret cremation ground (gopana-śmaśāna).
[This is the reading found in manuscript C. He should worship in the secret cremation ground, O Śivā. 12.
O Supreme Goddess, the hero should worship the secret Kalā mentally;
O Beloved, he may also worship her manifestly in an isolated place, even outdoors.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the manifest source (vyaktāyoni), which is twofold and bestows liberation— the indifferent [form] and the cremation ground— as the bhaga for householders.
From worshipping the cremation ground, one becomes a hero (vīra) with authority over the worship of the vulva (bhaga);
likewise, O Goddess, from mounting a corpse, one gains authority over mounting the vulva. || 15 ||

O Goddess, just as one becomes entitled to the knowledge of oneness through the knowledge of duality, so too, O Goddess, the cremation ground is proclaimed to be of two kinds: the funeral pyre and the womb.
O Mistress of the Gods, although the funeral pyre is manifest, it is also celebrated as the secret womb.
In the Nirvāṇatantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—through the yoga of the liquor of the *kalā*, one should perform the worship of the *kalā*. (17)
In the Kulārṇava:
"O Goddess, one should never engage in sexual union without liquor;
O Goddess, one should not practice the drinking of wine without sexual union. (18)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, the dharma of the householder is most praiseworthy;
for those who are indifferent, it is the seat of the corpse, while for householders, it is the seat of the liquor.
O beloved, *asava* is said to be that which has departed from life (the dead), while *madyapānāsava* refers to the distillation of fermented liquor.
In another tantra:
"Whether on a corpse or on liquor, the accomplishment of the task is certain;
the act of differentiation is performed on the seat of the corpse, while non-differentiation is on the seat of liquor. (20)
O Maheśānī, one should not perform the corpse-posture (śavāsana) upon a Śakti;
even by the mere sight of a Śakti, the ritual action of those who are indifferent [to her] comes to ruin.

O Goddess, the body of the male is the seat of the *āsavā*; the body of the *śakti* is the seat of the *puruṣa*. The *śakti* is the seat of the *puruṣa*, and the body of the *puruṣa* is the seat of the *śakti*.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the *Sarvollāsa* composed by the illustrious Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The sixty-second chapter.
Now, the definition of the nature of Prakṛti,
according to the Vṛhadyonitantra:
If one worships Kālī while knowing that primordial nature (prakṛti) is futile, his worship becomes in vain; it is like watering seeds that have already been parched. || 1 ||

O Goddess, for him who practices the knowledge of Brahman without knowing Prakṛti, that knowledge is in vain, like the embrace of a eunuch [or, as some read: like the union of power with those lacking power]. || 2 ||
(Śloka 232;
this verse is seen as an addition in manuscripts g, gh, and j: He who, having taken hold of the knowledge of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), effects the knowledge of Brahman.
His knowledge would be in vain, as would the union with power among the powers.
O Śivā, some meditate upon Prakṛti and others upon Puruṣa;
being knowers of Brahman, they regard both Prakṛti and Puruṣa as being of the nature of the Self.
Without Prakṛti there is no Brahman, and without Brahman there is no Śivā;
through the yoga of knowledge of both, one certainly knows Brahman. || 5 ||
In the Siddhalāharī Tantra: "Some speak of Prakṛti, some proclaim Puruṣa;
he who perceives both as one is certainly a knower of Brahman. (6)
Pārvatī said:
O Lord, this knowledge of Brahman is beyond speech, beyond action, and beyond the mind; it is eternal. Tell me, what is its primordial nature (prakṛti)?
Speak, O Lord! || 7 ||

In the Vṛhadyonitantra, the venerable Śiva said: "O Mother of the World, O Eternal One, that which is called eternal Prakṛti is herself the nature of the Yoni, the cause of the world's manifestation. (8)
In the *Siddhalāharītantra*:
"O Goddess, the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest certainly arise from *prakṛti*;
*sattva* and the other qualities are the roots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (9)
O Goddess of gods, in the three corners the triad of qualities (guṇatraya) is well-established;
the pervasive primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of light and composed of both the gross and the subtle, is situated there.
Her qualities are sattva and the rest, and she too has sattva and the rest as her qualities;
she transcends the qualities, for she who expresses them is beyond words.
the designator] || 11 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others arise from her by her own will;
again they dissolve into her, and from her they are born once more. (12)
O Pārvatī, when primordial nature (prakṛti) undergoes transformation (vikṛti), it perceives everything;
but when transformation returns to its primordial state, it perceives nothing at all.
In another Tantra it is said: "O Maheśvarī, that which is called Prakṛti is eternal; she is the transformation (vikṛti).
O Goddess, some say that Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are distinct."
And those living beings bound by the qualities (guṇas) lack the qualification for liberation. || 14 ||
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Mahādeva, if action exists as threefold by means of the three qualities (guṇas),
then how does a single state arise even within the three qualities, and from what is that quality born?
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Priyambadā, through the differentiation of the three qualities (guṇas), there is modification;
yet Prakṛti exists in a state of oneness, having the form and appearance of a chickpea.
In another tantra:

"That which is declared to be the eternal Prakṛti, whose form is shaped like a chickpea (caṇaka)—when differentiated, she is Śakti; when undifferentiated from Śiva, she is the chickpea within Śiva. (17)
The triangle is permeated by the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and the chickpea (*caṇaka*) consists of the three qualities. O Supreme Goddess, the three qualities are earth, water, and fire.
The earth is Kaṃ; Pāvaka is Dhruva. || 18 ||
Tamas, sattva, and rajas— these three qualities (guṇas)— are always present within the three triangles;
the entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded by these three qualities.
O beloved, the God, endowed with primordial power, has a form shaped like a chickpea; he is the manifest abode of the Nirguṇa and the abode of Mahākālī.
Where there is the oblation of bliss, that very thing is of the nature of bliss;
having become manifest as a gross form, it is revealed within the female body.
Arising within the subtle body, it is manifested in the bodies of men. || 21 ||
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*:
"The *liṅga* is difficult to traverse, the *bhaga* is difficult to traverse; the three worlds are enveloped therein.
The *yoni* is situated within the *liṅga*, and the *liṅga* is within the *yoni*."
Having abandoned both and both, it does not remain for even a single moment.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"O Goddess, that which is the supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and free from body and so forth, becomes possessed of form solely for the sake of awakening. (23)
Just as the orb of the sun is seen in many ways within mirrors and other surfaces, O Supreme Goddess, so too is this entire world perceived. (24)
The Supreme Brahman is indeed one, of the nature of light, and stainless;
yet, O beloved, if it should assume a form by its own will, then [it appears so].
The Great Source (Mahāyoni) is of the nature of light, awakening both the gross and the subtle; she is with form by her own will, and without form by her own will. (26)
When she is of a single form, then she is subtle and eternal;
and when she has become manifold, then she is celebrated as "Light" (Jyoti).
O Supreme Goddess, if She were endowed with a body and so forth, She would possess form;
yet even through manifold delight, She remains the revealer of light in the absence of [material] existence.
From non-existence (abhāva) arises the entire world, both stationary and moving;
O Dear One, the threefold form consisting of existence, consciousness, creation, maintenance, and dissolution [arises from it]. 29.
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa have their seed in the elemental; O Śivā, Prakṛti is to be known as elemental, and Puruṣa is to be known as elemental.
I declare that Brahman consists of both matter and spirit;
O Pārvatī, one should know that Bhaga is Prakṛti (Nature) and Puruṣa (Spirit) is Brahman. (31)
By nature, O Goddess, the Puruṣa is Brahman, and Prakṛti is the Sovereign (Īśvarī) in relation to the Puruṣa;
there, O Goddess, both Śṛṅgāra and Kāma are always present with Vāyu.
Wind, conjoined with space, permeated by wind, and consisting of all the elements—
just as limb and possessor of limbs, so too am I.
It consists of the five elements. || 33 ||

The impermanent is to be known as fivefold; the conception of the five as one is the notion of permanence. From such conception arises creation, and from conception arises dissolution. O Goddess, this Kaula knowledge is beyond all conceptual construction and is stainless.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
The sixty-third chapter.
In another Tantra, the illustrious Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, what are the three forms? And what, O Master, is the knowledge of Brahman?"
O Prāṇa, my beloved, tell me: what kind of knowledge is liberation?
Śrī Śiva said: O Sulocanā, this triad of forms— the gross form, the form of light, and the subtle form— is to be known as Brahman, the cause of knowledge.
Now, concerning the knowledge of Brahman. The venerable Śiva said:
From space (ākāśa) wind is born; from wind the sun is produced;
from the sun water is produced; and from water the earth is produced.
O Maheśvarī, whatever gross form consists of the five elements—whether born from an egg, born from sweat, born from a sprout, or born from a womb—[is all composed of these]. || 4 ||
O Goddess, birds and the like are born from eggs; mosquitoes and the like are born from sweat; and trees, shrubs, and so forth are born from sprouts—indeed, these are devoid of consciousness.
O Great Goddess [O Maheśānī], humans and animals are born from the womb;
among them, the knowledge of Brahman arises specifically within human beings. (6)
The twenty-four principles (tattvas) have been revealed as having the nature of light;
upon their dissolution, O Supreme Goddess, the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) is revealed.
"Listen, O beloved Prāṇā, to the twenty-four principles:
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (8)
The vital airs (vāyus) are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna.
Hearing, seeing, smelling, touching, and the perception of taste; || 9 ||
The anus, the genitals, the hands and feet, and speech, O Supreme Goddess;
renunciation, eroticism, and the fourfold group of mind and senses.
There are twenty-four principles (tattvas), and here Śakti is distinct from each one.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, the twenty-four principles have been described by you;
now I wish to hear the detailed glorification of their respective powers."
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, infinite powers are manifested within the body;
I am not able to describe them even at the end of the universe, O Pārvatī.
Among them, the most excellent is the form of emanation consisting of twenty-four forms;
among those, the most excellent is the form of emanation consisting of fourteen supreme natures.
O Maheśvarī, among them, the Śakti is the Self in four ways;
one is threefold and fourfold in nature.
Power has been described, O Maheśvarī. || 15 ||
Sundarī, Buddhirūpā, and Manorūpā are Kālikā;
Cittarūpā is Tārā.
Thus, she who is of the nature of action is said to be one in three ways.
Even Mahādeva became Śaṅkara through the very nature of ego (ahaṅkāra);
without even a mere trace of ego, nothing at all can come into being. (17)
From the non-conceptual Self, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is born;
from the stainlessness of the ego-sense, it is declared: "I am Brahman. (18)
O Goddess, as a jar exists in clay, as a bracelet in gold,
as silver in mother-of-pearl, and as waves and bubbles in water; || 19 ||
O Goddess, just as there is a snake in a rope or a coloring in crystal, so too, O Maheśānī, is the body manifested within the embodied soul. (20)
Just as clay remains when a jar is destroyed, and gold likewise when a bracelet is destroyed;
so too, when waves and bubbles perish, there is no doubt that only water remains.
Just as a rope exists when a snake is destroyed, and likewise a crystal when it is colored;
so too, when the body is destroyed, the body [remains], and I am alone, untainted.
That meditation whose nature is emptiness is undoubtedly samādhi;
it is non-duality, the supreme Brahman— I alone am the stainless one.
Transcending all, supremely peaceful, it awakens one's own self-knowledge;
when there is awakening to the supreme reality, I am alone, stainless.
This is to be known as stainless, beyond the reach of speech and mind;
that supreme Brahman, having pervaded all, remains as the one.
From that, the entire world is born; in that alone it always abides;
and into that indeed it dissolves again, O Pārvatī, like trees into the earth—or rather, into Brahman.
Creation proceeds precisely by reversing the order of its emergence; it dissolves into Brahman alone, and yet it is created again from that very source by His own will through His innate *māyā*. (27)
The play of Brahman is the entire world; this world is of the nature of Brahman.
For indeed, all this is Brahman; there is nothing else whatsoever. (28)
In the Viśvasāra:

"I bow to that which consists of the universe, which pervades all things from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, both the stationary and the moving, and whose essential nature is the Supreme Brahman. (29)
In another Tantra:
"The supreme state transcends all states; indeed, meditation transcends meditation;
action transcends action, yet it is endowed with action; pervading everything, it abides as one. (30)
All form transcends everything; it is both non-conceptual and imagined. Unchanging yet permeated by change, it stands as the one, pervading all. || 31 ||

One should ascertain that Brahman is that gain than which there is no greater gain, that happiness than which there is no greater happiness, and that knowledge than which there is no greater knowledge. 32.
In another tantra:
"The earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into the sun;
the sun dissolves into air; and air dissolves into space. (33)
The ether dissolves into the Real (Satya), the Real dissolves into Śiva;
Śiva dissolves into Power (Śakti); thereafter, Brahman is described.
In the *Nigamatattvasāra*:
"If one knows in reality that everything consists of the bliss of Brahman, then one attains liberation when one realizes Brahman. (35)
On the left she has the form of Prakṛti, and on the right the form of Puruṣa;
by the mere union of these two, the body is certainly produced.
All this, such as eating and so forth, occurs by His will;
even the desire for pleasure and the desire for pain are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

In the play of Brahman, one should not practice regarding the entire world as either faulty or faultless; for even a fault is entirely a virtue for Brahman, such as his laughter, curiosity, and so forth. (38)
O beloved, all dancing, singing, and so forth are like a magician's trick;
everything, including laughter and curiosity, is the playful sport of Brahman. (39)
And for the sake of play, the Supreme Brahman exists in embodied form moment by moment (or age by age).
That [nature] exists in a divine body as well as in insects and other such beings.
Having realized that everything is composed of Brahman, one should accomplish all ritual actions;
yet, having drunk the intoxicating wine of delusion, the omnipresent Lord himself becomes like one who is insane.
Having assumed a human body, he desires happiness and liberation;
having resorted to his elemental nature, he effects the destruction of the bodies of embodied beings. 42.
The imperishable one, appearing in the form of a thief, exists for the destruction of the wealth of those who possess it;
he is traditionally remembered as being without "mine-ness," without ego, and eternally composed of light.

In some places one is overcome by grief and the like; in some places one is beset by happiness and the like; in some places one is joined with laughter and the like; and in some cases, a certain person becomes exceedingly wealthy.
Resorting to the form of a woman within the bodies of women,
she who is intoxicated by desire and composed of desire seeks in every way the Supreme Brahman alone.
Resorting to a form of Madana, a man becomes overwhelmed. || 45 ||
Relying upon the form of the Guru, the world is delivered from existence;
one should not perform an action—whether faulty or faultless—merely by one's own will. (46)
All this is of the nature of Brahman; the world is composed of the nature of Brahman.
Its movement is in the upper void, and it is established in the middle void. (47)
Who truly knows the movement in the void below?
The state of dreaming in the void above is proclaimed as the *brahmarandhra*. (48)
The "void in the middle" is in the center of the eyebrows; there, one should contemplate knowledge and the rest.
The "void below" is in the *mūlādhāra*; there, one should contemplate desire and the rest. || 49 ||
Brahman plays at the end of the void; even the ignorant one does not fail to attain it. He abides as the Supreme Brahman, both by his own will and through divine play.
One attains perfection through knowledge; one does not attain perfection without knowledge.
O child, for him who does not know this knowledge of Brahman in its true essence, no perfection arises despite all his meditation, worship, and other such practices. (51)
Without the knowledge of Brahman, everything is considered a cause for failure;
for this very reason, O Great Lord, no accomplishment arises in the Kali age.
O Lord of the Kula, Brahman is indeed the cause of accomplishment in every respect;
he who knows this in its true essence becomes one with Brahman at the end of the body. || 53 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the Sarvollāsa composed by Śrī Sarvānandanātha. || 0 ||
